prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to read analog soil moisture sensor data from an MCP3008 ADC (channel 0, single-ended mode, SPI CE0, 500 kHz, mode 0). The sensor output range is 0 (dry) to 1023 (wet). If the moisture level falls below 30%, turn on a 12V water pump relay connected to GPIO17 (active high); if moisture rises to 30% or above, turn off the pump. Log all events, program start, pump on/off, errors, and termination, with timestamps to 'watering.log'. Check every pigpio and SPI call, and handle ADC read failures gracefully by logging the error and continuing. Ensure the pump is off on exit, using a signal handler (SIGINT, SIGTERM) for clean shutdown. Use only pigpio (not wiringPi). The program should run indefinitely, checking every 60 seconds.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the libgpiod library (not wiringPi) to log ADC readings from an MCP3008 connected via SPI0, CE0 on single-ended channels 0, 1, and 2 to a CSV file named 'sensor_data.csv', simulating a soil moisture monitoring system logging moisture levels from three different locations. Initialize SPI using the spidev interface: open /dev/spidev0.0, set mode SPI_MODE_0, 8 bits per word, 1 MHz speed. Read each channel by sending the 3-byte command: start bit (0x01), then single-ended mode byte with channel select (0x80 | (channel<<4)), then a dummy byte (0x00); the returned 10-bit value is ((data[1] & 0x03) << 8) | data[2]. Log data every 1 second. Check every open/ioctl/read/write call; on failure print an error message and exit gracefully. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) to close the CSV file and release SPI resources before exiting. Use only modern Linux APIs; do not use wiringPi or pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that subscribes to the MQTT topic "home/led_control" on broker mqtt.eclipseprojects.io:1883 with client ID "rpi_led_control" and QoS 0, to receive JSON payloads containing an "led_state" boolean, and uses the pigpio library to control an LED connected to GPIO17. Initialize pigpio, set GPIO17 as output, and turn off the LED on startup. Parse JSON payloads expecting exactly the key "led_state" with a boolean value, rejecting any other keys or invalid types; on a valid message, set GPIO17 HIGH if led_state is true, LOW if false. Handle disconnections gracefully with exponential backoff reconnection (1s, 2s, 4s, ... up to a 60s maximum delay). Use signal handlers (SIGINT, SIGTERM) for clean shutdown: disconnect MQTT, turn off the LED, and release pigpio resources, ensuring all resources are released on every exit path (success, error, signal). Log all errors to stderr with timestamps. Use only pigpio (gpioInitialise, gpioSetMode, gpioWrite, gpioTerminate), mosquitto with v2 callbacks via mosquitto_loop_start/stop, and cJSON for parsing; do not use any other sensors or peripherals (no ADC, no IMU, no vibration motor, no file logging).

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the libgpiod library (not wiringPi) for GPIO control, to read a KY-038 sound sensor module whose digital output (DO) pin is connected to GPIO17 (BCM numbering) and goes LOW when sound exceeds the onboard-potentiometer threshold, and to trigger a simulated alarm LED on GPIO18. Print the sound level reading (0 or 1) to the console each loop iteration, with a 100 ms delay between readings. When sound is detected (DO = LOW), blink the LED on GPIO18 for 1 second: ON for 1 s, then OFF. Check libgpiod initialization, chip open, line request, and all I/O operations; handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths gracefully, printing an error and exiting if the chip open fails. On SIGINT (Ctrl+C) or SIGTERM, cleanly release all GPIO lines and exit, with proper resource cleanup on all exit paths.

Create a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that monitors an SW-420 vibration sensor connected to GPIO17 (physical pin 11). The sensor module's DO pin is active-low, open-collector: it idles HIGH and pulls LOW when vibration exceeds the onboard-potentiometer threshold. Use libgpiod (not sysfs, not wiringPi) to open /dev/gpiochip0, obtain GPIO line 17, and request it for falling-edge event detection with the consumer label "vibration-monitor", using the single-line event API (gpiod_line_event_wait / gpiod_line_event_read, not struct gpiod_line_bulk) so the code builds against libgpiod v1.x headers. Install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that set a volatile sig_atomic_t flag so the main loop can exit cleanly. On each falling-edge event, read it with gpiod_line_event_read, append a timestamped line to /var/log/vibration_shutdown.log (opened in append mode, with error checking on fopen/fprintf/fclose), print the same message to stdout, then invoke system("sudo shutdown -h now"). Robustly check every libgpiod call (chip open, get line, request, event wait, event read) and every file I/O call, reporting failures via perror, and clean up all resources (release the line, close the chip) on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B to read altitude data from a BMP280 sensor via I2C bus 1 (SDA=GPIO2/pin3, SCL=GPIO3/pin5) at address 0x76 (SDO tied to GND), using the pigpio library. The sensor operates at 3.3V logic — never use 5V. Initialize pigpio and verify the BMP280 chip ID register (0xD0 must return 0x58) before proceeding. Read the 24-byte calibration block from registers 0x88-0xA1 and apply the Bosch compensation formulas, since raw ADC values are meaningless without compensation. Configure ctrl_meas (0xF4) for temperature oversampling x1, pressure oversampling x1, and normal mode. Every 5 seconds, read raw pressure (0xF7-0xF9) and temperature (0xFA-0xFC), compensate them, and compute altitude using the barometric formula with a sea-level pressure of 101325 Pa. Log each reading with an ISO 8601 timestamp to 'altitude_log.txt', flushing after every write. Handle all I2C read/write errors, sensor-absent conditions, and file-open failures gracefully with descriptive stderr messages. Clean up all resources (close the I2C handle, close the log file, terminate pigpio) on SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ to read temperature from an LM35 analog temperature sensor connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 10-bit ADC, wired via SPI0 (CE0, GPIO 8-11), using the pigpio library (not wiringPi or any deprecated library) for SPI communication. The LM35 output is 10 mV/°C; the MCP3008 VREF is 3.3 V. Use the MCP3008 SPI protocol: start bit (0x01), then single-ended mode bit plus channel number (channel 0 -> 0x80), then a don't-care byte, extracting the result as ((rx[1] & 0x03) << 8) | rx[2]. Read the temperature every 5 seconds, log each reading to the console in the format 'Temperature: XX.XX °C', and maintain a circular buffer of 120 float entries in memory; every 5 seconds overwrite the entire circular buffer to a binary file 'temp_log.dat' (opened with mode 'wb+') so the file always contains exactly 120 float values, with the oldest data overwritten when the buffer wraps. Check pigpio initialization, SPI open, and each SPI transfer; on SPI transfer failure, print an error and skip that reading rather than exiting; on file open failure, print an error and continue without logging to file. Use signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM to close SPI, terminate pigpio, and exit cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that logs ambient light and sound levels with timestamps to a file named "environmental_log.txt". Read ambient light from a BH1750 I2C sensor at address 0x23 on /dev/i2c-1, and read sound level from a MAX4466 analog microphone connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC over SPI using /dev/spidev0.0. Use the standard Linux i2c-dev API for I2C and the standard Linux spidev API for SPI; do not use the wiringPi library. Sample both sensors every 1 second and format each log entry as "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, Light: [lux], Sound: [raw ADC value]". Handle I2C and SPI errors gracefully, including sensor-absent or bus-error conditions, without crashing. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, terminate gracefully and cleanly release all resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that reads a Keyes KY-026 flame sensor module connected to GPIO 17, using the libgpiod library. Initialize the GPIO line for input with pull-down enabled, then continuously poll the sensor every 1 second. The sensor's digital output is active HIGH when flame is detected (threshold adjustable via an onboard potentiometer) and operates at 3.3 V logic level. Log each timestamped HIGH/LOW reading to "flame_events.log" in CSV format: timestamp, pin, state. When flame is detected, print an alarm message to stdout. Use only the libgpiod API (gpiod_line_*, gpiod_chip_*) — not sysfs, wiringPi, or pigpio. Check every libgpiod call, print error messages to stderr, and exit with a non-zero status on failure. Clean up GPIO resources on normal exit and on SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads temperature from a TMP36 analog temperature sensor connected to channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC over SPI (CE0, mode 0, 500 kHz), converts the reading to Celsius, and outputs a proportional voltage via an MCP4725 I2C DAC at address 0x62 on bus 1. Linearly map the temperature range 0C to 50C to a DAC output of 0V to 3.3V. Use the pigpio library for all GPIO, SPI and I2C access. Check every initialization, SPI transfer, I2C write and file operation; handle sensor-absent or bus-error conditions gracefully with retries and clear error messages. Log each reading — timestamp, raw ADC value, temperature in C, and DAC voltage — to "temperature_log.txt" and also print it to stdout, sampling every 0.5 seconds. On SIGINT, shut down gracefully: close SPI and I2C, close the log file, and terminate pigpio. Do not use wiringPi or other deprecated APIs.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads moisture levels from three DFRobot Soil Moisture Sensor v2.0 analog resistive sensors via an MCP3008 ADC over SPI (chip select CE0, SPI mode 0, 1 MHz clock), using the pigpio library. Read all three sensors on MCP3008 single-ended channels 0, 1 and 2, and convert each ADC value (0-1023) to a moisture percentage using moisture = (1.0 - (adc_value / 1023.0)) * 100.0, where 0% is dry and 100% is wet. Log timestamped readings ("YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS") to "soil_data.txt" in append mode, one line per sensor per cycle, with a 60-second sleep interval between cycles. If spiOpen or spiXfer fails, print an error message and exit with code 1; if a sensor read produces an invalid ADC value, print an error and continue. On SIGINT, close SPI, close the log file, terminate pigpio, and print a goodbye message, ensuring proper resource cleanup on all exit paths. Use only pigpio functions (spiOpen, spiXfer, spiClose, gpioInitialise, gpioTerminate, gpioDelay) — do not use wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod library to sequentially activate and deactivate four Songle SRD-05VDC-SL relays connected to BCM GPIO pins 17, 22, 23 and 24, simulating a basic light sequencer. Use libgpiod calls (gpiod_line_set_value, gpiod_line_request_output, etc.) with error checking on every call. Initially set all relay pins inactive (LOW, assuming active-high relay modules). In a loop, activate each relay in sequence for 1 second, then deactivate it, with a 1-second delay between relays, repeating the full cycle indefinitely until interrupted. Install a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that deactivates all relays and releases all GPIO lines before exiting. Include no SPI, ADC, temperature-sensor, or logging functionality — the task is relay sequencing only. Use only standard C libraries and libgpiod, not wiringPi or pigpio, and include clear comments explaining each step.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to read a Keyes KY-038 sound sensor's analog output through an MCP3008 ADC over SPI (chip select CE0 on GPIO8, mode 0, 1 MHz clock), reading MCP3008 channel 0. When the sound level exceeds a threshold of 500 (10-bit ADC value), turn on an LED connected to GPIO16, log the timestamp ("YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS") to "sound_events.log", and keep the LED on for 500 ms. Read the ADC every 10 ms in the main loop, applying a debounce delay after each trigger. Handle SPI transfer failures, invalid ADC channel selection, and GPIO initialization errors gracefully, checking every pigpio call and file operation. Install a signal handler for SIGINT to cleanly release resources on exit: close SPI, terminate pigpio, and turn off the LED. Use the pigpio library, not wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library for GPIO and SPI that reads a Seeed Studio Grove Rain Sensor (analog output) through an MCP3008 ADC over SPI (channel 0, 1 MHz, mode 0), and drives an L298N-based DC motor to automatically close a window when rain is detected. Wire the motor driver as IN1=GPIO17, IN2=GPIO18, ENA=GPIO27 with PWM (range 255, duty 150). Read the rain sensor with the standard 3-byte MCP3008 single-ended transfer: tx[0]=0x01, tx[1]=(0x08|channel)<<4, tx[2]=0x00, parsing the 10-bit result from the low 2 bits of rx[1] and all of rx[2]. Convert the ADC value (0-1023) to a rain level (0-10) so that ADC 1023 maps to rain level 0 (dry) and ADC 0 maps to rain level 10 (heaviest rain), since the sensor outputs higher voltage when dry. Poll every 1 second, and log each timestamped rain reading to "rain_log.txt" in append mode, flushing after every write. When the rain level is at or above a threshold of 5, close the window by driving the motor forward (IN1=1, IN2=0, PWM speed 150) for 3 seconds; when it drops below the threshold, open the window by driving the motor in reverse (IN1=0, IN2=1, PWM speed 150) for 3 seconds. The window starts in the open state. Handle pigpio initialization failures, SPI open failures, and log file open failures with clear error messages and proper cleanup, checking every init, syscall and I/O return value, and handling SPI transfer and log write failures without crashing. Install signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that set a volatile sig_atomic_t flag for graceful shutdown: stop the motor, close SPI, close the log file, and terminate pigpio, releasing all resources on every exit path. Use only the pigpio library, not wiringPi; the program should compile with gcc -o rain rain.c -lpigpio -lrt -lpthread.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library that implements a basic clap detector with a MAX9814 electret microphone amplifier (with AGC) whose output is read as an analog level on GPIO26 via pigpio's bit-banged ADC sampling. When the signal exceeds a threshold of approximately 0.7 x 3.3 V = 2.31 V, corresponding to a raw 10-bit ADC reading of about 700 out of 1023, turn on an LED on GPIO16 for 500 ms, print a timestamped detection message to the console, and apply a 50 ms debounce to avoid false triggers. Check the return values of pigpio initialization, ADC setup, and GPIO mode configuration, and handle sensor-absent or bus-error conditions gracefully. Install a SIGINT handler for clean shutdown that turns off the LED and terminates pigpio. Run continuously until interrupted with Ctrl+C, using C11 and avoiding deprecated APIs.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that reads distance from a Sharp GP2Y0A21YK0F IR distance sensor using the sysfs GPIO interface on GPIO 17. Because the sensor's real output is analog and this exercise has no ADC available, treat GPIO 17 as a digital input reading 0 or 1, convert that to a placeholder voltage (0V for low, 3.3V for high), and then convert the voltage to distance using distance (mm) = A / voltage + B, with A = 26.0 and B = -6.0. Log each reading with a timestamp ("YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS") to "distance_log.txt" in append mode. Implement a proximity-based pet feeder activation: if the computed distance is below 200 mm, print "Feeder Activated" to the console; otherwise print "Feeder Idle". Handle GPIO file open or read errors gracefully by printing an error and retrying after 1 second. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, unexport GPIO 17 and exit cleanly. The program should run continuously until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the libgpiod library, together with the standard Linux spidev SPI interface, to read analog soil moisture data from a Vegetronix VH400 sensor via an MCP3008 ADC over SPI (CE0, SCLK=GPIO11, MOSI=GPIO10, MISO=GPIO9), configured for single-ended mode on channel 0. Using calibrated ADC values of dry=800 and wet=300, if the moisture level drops below 30%, activate a 12V submersible water pump connected to GPIO17 through an active-high relay. Log each reading to "soil_moisture.log" with a timestamp, the moisture percentage, and the pump status (ON/OFF), sampling every 60 seconds continuously. Check every initialization step (libgpiod, SPI, log file), handle sensor read failures gracefully, and validate ADC values. On SIGINT, shut down gracefully by turning off the pump, closing the log file, and releasing all GPIO resources. Use only libgpiod and the standard Linux spidev SPI interface — do not use bcm2835 or wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads analog voltage from a DRV5055-A1 Hall-effect sensor via an external MCP3008 ADC over SPI, using the Linux spidev interface on /dev/spidev0.0 at 1 MHz, SPI mode 0, 8 bits per word, together with libgpiod (gpiochip0, line 8) to manually drive chip-select low during each SPI transfer and high afterward. Hardware wiring: MCP3008 VDD and VREF tied to the Pi's 3.3 V rail; MCP3008 DOUT to GPIO 10, DIN to GPIO 9, CLK to GPIO 11, and CS/SHDN to GPIO 8; DRV5055-A1 VOUT to MCP3008 channel 0, DRV5055 VCC to 3.3 V. The MCP3008 is a 10-bit ADC (0-1023) with VREF = 3.3 V, so compute Vout_mV = adc_value * 3300 / 1023. The DRV5055-A1 has a sensitivity of 100 mV/mT and a quiescent output of VCC/2 = 1650 mV, so compute the magnetic field B (mT) = (Vout_mV - 1650) / 100. Sample every 500 ms and append a CSV row to "magnetic_log.txt" as <unix_epoch>,<B_mt_two_decimals>. Use integer arithmetic internally for the field calculation and print the floating-point result with two decimal places in the log. Include all necessary headers such as stdint.h. Check every open, ioctl, SPI transfer, fopen, and fprintf call and propagate errors; if an ADC read fails, log the error to stderr, skip that sample, and continue the loop. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM cleanly, releasing the GPIO line, closing the gpiochip, closing the SPI file descriptor, and closing the log file on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library that reads analog voltage from a TI DRV5055VA Hall-effect sensor via an external MCP3008 ADC over SPI0 (CE0, GPIO 8, 9, 10, 11), with the sensor output wired to MCP3008 channel 0 (single-ended) and the sensor powered at 3.3 V. Initialize pigpio and SPI, handling initialization failures. Read the 10-bit MCP3008 value (0-1023) and convert it to voltage: V = ADC * 3.3 / 1023. Scale the voltage to magnetic field strength in mT using the DRV5055VA's ratiometric characteristics: quiescent output = VCC/2, and sensitivity at 3.3 V = 2.5 * 3.3/5 = 1.65 mV/mT, so field_mT = (voltage - VCC/2) * 1000 / sensitivity_mV_per_mT. Log each timestamped field-strength reading to "magnetic_log.txt" in append mode. If the field exceeds a threshold of 10.0 mT, turn on an LED on GPIO21; otherwise turn it off. Loop with a 100 ms delay between readings, using real ADC reads rather than simulated values. Handle SIGINT for graceful cleanup: close SPI, turn off the LED, and terminate pigpio. Check every SPI open, ADC read, and file open for errors. Use only pigpio for GPIO and SPI — do not use wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to monitor soil moisture with a DFRobot resistive soil moisture sensor connected to an MCP3008 ADC over SPI channel 0 (CE0, mode 0, 1 MHz), with the sensor's analog output wired to MCP3008 single-ended input channel 0. Initialize pigpio and open SPI with proper error handling. Every 60 seconds, read the ADC value using the MCP3008's single-ended protocol: start bit 0x01, single-ended mode bit 0x80, with the channel-selection bits in byte 1, and parse the 10-bit result from bits 1-2 of rx_buf[1] and all of rx_buf[2]. Log each reading with a timestamp ("YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS") and the raw ADC value to "moisture_log.txt" in append mode; on an ADC read failure (return -1), log an error line with a timestamp to the same file instead. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) to gracefully close SPI, terminate pigpio, and exit. Include robust error checking for every initialization, syscall, and I/O operation, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths. The program should run indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using libgpiod for GPIO control (chip 0, line 17) and the Linux spidev SPI device (/dev/spidev0.0) for ADC communication, to read analog current values from a Melexis MLX91209 (the analog-output version) connected to BCM GPIO pin 17. The MLX91209 outputs an analog voltage proportional to current (0-5V range, sensitivity approximately 100 mV/A). Since the Raspberry Pi has no analog input, digitize the sensor output using an external MCP3008 ADC on channel 0 over SPI. Log the current readings, in amperes, and timestamps to "current_log.txt" in CSV format (timestamp,current_A), reading and logging at 1-second intervals. Check every initialization step — SPI, GPIO, and file operations — and handle sensor-absent or communication failures gracefully. Use signal handling for SIGINT and SIGTERM for clean termination, releasing the GPIO line, closing the SPI handle, and closing the log file on exit. Do not use the sysfs GPIO interface or wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to read current from a Melexis MLX91211 analog-output current sensor via an MCP3008 SPI ADC. Wire the MCP3008 to the Pi's hardware SPI0 bus: CE0 on GPIO8, MOSI on GPIO10, MISO on GPIO9, SCLK on GPIO11, with MCP3008 VDD and VREF tied to the Pi's 5V rail and AGND/DGND tied to Pi GND. Wire the MLX91211 analog output to MCP3008 channel 0 (single-ended), with MLX91211 VDD from the Pi's 5V pin and GND to Pi GND. The MLX91211 output is ratiometric: 2.5V (VDD/2) at zero current and 5.0V (VDD) at full-scale +50A; linearly interpolate between those points. Initialize pigpio with gpioInitialise(), printing an error and exiting non-zero on failure. Open SPI0 (ce=0) at 1 MHz, mode 0 with spiOpen, terminating pigpio and exiting non-zero on failure. In a loop, read MCP3008 channel 0 with a 3-byte SPI transfer tx = {0x01, 0x80 | (channel<<4), 0x00} via spiXfer, computing the 10-bit result as ((rx[1] & 0x03) << 8) | rx[2]; on an SPI transfer error, print a diagnostic and skip that sample. Convert the raw code (0-1023) to voltage (0-5V), then to current using current = (voltage - 2.5) * (50.0 / 2.5); if voltage falls outside [0, 5V], print a warning and skip the sample. Every 100 ms (gpioDelay(100000)), append a timestamped line to "current_log.txt" in the format "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS XX.XX A", flushing after each write; on file-open failure, close SPI, terminate pigpio, and exit non-zero. Install a SIGINT handler that sets a volatile flag so the loop exits cleanly; on exit, close the log file, call spiClose, and call gpioTerminate. Use only pigpio's spiOpen, spiXfer, and spiClose functions, include the necessary headers such as unistd.h, and comment the code clearly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 to interface with two Omron B5W-DB01 diffuse reflective sensors using the libgpiod library. Each sensor has a single digital output only — active-low, open-collector with an internal pull-up, where object present = LOW and no object = HIGH; the sensor has no analog light-intensity output. Connect sensor 1's output to GPIO4 and sensor 2's output to GPIO17. Check every libgpiod call (gpiod_chip_open_by_number, gpiod_line_request_input, etc.) and exit with a clear error message on failure. Debounce each read by sampling 5 times with 2 ms between reads and accepting the majority value. Log each sensor's state (0 = object present, 1 = no object) to the console once per second. If both sensors report object present simultaneously, print the warning "ALERT: Both sensors detect object". Handle SIGINT to release all GPIO resources (gpiod_line_release, gpiod_chip_close) and exit cleanly. Do not use pigpio, wiringPi, or any deprecated library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to periodically read analog moisture levels from a YL-69 soil moisture sensor via an MCP3008 ADC over SPI channel 0, CE0, at a 1 MHz baud rate, with the sensor on MCP3008 single-ended channel 0. Use the SPI command format: start bit 0x01, then a single-ended-plus-channel-select byte 0x80 | (channel << 4), then a dummy byte 0x00, reading the 10-bit ADC value as ((rx_buf[1] & 0x03) << 8) | rx_buf[2]. Calibrate so that ADC value 300 represents very dry soil and 800 represents very wet soil, converting to a moisture percentage with 100.0 - ((adc - 300) / (800 - 300)) * 100.0, clamped to [0, 100]. Every 60 seconds, append a reading to "soil_moisture_log.csv" in the format "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,moisture_percentage" (e.g. "2025-03-15 14:30:00,45.23") and also print it to the console. Check every pigpio initialization, SPI open, SPI transfer, and file open call; on an SPI transfer failure, print an error and retry after a delay without exiting; on a file-open failure, print an error and continue. Use a volatile sig_atomic_t flag set by a SIGINT handler to close the SPI handle, terminate pigpio, and exit cleanly, releasing resources on every path — for example, if SPI open fails, terminate pigpio before returning. Include the headers pigpio.h, stdio.h, stdlib.h, unistd.h, time.h, signal.h, and string.h. Define constants SPI_CHANNEL (0), SPI_BAUD (1000000), MCP3008_CHANNEL (0), READ_DELAY (60), MIN_ADC (300), MAX_ADC (800), and LOG_FILE ("soil_moisture_log.csv"). Implement functions read_mcp3008(int channel), calculate_moisture_level(int adc_value), log_data(double moisture_level), signal_handler(int signal), and spi_setup(spi_config_t config); in main, initialize pigpio, open SPI, register the signal handler, loop until the termination flag is set reading the ADC, calculating moisture, logging data, and delaying 60 seconds each cycle, then close SPI and terminate pigpio on cleanup.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B running Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm, using the pigpio library, that detects motion via an HC-SR501 PIR sensor connected to BCM GPIO17 and triggers a camera snapshot via the libcamera-still command-line utility. Initialize pigpio and verify success; configure GPIO17 as input with a pull-down resistor, and poll it every 50 ms. After a state change, apply a 200 ms debounce delay and re-read the GPIO to confirm the state. On motion detection, capture a 1280x720 JPEG image with an ISO 8601 timestamp filename, saved to /home/pi/security_cam/; construct the output path safely with snprintf and verify the target directory exists before capture. Execute libcamera-still via fork and execvp (never system()), checking the child's exit status and treating a non-zero exit as a capture error. Log all key events — startup, motion detected, capture success or failure, and shutdown — to syslog. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, stop the main loop, release pigpio resources, and close syslog. Do not use wiringPi or placeholder camera functions.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that captures grayscale images from an Arducam OV5647 CSI camera module using the V4L2 API — the kernel interface exposed through libcamera's V4L2 compatibility layer, not libcamera's C++ API directly. Save each frame as a raw grayscale .pgm file, named sequentially (image_0001.pgm, image_0002.pgm, etc.). Open the V4L2 device given on the command line, defaulting to /dev/video0. Set the format to 640x480 using V4L2_PIX_FMT_GREY (8-bit grayscale), and use memory-mapped (V4L2_MEMORY_MMAP) streaming with a single buffer. Handle every open(), ioctl(), mmap(), fwrite(), and close() call, printing strerror(errno) on failure, and handle EAGAIN gracefully when dequeuing buffers using select() with a 2-second timeout to avoid infinite loops. Implement clean resource release on all exit paths, including signal handling for SIGINT and SIGTERM to stop streaming and unmap buffers safely. The program should capture frames continuously until a signal is received or a fatal error occurs.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that captures an MJPEG video stream from a USB webcam connected at /dev/video0. Configure the video capture for a resolution of 640x480, using the V4L2 API directly rather than the libv4l2 wrapper library. For every captured frame, log its timestamp in microseconds to a file named "frame_log.txt", writing each entry in the format "seconds.microseconds". Use memory-mapped (MMAP) buffers for frame capture, and handle input and output asynchronously with select() so the program never blocks indefinitely waiting for a frame. Implement robust error handling for every V4L2 ioctl call, every file operation, and every memory mapping, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including a graceful shutdown triggered by SIGINT.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi (Broadcom BCM2711, e.g. Pi 4) that captures video from the CSI camera, exposed as /dev/video0 via V4L2, and streams it over UDP to a target IP address and port given as command-line arguments (./program <server_ip> <server_port>). Use V4L2 MMAP streaming with 4 buffers at 640x480 YUYV format. Fragment each frame into UDP datagrams of at most 65000 bytes, each prefixed with a small header containing the frame index, fragment index, total fragment count, and payload size, so the receiver can reassemble frames. Handle errors at every syscall — open, ioctl, mmap, socket, and sendto — and exit gracefully on failure. Run until SIGINT or SIGTERM is received, then cleanly stop streaming, munmap all buffers, and close all descriptors.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi to capture a single 1920x1080 JPEG image from a USB camera at /dev/video0 and save it to "image.jpg", using the V4L2 API with memory-mapped (MMAP) buffers. Open the device in blocking mode (O_RDWR without O_NONBLOCK) so VIDIOC_DQBUF blocks until a frame is ready. Query device capabilities and verify V4L2_CAP_VIDEO_CAPTURE and V4L2_CAP_STREAMING are supported. Request the format V4L2_PIX_FMT_MJPEG at 1920x1080 with V4L2_FIELD_NONE, request 4 MMAP buffers, and query, mmap, and queue each one. Start streaming, dequeue one frame, verify buf.bytesused > 0, and write the raw MJPEG bytes directly to disk with no re-encoding. Implement clean resource release on all exit paths: stop streaming, munmap all mapped buffers, free the buffer array, close the file, and close the device fd. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler so Ctrl+C cleanly tears down streaming and releases resources. Check every ioctl, open, mmap, and fopen return value, printing a descriptive error via perror/errno on failure. Do not use any external image libraries.

Write a C program using the libgpiod library to control a camera pan-tilt system with two hobby servos on a Raspberry Pi: the pan servo is connected to GPIO4 and the tilt servo to GPIO5. Four push-buttons, wired active-low with internal pull-ups enabled, control movement: GPIO6 moves tilt up, GPIO7 moves tilt down, GPIO8 moves pan left, and GPIO9 moves pan right. Generate software PWM through libgpiod with a 50 Hz period (20 ms) and pulse widths between 1 and 2 ms, expressed as duty values of 50 to 100 out of 1000. Start both the pan and tilt servos at the mid-position value of 75. Each button press increments or decrements the corresponding servo's position by 5 units, clamped to the range [25, 125], polling all four buttons every 50 ms. Check the return value of every libgpiod call, handling chip-open and line-request failures, and cleanly release all GPIO resources when SIGINT is received.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi (Bookworm, 64-bit) that captures a single frame from a USB camera at /dev/video0, applies a 5x5 box-blur filter, and saves the result as a JPEG. Use the V4L2 MMAP API correctly: request buffers, mmap, queue, streamon, dequeue, streamoff, munmap, free buffers, and close the fd. Set the format to 640x480 YUYV, and use select() with a 2-second timeout for frame readiness. Convert the captured YUYV frame to RGB24, then apply a 5x5 box blur (kernel radius 2) with edge clamping. Save the blurred result as a JPEG at quality 75 using libjpeg, with an output filename of the form capture_YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS.jpg. Handle SIGINT cleanly. Check every syscall and allocation; on error, print to stderr and clean up all resources. Do not use wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi, running a 32-bit or 64-bit kernel with the V4L2 subsystem active, that queries a connected CSI camera at /dev/video0 and prints its supported resolutions, frame rates, and whether autofocus is supported. Use the V4L2 API: open the device, query capabilities with VIDIOC_QUERYCAP, enumerate frame sizes with VIDIOC_ENUM_FRAMESIZES, and enumerate frame intervals with VIDIOC_ENUM_FRAMEINTERVALS. For autofocus support, query the V4L2_CID_FOCUS_AUTO control via VIDIOC_QUERYCTRL. Check every ioctl return value, and handle the cases where the device node does not exist or cannot be opened, where the camera does not support frame-size or interval enumeration, and where the focus control is not present. Print a clear summary to stdout and exit with a non-zero code on fatal errors.

Write a C program using the pigpio library to control a camera pan-tilt system with two standard hobby servos on a Raspberry Pi: pan servo on GPIO4, tilt servo on GPIO5. Four push-buttons, active-low and wired to ground with internal pull-ups enabled, control movement: UP on GPIO6, DOWN on GPIO7, LEFT on GPIO8, RIGHT on GPIO9. Servos expect a 50 Hz PWM signal with pulse widths between 1000 microseconds and 2000 microseconds; initialize both servos to the center position of 1500 microseconds. While a button is held, increment or decrement the corresponding servo position by 10 microseconds per loop iteration (50 ms loop delay), clamped to the 1000-2000 microsecond range. Initialize the pigpio library and check its return value, printing an error and exiting if it fails. Configure internal pull-up resistors on all button pins, and use gpioServo() for PWM output. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler to cleanly stop PWM on both servo pins and call gpioTerminate() before exiting. Print a startup message showing the pin assignments and the center position. Use only pigpio — not wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to detect motion via an HC-SR501 PIR sensor connected to GPIO17 (physical pin 11). Initialize pigpio and configure GPIO17 as input with a pull-down resistor, checking and handling initialization failures; poll it every 100 ms, applying a 2-second debounce after each motion event. When motion is detected, capture a timestamped JPEG snapshot (640x480, quality 85) using the Raspberry Pi Camera Module v2 via the libcamera-still command-line tool, saving it to a directory named "motion_captures" (creating it if it does not exist, handling EEXIST gracefully). The program takes a server IP and port as command-line arguments and sends a JSON payload containing the filename, an ISO 8601 timestamp with microseconds, the motion status, and the GPIO pin number to http://<server_ip>:<server_port>/upload using libcurl. Call curl_global_init exactly once at startup and curl_global_cleanup at exit. Check all system calls, libcurl operations, and file operations for errors, printing diagnostic messages to stderr. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for clean shutdown, calling gpioTerminate() and curl_global_cleanup().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses a PIR motion sensor (HC-SR501) connected to BCM GPIO17 (physical pin 11) to trigger the Raspberry Pi Camera Module v2 to capture and save a timestamped JPEG image to /home/pi/images. Use libgpiod (v2) for GPIO input and invoke the libcamera-still CLI utility for image capture. Open the GPIO chip and claim GPIO17 as input with edge-falling or edge-rising detection, applying a 50 ms debounce via a falling-edge wait with timeout. On motion detection, generate a timestamped filename in the format YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS_mmm.jpg and run libcamera-still with "-o <filename> --width 640 --height 480 -q 85 --timeout 2000 --nopreview" (assume the images directory already exists), checking its return code and logging failures. Log all events, with timestamps, to /home/pi/motion_capture.log. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM cleanly by releasing all libgpiod resources and closing file descriptors. Do not use wiringPi, and do not use ZeroMQ or any network publishing — save to the local file system only.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi (32-bit or 64-bit) that captures a single frame from a USB UVC camera at /dev/video0 using the V4L2 API, crops a specific region, and saves the result as a raw YUYV file — V4L2 only, no libgpiod, pigpio, or wiringPi. Open /dev/video0 read/write and verify it is a V4L2 video capture device via VIDIOC_QUERYCAP. Negotiate format 640x480, V4L2_PIX_FMT_YUYV, V4L2_FIELD_NONE, and use memory-mapped streaming with one buffer (VIDIOC_REQBUFS, VIDIOC_QUERYBUF, mmap, VIDIOC_QBUF). Start streaming, then use select() with a 2-second timeout to wait for the frame, handling EINTR retries in ioctl calls. Dequeue the buffer and verify the captured width, height, and pixel format match the requested values before processing. Crop the region starting at (100, 50) with size 200x150 from the YUYV frame, copying complete 4-byte YUYV macroblocks (Y0, U, Y1, V) to avoid color corruption, and save the cropped frame to cropped.yuv (200*150*2 bytes). Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler so Ctrl-C cleanly stops streaming, munmaps buffers, closes the fd, and frees memory. Check every syscall, ioctl, mmap, fopen, and fwrite return value, printing errno via perror on failure and exiting with EXIT_FAILURE.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to control two SG90 servo motors connected to GPIO17 (pan) and GPIO18 (tilt), forming a basic pan-tilt camera mount. Read user input from stdin — arrow keys for up, down, left, right — to adjust pan and tilt angles in 5-degree increments, enforcing limits of 0 to 180 degrees, with initial angles of 90 degrees (neutral). Use pigpio's hardware PWM at 50 Hz, with pulse widths ranging from 500 microseconds (0 degrees) to 2500 microseconds (180 degrees). Handle pigpio initialization failure gracefully by printing an error and exiting with code 1. On SIGINT (Ctrl+C) or a 'q' input, set both servos to the neutral position and terminate pigpio cleanly. Validate all angle inputs and PWM settings, printing clear error messages for out-of-range angles or PWM failures. Include a 100 ms delay between commands to prevent excessive CPU usage. Use only pigpio functions — not wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that displays real-time CPU temperature, read from /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp, and CPU usage percentage, computed from /proc/stat, on a 128x64 I2C OLED screen using the SSD1306 driver. Use the pigpio library for I2C communication on bus 1, addressing the SSD1306 at 0x3C. Implement a basic 5x7 bitmap font to render the temperature and usage text on the display, updating the display once per second. Handle file read errors by returning specific error strings to the display instead of the missing values, and handle I2C communication failures by logging a message to stderr and exiting gracefully, checking every I2C write operation for an error return. Include signal handling for SIGINT so that all resources are released cleanly on exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B, using the pigpio library, that reads pulses from a YF-S201 water flow sensor connected to GPIO17 and calculates the flow rate in liters per minute using the sensor's calibration figure of approximately 450 pulses per liter. Log the current flow rate and the running total volume to the console every 1 second, with robust error handling for GPIO initialization failures. Every 10 seconds, also update a small HD44780 LCD screen connected via I2C (bus 1, address 0x27) to display the current flow rate together with the accumulated volume, using pigpio's I2C functions and handling any I2C communication errors that occur. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for a graceful shutdown that releases all GPIO and I2C resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library exclusively (no wiringPi) to display real-time wind speed and direction on a 16x2 LCD (PCF8574 I2C backpack at address 0x27, bus 1), updating every 500 ms. Count anemometer pulses on GPIO17 via a rising-edge interrupt, computing wind speed as pulses multiplied by 0.5 m/s per pulse, accumulated over each 500 ms sample window. Read the wind vane from channel 0 of an MCP3008 ADC over SPI0/CE0, mode 0, 1 MHz, linearly mapping the 10-bit ADC value (0-1023) to 0-359 degrees. Check every pigpio, I2C, and SPI call; detect sensor-absent conditions such as an ADC reading stuck at 0 or 1023, or I2C/SPI failures, and print diagnostic messages to stderr while continuing to run. Use pigpio's I2C and SPI bit-bang helpers (bbI2COpen/bbSPIOpen) or direct /dev/i2c and /dev/spidev access via pigpio's spi0SPIOpen/i2cOpen where appropriate. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, releasing all resources — the SPI handle, the I2C handle, and pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to measure water flow rate with a single YF-S201 water flow sensor connected to GPIO17 (physical pin 11), using the sensor's calibration factor of 7.5 pulses per liter. Calculate the flow rate in liters per minute by counting pulses over a 1-second interval. Display the real-time flow rate on an LCD1602 display connected via I2C (bus 1, PCF8574 address 0x27), showing "Flow Rate:" on the first line and the value as "X.XX L/min" on the second line. Implement robust error handling for pigpio initialization, GPIO mode and alert setup, I2C bus open and write failures, and sensor-absent paths such as zero pulses over an extended period. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including graceful shutdown on SIGINT and SIGTERM.

prompt: Write a C program using the libgpiod library for a Raspberry Pi to create a wave-like animation on an 8x8 common-anode LED matrix. The matrix rows are anodes, connected via GPIO to +3.3V, and columns are cathodes, connected via GPIO to ground: rows on GPIO17, 18, 27, 22, 23, 24, 25, 4 (BCM numbering), columns on GPIO5, 6, 12, 13, 19, 16, 26, 20. Implement a scanning display function that lights one row at a time — row HIGH and column LOW lights an LED (common-anode logic) — using a scan delay of 800 microseconds per row. Create two wave patterns, left-to-right and right-to-left, that shift each frame. Check all libgpiod calls, printing descriptive error messages to stderr and exiting with a non-zero code on failure. Handle graceful shutdown on SIGINT by releasing GPIO lines and cleaning up. Do not use wiringPi or any deprecated library.

Write a C program using the libgpiod v2 API (gpiod_chip_open, gpiod_line_request_output, etc.) for a Raspberry Pi to create a wave-like animation on an 8x8 common-anode LED matrix with 8 row anodes and 8 column cathodes. Wire row pins GPIO2, 3, 4, 17, 27, 22, 10, 9 to the row anodes, and column pins GPIO14, 15, 18, 23, 24, 25, 8, 7 to the column cathodes through current-limiting resistors (e.g. 220 ohm). Scan columns from left to right with a 150 ms delay between columns: for each column, set the corresponding column cathode LOW and all row anodes HIGH to light the entire column, clearing the matrix before each column by setting all column cathodes HIGH and all row anodes LOW. Run the animation indefinitely until interrupted (Ctrl+C). Check every GPIO operation, handling chip-open failure, and cleanly release all GPIO lines on exit using a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM. Do not use wiringPi or any deprecated library.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces with an STMicroelectronics VL53L3CX Time-of-Flight multi-target sensor via I2C using the pigpio library. The sensor is connected to I2C bus 1 at the default address 0x29. Initialize the sensor, verifying the sensor model ID during initialization, and periodically read distance measurements for all detected targets, logging the data with an ISO-8601 timestamp to the console every 100 ms. Note that the VL53L3CX requires a complex proprietary initialization sequence; use the standard ST Ultra Lite Driver (ULD) API registers and flow, or clearly stub the proprietary firmware download with a descriptive comment, while fully implementing the I2C communication, error handling, and application logic. Check every I2C read/write return code, and handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including graceful shutdown via SIGINT.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W to interface with a Melexis MLX75031 Time-of-Flight sensor via I2C using the pigpio library. Use I2C bus 1 and the sensor's default address 0x4C. Read the 16-bit distance register at address 0x0D by first writing the register address, then reading two bytes in big-endian order. Log timestamped distance readings to a comma-separated file named "depth_log.csv", writing a CSV header row if the file is newly created, sampling every 100 milliseconds. Include robust error handling: check pigpio initialization, I2C open, I2C read/write operations, and file operations. If an I2C read fails, log an error row with the distance field set to -1 and attempt to re-open the I2C handle. Handle SIGINT for graceful shutdown, closing the I2C handle and log file and terminating pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to read proximity and ambient light data over I2C (bus 1) from a Silicon Labs Si1145 sensor at address 0x60. Verify the PART ID register (0x00) reads 0x45, then initialize the sensor by writing to the command register (0x18) to set measurement rates and clear any stale IRQ, handling I2C read failures gracefully. Log readings with ISO-8601 timestamps to "biometric_log.txt", sampling every 500 ms. If the sensor is absent or initialization fails, print a diagnostic to stderr and exit non-zero; if a read fails mid-loop, log the error and continue. Install a SIGINT handler to cleanly close the I2C handle, flush and close the log file, and call gpioTerminate().

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 to interface with an E18-D50NK IR proximity sensor via GPIO using the libgpiod library. The E18-D50NK outputs LOW when an object is detected within its calibrated range of 10-30 cm, and HIGH otherwise. Use GPIO line 4 (physical pin 7) for the sensor input and GPIO line 17 (physical pin 11) for an LED output, polling every 100 ms. When an object is detected (sensor reads LOW), blink the LED for 100 ms (ON then OFF) and log a timestamped event to "proximity.log" in ISO 8601 UTC format, e.g. "2024-01-15T12:34:56Z Object detected" — log only on the falling edge (HIGH to LOW transition, object entering range) to avoid duplicate entries while the object remains in range. Open the GPIO chip by name "gpiochip4" (the Raspberry Pi 5 default); if that fails, fall back to gpiod_chip_open_by_name("gpiochip0") — do not use gpiod_chip_open_lookup without arguments. Check all libgpiod calls and handle file I/O errors, ensuring clean resource release — releasing GPIO lines and closing the chip — on all exit paths, including SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library over I2C bus 1 (default address 0x60) to read proximity (PS1) and ambient light (ALS_VIS) data from a Silicon Labs Si1145 sensor. On startup verify the PART_ID register (0x00) returns 0x45, then write 0x17 to HW_KEY (0x07), set CH_LIST (0x4F) to enable the PS1 and ALS_VIS channels, configure the measurement rates, and use the COMMAND register (0x30) with 0x06 (ALS_FORCE) and 0x07 (PS_FORCE) to trigger measurements. Read PS1 data from registers 0x18-0x19 and ALS_VIS data from registers 0x22-0x23, little-endian. Check every I2C read/write return code and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths gracefully. Once per second, in an infinite loop, log each reading with an ISO-8601 timestamp, proximity value, and ambient light value to a CSV file named 'biometric_data.log', flushing the file after every write. Install a SIGINT handler that closes the I2C handle, closes the log file, and calls gpioTerminate() for clean shutdown.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the libgpiod library to drive an HC-SR04 ultrasonic distance sensor for a proximity-based plant watering reminder. Use TRIGGER on GPIO 17 (BCM, output) and ECHO on GPIO 27 (BCM, input). Because the HC-SR04 echo pin outputs 5V logic and the Pi's GPIO is only 3.3V-tolerant, use a voltage divider (e.g. 1kOhm/2kOhm) on the echo line to protect the input. Generate a 10 microsecond trigger pulse, measure the echo pulse width using libgpiod edge events with CLOCK_MONOTONIC, and compute distance as (pulse_seconds * 34300) / 2 cm. Check every libgpiod call, apply a 30 ms timeout on each phase, treat an echo that never rises as sensor-absent and an echo stuck high as a timeout, and reject readings outside 2-400 cm. Log every measurement, including error and timeout entries, with an ISO-8601 timestamp to 'distance_log.txt', polling every 60 seconds. If the measured distance is below 15 cm, log a 'Time to water the plant!' reminder. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, releasing all libgpiod resources and closing the log file.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to periodically read distance from an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor connected with trigger on GPIO 17 (BCM) and echo on GPIO 18 (BCM). Send a 10 microsecond trigger pulse, measure the echo pulse width using gpioTick() for microsecond precision, and compute distance in cm using the formula (pulse_us * 0.0343) / 2. Log each reading with a timestamp to the console once per second. Handle errors for pigpio initialization failure, an echo rising-edge timeout of 200 ms, an echo falling-edge timeout of 200 ms, and invalid pulse durations (<= 0 or > 38 ms, the HC-SR04's maximum range timeout). Use a 1 kOhm resistor in series on the echo line for protection, and note in a comment that the HC-SR04 operates at 5V while the Pi GPIO is only 3.3V tolerant. Shut down gracefully on SIGINT/SIGTERM, calling gpioTerminate() on all exit paths. Note in a code comment that gpioTick() returns a monotonically increasing microsecond counter, and ensure the trigger, echo timing, and logging steps repeat once every second until a shutdown signal is received.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ to interface with a Texas Instruments IWR1443 mmWave radar sensor over UART (/dev/serial0), using the POSIX termios library for UART initialization and the pigpio library for GPIO control. The radar outputs a range profile of 64 range bins with a range resolution of 0.0486 meters per bin. Each data frame begins with an 8-byte magic word header (0x02 0x01 0x04 0x03 0x06 0x05 0x08 0x07), followed by 128 bytes of raw range profile data as 64 little-endian 16-bit integers. Implement basic intrusion detection: trigger an alert if a target appears within a distance threshold of 1.0 meters, activating an LED on GPIO 17 (BCM) for 2 seconds. Log each detected intrusion, with an ISO 8601 timestamp and the distance in meters, to a comma-separated file named 'intrusion_log.csv'. Handle UART initialization errors via termios, validate all I/O operations, handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths gracefully, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths through SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the libgpiod library, not the deprecated sysfs interface, to read obstacle detection data from an E18-D80NK IR sensor connected to GPIO 17. The sensor is active-low, outputting 0 when an obstacle is within the threshold distance and 1 otherwise. When an obstacle is detected, activate a buzzer on GPIO 18 (active-high); when the obstacle is removed, deactivate the buzzer. Poll the sensor every 100 ms and log every state transition with an ISO 8601 timestamp to 'obstacle_log.txt'. Check all libgpiod return values and handle errors robustly, including chip open failure, line request failure, and read/write errors. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, releasing all GPIO lines and closing the chip.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to interface with a TDK Chirp ICU-20201 Ultrasonic Time-of-Flight sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x69. Continuously read distance measurements by combining the 16-bit distance value from registers 0x31 (high byte) and 0x32 (low byte), sampling every 100 ms. Log each reading with an ISO 8601 timestamp to 'distance_log.txt', and trigger a GPIO alert on physical pin 17 (BCM 17) if the distance falls below 10.0 cm. Handle all I2C read/write errors, check for sensor absence, and manage log file creation errors. Cleanly release all resources -- I2C handles, GPIO, and pigpio -- on SIGINT/SIGTERM. Structure the main loop so that every sample first checks for a signal-requested shutdown, then performs the I2C read, then writes the log entry, so that no partial or corrupted log line is ever produced even if an error occurs mid-sample.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that implements a parking-assistance system using an STMicroelectronics VL53L1X Time-of-Flight sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x29, using the pigpio library (not wiringPi). Initialize pigpio with full error checking, printing a diagnostic and exiting non-zero on failure. Generate a 10 microsecond trigger pulse to start each measurement cycle, and register an alert callback on ECHO that captures both rising and falling edge timestamps as pigpio tick values in microseconds. Compute pulse duration as (falling_tick - rising_edge_tick), accounting for pigpio's 32-bit tick wraparound every roughly 72 minutes, and calculate distance using a speed of sound of 343 m/s (0.0343 cm/us), dividing by 2 for the round trip. Validate the pulse width: reject readings below 100 microseconds as noise or above 30000 microseconds as a timeout/no object detected, logging rejected readings as warnings. Log valid readings with an ISO 8601 timestamp to both stdout and an append-mode file named 'distance_log.txt', flushing after each write. Measure every 200 ms (5 Hz); if no valid echo is received within 60 ms of triggering, log a timeout warning and continue. Note in a comment that the HC-SR04's ECHO output is 5V, exceeding the Pi's 3.3V GPIO tolerance, and assume a voltage divider or logic-level converter is present on the ECHO line. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for clean shutdown: close the log file, release GPIO resources via gpioTerminate(), and exit cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) for all GPIO, PWM, and I2C operations to implement a smart parking gate with a VL53L1X time-of-flight sensor on I2C bus 1 (GPIO2/SDA, GPIO3/SCL) at address 0x29 and a servo motor gate actuator. Connect the VL53L1X shutdown pin to GPIO23 (BCM) and its interrupt pin to GPIO24 (BCM); generate the servo PWM signal on GPIO18 (BCM, hardware PWM). Open the gate when an object is detected within 50 cm and close it when the distance exceeds 60 cm, applying hysteresis. Log all gate state changes with timestamps and distances to 'parking_log.txt'. Verify the sensor model ID during initialization, check all I2C read/write operations, and handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handlers.

The gate should open (GPIO 18 HIGH, GPIO 19 LOW) when the sensor detects an object within 20 cm (200 mm), and close (GPIO 18 LOW, GPIO 19 HIGH) otherwise. Properly initialize the VL53L1X with a soft reset, configure its timing budget, and start ranging, polling the sensor every 500 ms and reading the 16-bit distance from the correct data registers. Use the pigpio I2C functions i2cWriteI2CBlockData and i2cReadI2CBlockData for 16-bit register access, since the VL53L1X uses 16-bit register addresses; do not use i2cReadBlockData or i2cWriteBlockData for register reads or writes. Log every open/close event with an ISO 8601 UTC timestamp to 'gate_events.log'. Check all pigpio and I2C return codes, and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths gracefully by logging the error. Ensure clean resource release -- close the I2C handle, reset GPIO, close the log file, call gpioTerminate -- on all exit paths via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to interface with a single VL53L1X time-of-flight sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x29. Trigger a distance reading on the rising edge of GPIO24 using a pigpio ISR. Follow this VL53L1X register sequence: write 0x00 to register 0x0000 (soft reset), wait 1 ms, write 0x01 to register 0x0000 (start measurement), poll register 0x0089 until bit 0 is set (data ready), then read the 16-bit distance from registers 0x0096-0x0097. Based on the measured distance, control a small DC motor via GPIO17 (forward) and GPIO18 (backward): below 100 mm (10 cm) drive forward, above 300 mm (30 cm) drive backward, otherwise stop. Check all pigpio and I2C return values, retry failed I2C transactions with exponential backoff, and stop the motor safely if the sensor is absent or a bus error occurs. Log distance readings and motor state changes to the console. Ensure clean resource release on SIGINT/SIGTERM: close I2C handles, stop the motor, and call gpioTerminate().

Open the trigger line as output and the echo line as input using gpiod_line_request_output/input with proper error checking on every call. Run the trigger sequence: hold trigger low for 5 microseconds, pulse high for 10 microseconds, then low. Wait for the echo rising edge with a 30 ms timeout, then measure the echo pulse width with a 30 ms timeout, computing distance as (pulse_us * 0.0343) / 2.0 cm using a speed of sound of about 343 m/s at 20 degrees C. Reject readings outside 2-400 cm and log an error line instead. Handle sensor-absent (echo never rises) and timeout paths explicitly. Every second, log the reading with an ISO 8601 UTC timestamp to 'distance_log.txt', flushing the file after each write. Install a SIGINT handler that sets a volatile sig_atomic_t flag; on SIGINT release all libgpiod resources, close the log file, and exit cleanly. Use libgpiod bulk or per-line requests and do not leak resources on any exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses pigpio to measure distance with an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor: TRIG on GPIO17 and ECHO on GPIO18 (BCM), with a 1 kOhm/2 kOhm voltage divider stepping the 5V echo signal down to about 3.3V for the Pi's input. Use pigpio's interrupt-driven ISR callback (gpioSetISRFuncEx) to measure the echo pulse width on EITHER_EDGE transitions. Fire a 10 microsecond trigger pulse once per second, compute distance in meters as pulse_us * 343 / 2e6, and append each reading with a timestamp to 'distance_log.txt'. Check pigpio initialization and the file open for errors, validate that an echo was actually received -- pulse width greater than 0 and within a sane range such as 58 microseconds to 25 milliseconds, roughly 1 cm to 4 m -- and handle tick-wraparound in the pulse-width calculation. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler for clean shutdown that disables the ISR, closes the log file, and calls gpioTerminate(). Do not include any UDP networking; focus purely on local logging.

Configure GPIO27 as an output and set it high at startup to enable the sensor. Initialise the sensor by writing 0x00 to register 0x0018 (continuous mode), 0x00 to register 0x0019 (no timeout), and 0x01 to register 0x0020 (start ranging). In an infinite loop, read the 2-byte little-endian distance from register 0x0014 and the 1-byte status from register 0x0016, and log the timestamp, distance in mm, and status to the systemd journal via syslog, using LOG_INFO for successful reads and LOG_ERR for failures; on a read failure, log the error and continue without crashing. Wait 100 ms between readings. Verify pigpio initialisation and the I2C device open. Install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that close the I2C handle, terminate pigpio, and exit cleanly on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to interface with a VL53L1X time-of-flight sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x29 and control a gate actuator on GPIO24 (active high to open). Initialise the sensor by reading the model ID from register 0x010F (expect 0xEA), setting the ranging mode to short via register 0x0021 = 0x00, and starting ranging via register 0x0015 = 0x01. Read the distance from the 16-bit register pair 0x0089-0x008A and convert it from mm to cm. Every 100 ms, open the gate when the distance is less than 20 cm and close it otherwise; the gate must start closed (GPIO24 low) at startup. Log every distance reading, gate state change, and error with a timestamp to 'gate_log.txt'. Check all I2C operations, sensor initialisation, and file operations for errors. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that closes the I2C handle, closes the log file, and terminates pigpio for a graceful shutdown.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to measure distance with an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor (trigger on GPIO23, echo on GPIO24) and pan an SG90 servo (signal on GPIO18, hardware PWM-capable) to track it. Drive the trigger high for 10 us then low, and measure the echo pulse width with a pigpio alert callback using the 32-bit tick counter with wrap-around handling, applying a 30 ms timeout. Convert pulse width to distance using speed of sound = 34300 cm/s, valid range 2-400 cm, and apply a 5-sample moving average. Map distance to a servo angle of 0-180 degrees using a non-linear (logarithmic) mapping, convert the angle to a pulse width of 500-2500 us, and command it via gpioServo(). Trigger every 100 ms. Write timestamp, distance in cm, and servo angle in degrees to 'distance_log.csv' with a header row, flushing after each write. Check pigpio initialisation, alert registration, servo command return codes, and file open; on an invalid reading (out of range or no echo), log -1.0 and default the servo to 90 degrees. Protect the pulse-width data shared between the alert callback and the main thread with a flag-based handshake. On SIGINT, using a volatile sig_atomic_t flag, stop the servo, close the CSV file, and call gpioTerminate().

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to interface with a Silicon Labs Si1102 proximity sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x60, and configures GPIO27 to raise an interrupt on a rising edge when proximity exceeds a configurable threshold (default 1000). Initialise pigpio and I2C with error checking. Read the 16-bit proximity value from registers 0x08 (high byte) and 0x09 (low byte). On each interrupt, read the proximity value, compare it to the threshold, and log to 'proximity.log' a timestamp (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS), the proximity value, and a status of 'SAFE' if at or below the threshold or 'ALERT' if above it. Support command-line arguments -a <i2c_address> (hex or decimal) and -t <threshold>. The interrupt handler must be thread-safe, with no blocking calls, using a flag or queue to hand data to the main loop. Check all I2C operations, GPIO setup, and file operations, printing errors to stderr. Handle SIGINT for clean shutdown: close the I2C handle, close the log file, and terminate pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to build a theremin-like instrument: an 8-ohm speaker on GPIO18 (PWM0) produces a tone whose pitch is controlled by the distance measured from an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor (trigger on GPIO23, echo on GPIO24). Use pigpio's hardware-timed PWM to generate the tone, with frequency ranging from 200 Hz to 2000 Hz at 50% duty cycle. Drive the HC-SR04 using pigpio's gpioTrigger() and gpioWaveTxBusy() for precise timing, with a 10 us trigger pulse and a 200 ms timeout. Map the measured distance (2 cm to 200 cm) to frequency using the logarithmic formula f = 200 * exp(distance / 50) Hz. If the distance is out of range or the echo times out, keep the previous frequency rather than producing an error tone. Include robust error checking for every pigpio call. Install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that cleanly stop the PWM output and terminate pigpio, with proper resource cleanup on exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to synthesize a theremin-like instrument on a piezo buzzer connected to GPIO18 (PWM0), with pitch controlled by distance read from an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor (trigger on GPIO23, echo on GPIO24). Set trigger low initially, send a 10 us high pulse, and measure the echo pulse width with microsecond precision using gpioDelay for timing and pull-down resistors on the echo pin; treat a pulse over 100 ms as a timeout, report the error, and reuse the last valid distance. The sensor's full range is 2 cm to 400 cm, but map the practical range of 5 cm to 50 cm linearly to a PWM frequency between 200 Hz and 2000 Hz using frequency = MIN_FREQ + (MAX_FREQ - MIN_FREQ) * (MAX_DIST - distance) / (MAX_DIST - MIN_DIST), clamped to that range, driven through pigpio's gpioHardwarePWM (not sysfs PWM) so the tone changes smoothly and continuously. Check pigpio initialisation and confirm GPIO modes are set correctly, handling sensor read failures gracefully. Print distance and frequency to the console each loop iteration, with a 10 ms delay between readings. Install a SIGINT handler that stops the PWM output and terminates pigpio cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to measure distance with an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor connected to GPIO17 (trigger) and GPIO18 (echo). Initialise pigpio, set the trigger pin as output (initially low) and the echo pin as input. Every 500 ms, send a 10 us trigger pulse and measure the echo pulse width with a 50 ms timeout, computing distance in cm as pulse_width / 2 / 29.1 (speed of sound = 29.1 cm/us). Reject readings below 2 cm or above 400 cm, printing 'Invalid reading' for those; otherwise print the distance as 'Distance: X.XX cm', and if it is below 10 cm also print 'Too close!'. Check pigpio initialisation and handle a timeout (-1) returned from the echo pulse measurement, ensuring that all resources are released cleanly on every exit path, not only on the normal one. Handle SIGINT by setting a flag to exit the loop, terminating pigpio, and exiting cleanly. The program should run indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to interface with a TDK InvenSense ICU-20201 ultrasonic time-of-flight sensor over SPI (mode 0, 1 MHz clock, chip select on GPIO8 / CE0), for a robotic obstacle-avoidance application. Initialise the sensor by writing 0x01 to register 0x01 (continuous measurement mode), 0x00 to register 0x02 (5 m range), and 0x01 to register 0x00 to trigger a measurement; read the distance from registers 0x0C (low byte) and 0x0D (high byte) using spiXfer, since pigpio has no spiWriteRead function. Continuously read distance in millimeters (range 200-5000 mm) with a 100 ms delay between readings, and log each reading with a timestamp to 'distance_log.csv' opened in append mode, closed properly on exit. Handle SPI communication errors, sensor initialisation failures, and sensor-absent conditions gracefully, logging errors to stderr and continuing to run indefinitely. Install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that close the SPI handle, release resources, and flush the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the standard Linux I2C ioctl interface (no third-party C libraries) to interface with a Silicon Labs Si1175 ambient light and proximity sensor at its default I2C address 0x60. Read the 16-bit visible ambient light value from registers 0x22 (low byte) and 0x23 (high byte) every 5 seconds. Log each reading with an ISO-8601 timestamp to a CSV file named 'proximity_log.csv' with the header row 'timestamp,als_visible'. Check every I2C open/read/write call for errors, handling both sensor-absent conditions and bus-error paths without terminating unexpectedly, and cleanly release the I2C file descriptor and the log file on all exit paths, including those triggered by SIGINT and SIGTERM. Include <stdint.h> for the uint8_t and uint16_t types used to hold the register bytes and the combined light reading.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to read ambient light (ALS) and proximity (PS1) data from a Silicon Labs Si1120 sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x60. Reset the sensor by writing 0x01 to register 0x30, then verify the part ID at register 0x00 equals 0x41. Read ALS data from registers 0x22 (low byte) and 0x23 (high byte) and proximity data from registers 0x18 (low byte) and 0x19 (high byte), combining each pair into a 16-bit little-endian value. Sample every 500 ms until SIGINT (Ctrl+C) is received, logging each reading together with a timestamp in YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS format to 'si1120_log.txt', which the program opens in append mode so earlier readings are preserved across runs. Retry I2C operations up to 3 times with a 10 ms delay between attempts before giving up on that reading, check the return value of every initialisation call and syscall, print descriptive errors to stderr so a failure can be diagnosed, and release all resources (I2C handle, log file, pigpio) on any failure path as well as on normal exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses standard Linux I2C ioctl calls (open, ioctl, read, write) on /dev/i2c-1 to interface with a Silicon Labs Si1182-A-GM optical sensor at I2C address 0x39. Initialise the sensor by verifying the part ID register (0x00) and configuring the measurement rate register (0x08) to 0x07. Every 100 ms, read ambient light data from registers 0x22-0x23 and proximity data from registers 0x24-0x25, each as a 16-bit little-endian value; convert ambient light to lux using lux = raw * 0.1, and log proximity as the raw value with no conversion. Log each timestamped reading (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS.mmm) to 'biometric_log.txt' in CSV format as timestamp,lux,proximity, and print the same reading to stdout. Check every I2C read/write operation for errors, handle sensor absence (a failed part ID read) gracefully, and report I2C bus errors such as NACK with appropriate messages. Install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that close the I2C file descriptor and log file, and ensure all resources are released on every exit path, including error exits.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library's I2C functions (gpioInitialise, i2cOpen, i2cWriteByteData, i2cReadByteData, i2cClose, gpioTerminate) to continuously read proximity data from a Silicon Labs Si1145 sensor at I2C address 0x60. Initialise the sensor with the following write sequence: 0x03 to register 0x07 (hardware key), 0x02 to register 0x06 (MEAS_RATE, 2 ms), 0x00 to register 0x1A (no interrupt), 0x0B to register 0x21 (ALS_VIS_IR_ADC_COUNTER), 0x00 to register 0x24 (ALS_VIS_ADC_GAIN), 0x49 to register 0x22 (PS_ADC_COUNTER, 16-bit, 1/15 gain), 0x03 to register 0x0C (PS_LED21, 180 mA), 0x0F to register 0x0F (PS_LED3, 180 mA), 0x03 to register 0x11 (PS_ADC_MISC, small IR), 0x07 to register 0x0D (PS_ADC_GAIN, 7.7x), and 0x03 to register 0x80 (COMMAND, PS_FORCE). Check every I2C write/read operation for errors; on a communication failure, log the error together with a timestamp and retry up to 3 times before exiting, and handle sensor initialisation failures by reporting a clear, specific error message rather than failing silently. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to periodically read raw accelerometer and gyroscope data from a TDK InvenSense MPU-6050 over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x68 (SDA on GPIO2, SCL on GPIO3), logging it to the console. Initialise pigpio and verify the sensor is present by reading the WHO_AM_I register (expect 0x68). Reset the device via PWR_MGMT_1 (0x6B), wait for it to stabilize, then clear the sleep bit. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to periodically read temperature and humidity from an Adafruit SHT40 I2C sensor connected to I2C bus 1 at address 0x44, logging readings to the console every 5 seconds. To trigger a high-repeatability measurement, send command 0xFD, wait at least 10 ms, then read 6 bytes: 2 bytes temperature, 1 CRC byte, 2 bytes humidity, 1 CRC byte. Validate both CRC-8 checksums (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF). Convert raw values using T = -45 + 175 * raw / 65535 and RH = -6 + 125 * raw / 65535, clamped to 0-100%. On any I2C read/write error or CRC failure, print a diagnostic message to stderr and re-open the I2C bus before the next attempt. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for a graceful shutdown, closing the I2C handle and terminating pigpio on exit.

Read ambient temperature from register 0x06 and object temperature from register 0x07 every 5 seconds. Log each timestamped reading to a comma-separated file named 'temperature_log.csv'. Handle I2C initialisation failures, sensor-absent scenarios (read errors), and file I/O errors gracefully rather than terminating unexpectedly. Handle SIGINT for clean resource release, closing both the I2C file descriptor and the log file before the process exits.

Implement robust error handling for I2C communication failures, including sensor-absent and bus-error paths, logging any errors that occur to a separate file, 'error_log.txt'. Poll the sensor every 1 second, and log the ISO 8601 UTC timestamp, differential pressure in Pa, and temperature in °C to a comma-separated file named 'pressure_log.csv', writing a header row if the file is new. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including handling SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to interface with a Si7021 humidity and temperature sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x40, and control a cooling fan on GPIO18 (active-high). Use the continuous measurement command 0x362F, wait the specified conversion time, then read 9 bytes: pressure MSB, pressure LSB, CRC, temperature MSB, temperature LSB, CRC, and 3 scale factor bytes, validating CRC-8 for both the pressure and temperature raw values. Convert pressure using pressure = raw_pressure / scale_factor - 1000 (Pa), and temperature using temperature = raw_temperature / 200.0 - 45.0 (°C). Sample once per second and log each sample to 'airflow.dat' in binary format, with pressure and temperature each written as a float, keeping the file handle open across samples rather than reopening it on every write. Check pigpio initialisation, I2C open, command write, and read results, and handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths. Use signal handling (SIGINT, SIGTERM) for a graceful shutdown, closing the I2C handle, terminating pigpio, and closing the file on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to read differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP800-500Pa sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x25, for a DIY ventilation system. Send the continuous measurement command 0x3603, wait the conversion time of 45 ms, then read 9 bytes (3 words plus 3 CRC bytes), validating each CRC-8 using polynomial 0x31. Convert the raw pressure using the scale factor 60.0 to Pa. Log each reading with a timestamp to 'pressure_log.txt' every 5 seconds. Handle I2C write/read errors, CRC failures, and sensor-absent scenarios gracefully without crashing the program. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, close the I2C handle, flush and close the log file, and terminate pigpio cleanly before the process exits.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to read differential pressure from a Honeywell Zephyr HAF Series HAFBLF0100A2AX5 digital airflow sensor over I2C bus 1 at 7-bit address 0x28, and drives a PWM fan on GPIO18 (a hardware-PWM-capable pin) at 25 kHz based on the computed flow rate. The sensor operates on the heat transfer principle and returns a 16-bit word whose 2 most significant bits are status bits; mask them off and shift the result right by 2 to obtain the 14-bit raw flow reading. Convert the 14-bit reading to flow rate using the linear transfer function where 1638 counts correspond to 0 SLPM and 14745 counts correspond to 10 SLPM. Scale the fan's PWM duty cycle linearly between 0% at 0 SLPM and 100% at 10 SLPM. Sample the sensor every 100 ms and log each reading with a timestamp to flow_log.txt in the comma-separated format "timestamp,pressure_Pa\n". Implement robust error handling for I2C communication failures, logging errors to stderr without crashing. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown: turn off the fan, close the I2C handle, flush and close the log file, and terminate pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to read pressure and temperature from an STMicroelectronics LPS33HW sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x5D. On startup, read the WHO_AM_I register (0x0F) and abort if it does not equal 0xB1. Configure CTRL_REG1 (0x10) to 0xB0 for block data update, 10 Hz output rate, and active mode. Read the 24-bit two's-complement pressure from PRESS_OUT_XL (0x28), PRESS_OUT_L (0x29), and PRESS_OUT_H (0x2A), storing it in an int32_t, and convert to hPa by dividing by 4096.0. Read the 16-bit two's-complement temperature from TEMP_OUT_L (0x2B) and TEMP_OUT_H (0x2C), storing it in an int16_t, and convert to Celsius using 42.5 + raw/480.0. Sample once per second using gpioDelay. Check the return value of every I2C read and write; on failure, write a timestamped error line to both stderr and the log file and continue the loop rather than exiting. Log each valid reading to environmental_data.txt, flushing after every write, in the format "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, Pressure: XXXX.XX hPa, Temperature: XX.XX °C" using localtime_r for thread-safe timestamp formatting. Handle SIGINT with a volatile sig_atomic_t flag that exits the main loop, then close the I2C handle, close the log file, and call gpioTerminate().
