prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to read an STLM75 digital temperature sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x48, reading temperature register 0x00 once per second. The STLM75 returns a 16-bit two's-complement word with 9-bit resolution (sign bit, 8 data bits, and the low 7 bits always 0); because pigpio's i2cReadWordData returns bytes in little-endian order, swap the two bytes before extracting the value, then right-shift by 7 and divide by 2 to get degrees Celsius. Store each reading in a 10-element circular buffer in memory and compute the running average. Turn on an LED on GPIO 17 when the average temperature exceeds 28.0 °C and turn it off otherwise. Check pigpio initialization, the I2C bus open, and every I2C read; if a read fails, skip that iteration and continue. Install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM so the program shuts down cleanly, turning off the LED, closing the I2C handle, and calling gpioTerminate() before exiting.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (gpioInitialise, i2cOpen, i2cClose, i2cReadDevice, i2cWriteDevice, gpioTerminate) to interface with a Sensirion SCD30 CO2 sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x61. Set the measurement interval to 2 seconds and start continuous measurement with ambient pressure compensation disabled (0). Before each read, poll the data-ready flag with command 0x0202, then read the measurement with command 0x0300, returning 18 bytes (3 values of 4 data bytes plus 2 CRC bytes each). Implement the SCD30 CRC-8 checksum (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF) for every write command that carries arguments and verify the CRC on every value read. Log CO2 (ppm), temperature (°C), and humidity (%RH) with ISO 8601 UTC timestamps as comma-separated values to air_quality.log, flushing after each write, and drive a simulated ventilation system from the CO2 reading: OFF below 800 ppm, LOW between 800 and 1199 ppm, and HIGH at 1200 ppm or above. Handle every error path — pigpio initialization failure, I2C open/write/read failures, sensor non-response, data-not-ready, and CRC mismatches — by logging the error and continuing the loop rather than crashing. Use sigaction to catch SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown: stop periodic measurement, close the I2C handle, close the log file, and call gpioTerminate(). In a mocked or emulated environment where the I2C hardware may be absent, initialize pigpio and open the I2C bus, and if sensor initialization or reads fail, log the error and exit gracefully with code 0 rather than crashing or returning a nonzero status.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to periodically read differential pressure from a Sensirion SDP32 (±125 Pa) sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x21. Send the continuous-measurement command bytes 0x36, 0x2F to start the sensor, then poll 9 bytes per reading: pressure MSB, pressure LSB, pressure CRC, temperature MSB, temperature LSB, temperature CRC, scale-factor MSB, scale-factor LSB, and scale-factor CRC. Verify the CRC-8 checksum on the pressure, temperature, and scale-factor words, and convert the raw pressure using pressure_pa = raw_pressure / scale_factor. Log each timestamped reading to the console at a default sampling interval of 1000 ms, configurable via a command-line argument. Implement robust error handling for I2C communication failures, including sensor-absent and bus-error paths; if the sensor is not physically connected, detect the I2C read/write failures and exit with a clear diagnostic message rather than crashing. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths through signal handling, and make sure the program compiles and runs cleanly in a mocked or emulated environment, exiting with code 0 when terminated by SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, closing the I2C handle and calling gpioTerminate() on all exit paths.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B running a 64-bit kernel to periodically read temperature and humidity from a Texas Instruments HDC1000 sensor on I2C bus 1 (/dev/i2c-1, GPIO 2 = SDA, GPIO 3 = SCL) at its default 7-bit address 0x40, using the Linux i2c-dev API (open(), ioctl(), read(), write()) rather than the deprecated wiringPi library. Configure the Configuration Register (pointer 0x02), setting bit 12 to enable a combined temperature-and-humidity measurement at 14-bit resolution. To read a sample, write the temperature register pointer 0x00 to the sensor, wait at least 20 ms for the 14-bit conversion (the DRDYn pin is not connected, so rely on this fixed delay), then read 4 bytes — 2 bytes temperature followed by 2 bytes humidity — in a single I2C read transaction. Convert the raw 16-bit values using Temperature (°C) = (raw / 65536.0) * 165.0 - 40.0 and Humidity (%RH) = (raw / 65536.0) * 100.0. Check the return value of every open(), ioctl(), read(), and write() call, and handle the sensor-absent path where the device file cannot be opened or the sensor fails to acknowledge. Log readings to the console every 5 seconds in the format "Temperature: XX.XX C, Humidity: XX.XX %"; on a read failure, print an error to stderr and continue the loop without exiting. Install a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM so the program closes the I2C file descriptor and exits cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to periodically read temperature from a Silicon Labs Si7051 sensor over I2C bus 1 (GPIO 2/3 for SDA/SCL) at its default 7-bit address 0x40. Log the temperature in degrees Celsius to the console every 5 seconds. Implement robust error handling for I2C communication failures, including sensor-absent conditions, bus errors, and read/write timeouts, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including graceful shutdown on SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (never wiringPi) to periodically read pressure values from a Melexis MLX90833 absolute pressure sensor connected over I2C bus 1 at its manufacturer-default 7-bit address 0x60. Log each reading to the console every 500 ms with a timestamp. Check all pigpio initialization and I2C read/write operations, handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to periodically read pressure and temperature from a TDK ICP-10101 barometric pressure sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x63. On startup, read the 4 calibration coefficients from the sensor's OTP memory with command 0x50 (8 bytes) and compute the scale_factor_lut, scale_factor_h, and scale_factor_p scaling factors per the datasheet. Every 5 seconds, trigger a high-precision measurement with command 0x40, wait 7 ms, then read 6 bytes — 2 bytes temperature followed by 4 bytes pressure — and apply the datasheet compensation formulas to convert the raw values to Celsius and Pascals. Log each reading to stdout with an ISO-8601 timestamp, for example "2024-01-15T14:30:00 - Temperature: 22.45 C, Pressure: 101325.00 Pa". Check the return value of every pigpio I2C call, detect a sensor-absent condition when a read returns a negative value or all bytes are 0xFF, and log such errors to stderr without crashing. Install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers for graceful shutdown, closing the I2C handle and calling gpioTerminate() on all exit paths.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the Linux i2c-dev interface (open() and ioctl() on /dev/i2c-1) to periodically read pressure values from a Melexis MLX90819 (digital I2C version) sensor on I2C bus 1 at 7-bit address 0x60. Trigger a measurement and read the 16-bit raw pressure value from the sensor's pressure registers, MSB at 0xAA and LSB at 0xAB, once per second. Convert the raw value to kPa using a linear scaling factor of 0.1. Log each reading to stdout with a timestamp. Handle I2C communication failures, including read/write errors and a sensor-absent condition, by printing to stderr and continuing. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler so the program exits cleanly on Ctrl+C, closing the I2C file descriptor.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface (open() and ioctl()) rather than the deprecated wiringPi library to interface with a Sensirion SDP800-500Pa differential pressure sensor connected on I2C bus 1, with SDA on GPIO 2 and SCL on GPIO 3, at address 0x25, for a do-it-yourself HVAC airflow monitoring system. Send the continuous-measurement command 0x362F, wait 45 ms, then read 9 bytes forming 3 words: pressure, temperature, and their CRCs. Validate each word's CRC-8 (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF), then convert the raw values using pressure = raw / 60.0 (Pa) and temperature = raw / 200.0 (C). Log the timestamp, differential pressure, and temperature as comma-separated values to pressure_log.txt. Handle I2C open/write/read errors and sensor-absent paths gracefully, and release all resources cleanly on SIGINT/SIGTERM.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (never wiringPi) to read differential pressure data from a Sensirion SDP800-500Pa sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x25. Use the continuous-measurement command bytes 0x36, 0x2F to trigger readings, wait at least 8 ms for the measurement to complete, then read 3 bytes: 2 data bytes plus 1 CRC byte. Verify the CRC-8 checksum (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF) of the data bytes, and convert the raw 16-bit signed value to pressure in Pa using raw / 60.0. Check every pigpio I2C call, and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths gracefully. Log the pressure reading and a timestamp (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS) once per second as comma-separated values to a CSV file named airflow_log.csv, writing a header row if the file is newly created. Include the necessary POSIX headers, such as unistd.h for access()/F_OK, so the code compiles cleanly with gcc -Wall -Wextra. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including graceful shutdown on SIGINT and SIGTERM.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that implements a PID-controlled greenhouse heater. Read temperature from a DS18B20 sensor on GPIO4 (physical pin 7) via the w1-gpio kernel module through sysfs at /sys/bus/w1/devices/, validating the CRC in each reading. Control a 12V heater using a relay on GPIO17 (physical pin 11) for enable/disable and a hardware PWM signal on GPIO18 (physical pin 12) for duty cycle modulation, using libgpiod for all GPIO control (not wiringPi). Accept command-line arguments for setpoint temperature and PID gains Kp, Ki, Kd. Every 5 seconds, log timestamp, average temperature, setpoint, PID output, and PWM duty cycle to greenhouse.log. Check all I/O operations and handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths. Ensure clean resource release — turn off the relay, set PWM to 0, close the GPIO lines, close the chip, and close the log file — on all exit paths via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the libgpiod library to read humidity from an AHT20 sensor over I2C bus /dev/i2c-1 at address 0x38, activating a dehumidifier relay on GPIO 17 (active-high) when humidity exceeds 60% and turning it off when humidity falls below 55%. Perform the AHT20 initialization sequence (0xBE 0x08 0x00) once at startup, then in a loop send the measurement trigger command (0xAC 0x33 0x00), wait 80 ms, and read 6 bytes of data, verifying the status byte indicates the sensor is calibrated and not busy before reading. Retry failed I2C transactions up to 3 times with a 10 ms delay between retries, and poll every 5 seconds. Log each reading to the console with a timestamp. If the sensor is absent or I2C communication fails after all retries, print an error to stderr and continue the loop rather than crashing. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM cleanly by releasing the GPIO line, closing the I2C file descriptor, and exiting with code 0.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads relative humidity from an HTU21D sensor over I2C at address 0x40 on /dev/i2c-1 every 60 seconds, and POSTs the reading as JSON to http://api.example.com/humidity. Use the standard Linux I2C dev interface (linux/i2c-dev.h with open(), ioctl(), read(), write()) rather than the bcm2835 library. Implement robust error handling for I2C communication failures — NACKs, bus errors, CRC mismatches, sensor absence — and for HTTP failures. Implement the HTTP POST client using standard POSIX sockets rather than an external library such as libcurl, and use syslog for logging. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, closing all file descriptors cleanly.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to monitor a Bosch BMP280 pressure sensor over I2C-1 at address 0x76. Verify the chip ID equals 0x58 at register 0xD0 before proceeding, then read the 24-byte calibration block starting at 0x88 and apply the Bosch compensation formulas. Configure ctrl_meas (register 0xF4) for 1x oversampling on temperature and pressure in forced mode (0x27), triggering a measurement by writing the forced mode bits (0x01) each loop, and wait about 10 ms for conversion completion before reading 6 bytes of raw data from register 0xF7. Sample every 2 seconds and log timestamped pressure threshold breaches — above 1020 hPa or below 980 hPa — to pressure_log.txt. Handle I2C errors gracefully with up to 3 retry attempts that re-open the bus and re-verify the chip ID. Use signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM to shut down cleanly, closing the I2C handle and calling gpioTerminate() on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4B that logs temperature from a TMP117 sensor (I2C address 0x48, temperature register 0x00, 16-bit signed big-endian, LSB = 0.0078125 °C), humidity from an AHT20 sensor (I2C address 0x38, init command 0xBE 0x08 0x00, measure command 0xAC 0x33 0x00, 7-byte response with busy bit in data[0] bit 7, 20-bit humidity and temperature raw values), and motion detection from a PIR sensor on GPIO 17, into daily timestamped CSV files. Use libgpiod for GPIO access (gpiochip4, line 17, input direction) and the standard Linux I2C interface (/dev/i2c-1) via ioctl for the sensors. Sample every 1 second, handle I2C errors with up to 3 retries and a 10 ms backoff, and check sensor presence at startup — print a warning but continue if a sensor is absent. Create a new log file each day at midnight with CSV header 'Timestamp,Temperature(C),Humidity(%),MotionDetected'. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling. Build with: gcc -o logger logger.c -lgpiod -lrt.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 using the libgpiod library, through the Linux GPIO character-device interface, to monitor a YL-83 rain sensor connected on GPIO17, reading it as an active-low digital output where a value of 0 means rain has been detected, polling the line every 2 seconds. When rain is detected, close a window by driving an L298N motor driver board, with its enable line ENA on GPIO22, its first direction input IN1 on GPIO23, and its second direction input IN2 on GPIO24, so that the motor runs forward for 5 seconds and then stops. Check the return value of every libgpiod call, and explicitly handle the case where the GPIO chip cannot be opened at startup. Ensure the motor is stopped and every requested GPIO line is released back to the system on program exit, whether that exit is triggered by SIGINT or SIGTERM signal handling, and log each event with a timestamp to stdout. Do not include any DHT22 or humidity-sensing code in this program — the scope is limited strictly to the rain sensor and the motor control it drives.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library, and not wiringPi, to modulate a common-anode RGB LED, whose Red, Green, and Blue cathodes are wired to GPIO 17, 22, and 27 respectively, so that its color visually represents the current CPU load. Use hardware PWM through pigpio to control the brightness of each channel, clamping every PWM value to the 0-255 range. Map CPU load, computed by reading /proc/stat and comparing successive samples, onto a color gradient: 0% load renders Green (0,255,0), 50% load renders Yellow (255,255,0), and 100% load renders Red (255,0,0), sampling and updating every 500 ms. Handle any pigpio initialization failure by printing an error message to stderr and exiting with status code 1. Install handlers for both SIGINT and SIGTERM that turn the LED fully off, which for a common-anode LED means driving all channels to full off, and then cleanly call gpioTerminate() before the process exits. Do not include any temperature-sensor code in this program; the scope here is CPU load alone.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to read temperature and pressure from a Bosch BMP280 sensor over I2C-1 (SDA=GPIO2/pin3, SCL=GPIO3/pin5) at address 0x76, sending the data as a JSON string over UDP to 192.168.1.100:5000 every 5 seconds. Verify the chip ID equals 0x58 at register 0xD0 before proceeding, read the 24-byte calibration block at 0x88-0xA1, and apply the Bosch 64-bit compensation formulas. Use forced mode (write to register 0xF4) for low power, waiting for the measurement to complete before reading 6 bytes from register 0xF7. Handle all I2C read/write errors, sensor-absent paths, and UDP send failures gracefully. Ensure clean resource release of the I2C handle, UDP socket, and pigpio library on all exit paths via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to dynamically control a PWM-driven cooling fan on GPIO18 (BCM) based on temperature readings from a MAX31855 thermocouple amplifier over SPI0 (CE0, GPIO8). Initialize pigpio and open SPI channel 0 at 500 kHz, mode 0. Every 1 second, read the 32-bit MAX31855 register, extracting the signed 14-bit thermocouple temperature at 0.25°C resolution and checking the fault bit (bit 16) plus fault type bits OC (bit 0), SCG (bit 1), and SCV (bit 2). Drive the fan via hardware PWM on GPIO18 at 1 kHz with a 0-255 duty range, using a piecewise curve: 0% below 25°C, a linear ramp of 0-50 between 25-40°C, a steeper ramp of 50-200 between 40-60°C, and 100% above 60°C. Log each valid reading — timestamp, temperature, PWM duty cycle — into a 20-entry circular buffer. On SPI transfer errors or MAX31855 faults, print a diagnostic message to stderr and skip the fan update for that cycle. Handle SIGINT gracefully: stop PWM, close SPI, print the full buffer contents, and terminate pigpio before exiting. Check every pigpio call, including gpioInitialise, spiOpen, spiXfer, and gpioPWM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library. Configure GPIO2 as a falling-edge triggered interrupt, with the internal pull-up enabled, to toggle data logging on and off from a BMP180 sensor connected over I2C bus 1 at address 0x77. Use oversampling setting OSS=3 for pressure. Log timestamped pressure (Pa) and temperature (Celsius) readings to altitude_log.txt in CSV format (timestamp,temperature,pressure), polling the main loop at 1-second intervals. Handle I2C read and write errors at every step and verify the calibration data reads. Ensure graceful exit on SIGINT by closing the I2C handle, closing the file, and releasing the GPIO.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that reads temperature from a MAX31865 RTD-to-digital converter over SPI0 (CE0, GPIO8, 1 MHz) and logs readings with timestamps to rtd_log.csv, every 5 seconds. Use the libgpiod library for chip-select line management and the standard Linux spidev interface for SPI communication (do not use wiringPi). Initialize the MAX31865 for 3-wire RTD mode with bias voltage enabled, read the RTD registers, check the fault status register, and calculate temperature using the Callendar-Van Dusen equation. Implement robust error handling for SPI communication failures and sensor read errors, handling sensor-absent and SPI bus-error paths by logging errors without crashing. Implement graceful shutdown on SIGINT/SIGTERM, properly closing the SPI device file descriptor and the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that logs temperature, humidity, and pressure from a BME280 sensor at I2C address 0x76 on I2C bus 1 (GPIO2=SDA, GPIO3=SCL, /dev/i2c-1) to bme280_log.csv every 5 seconds, with a timestamp in YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS format. Use the standard Linux I2C dev interface (linux/i2c-dev.h and sys/ioctl.h) rather than the deprecated wiringPi library. The CSV must contain columns timestamp, temperature_C, humidity_percent, and pressure_hPa. Check all I2C read and write syscalls, verify the BME280 chip ID equals 0x60 during initialization, and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths gracefully. Ensure clean resource release of file descriptors and file pointers on all exit paths via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling.

Create a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to sample a BMP180 pressure sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x77 every 50 ms, using a pigpio hardware timer (gpioSetTimerFuncEx). Use pigpio's i2cOpen, i2cReadByteData, and i2cWriteByteData functions for I2C communication, and read the 11 calibration coefficients starting at register 0xAA. Use oversampling OSS=0 (ultra-low power) for pressure conversion by writing 0x34 to register 0xF4 and waiting 5 ms. Log timestamped pressure readings to a circular buffer sized for 60 seconds of data, and trigger an alert on GPIO24 (active-HIGH) if the current pressure deviates by more than 5 hPa from the rolling average of the last 60 seconds. Implement robust error handling for I2C failures and sensor absence, and log alerts and errors to stderr. Ensure clean resource release on SIGINT by closing the I2C handle, resetting GPIO, and terminating pigpio.

Create a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library and a hardware timer interrupt to sample a single BMP180 pressure sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x77. Validate the calibration data read from registers 0xAA-0xBF before starting measurements, then use oversampling setting 0 (ultra low power) to log temperature (°C) and pressure (Pa) readings to bmp180_log.txt every 500 ms. Implement robust error handling for I2C communication failures — sensor absent, bus errors, read/write timeouts — and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths via signal handling for SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to control a PWM-driven cooling fan on GPIO18 (BCM), adjusting fan speed based on CPU temperature read from /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp. Use a linear mapping: 0% duty at 40°C, 100% duty at 70°C, clamped below 40°C and above 70°C. Set the PWM frequency to 25 kHz with a 0-255 duty range. Log timestamp, temperature, and duty cycle to fan_log.txt every 5 seconds. Handle file write errors, temperature read failures, and pigpio initialization failures gracefully. Clean up all resources on SIGINT/SIGTERM — stop the fan, close files, and terminate pigpio. Do not use wiringPi or ZeroMQ.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that reads temperature and pressure from a Bosch BMP280 sensor over I2C bus 1 (/dev/i2c-1, SDA=GPIO2/pin3, SCL=GPIO3/pin5) and logs readings with timestamps to weather_data.txt in append mode, using only the Linux i2c-dev interface (no wiringPi, no pigpio). The default BMP280 address is 0x76 (SDO tied to GND); also try 0x77 as a fallback. The sensor is powered from the 3V3 rail, never 5V. Read chip_id from register 0xD0 and verify it equals 0x58, aborting with a clear error if it does not match, then read the 24-byte calibration block starting at register 0x88 (dig_T1..dig_P9) and apply the Bosch 64-bit compensation formulas. Configure ctrl_meas (register 0xF4) for forced mode with oversampling x1 for temperature and pressure, re-writing ctrl_meas each loop to trigger each measurement, and poll the status register (0xF3) bit 3 (measuring) until it clears, with a timeout, before reading 6 bytes of raw data from register 0xF7 (press_msb) and combining into 20-bit values. Log every 5 seconds in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, Temperature: XX.XX °C, Pressure: YYYY.YY hPa'. Check every I/O call — open, ioctl, read, write, fopen, fputs — and handle failures gracefully. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to exit the loop cleanly, closing the I2C file descriptor and exiting 0. If the sensor disappears mid-run, log the error to stderr and attempt to continue or exit gracefully.

Read the 16-bit temperature register (0x00) every 1 second; the value arrives two's-complement, MSB first, left-shifted by 5 bits (bits [15:5] hold the temperature, bits [4:0] are always 0), so divide the signed 16-bit value by 256.0 to get degrees Celsius. Log each reading to an in-memory circular buffer with a capacity of 60 samples and compute the running average. Trigger an LED on GPIO 18 (BCM numbering) if the temperature exceeds 28.0°C, turning it off otherwise. Use a background thread with a mutex-protected circular buffer for data acquisition. Check every I2C read/write and GPIO init call, handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths by logging to stderr and attempting re-initialization, and ensure clean resource release — close the I2C file descriptor, release the GPIO lines, destroy the mutex — on all exit paths including SIGINT.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that regulates a resistive heater connected through a logic-level MOSFET on GPIO18 (hardware PWM) using the pigpio library (not wiringPi). Measure temperature with a PT100 RTD through a MAX31865 RTD-to-digital converter over SPI0 (CE0, SPI mode 1, 500 kHz), using a 430-ohm reference resistor for the PT100 (nominal resistance 100 ohms). Initialize the MAX31865 by writing 0xC1 to the configuration register (0x80) to enable VBIAS, enable auto-conversion, and clear faults. Read the 15-bit RTD code from registers 0x01 (MSB) and 0x02 (LSB), check the fault bit (D0 of MSB), and read the fault status register (0x07) to diagnose open, over-voltage, or under-voltage faults. Convert the RTD code to resistance using R_rtd = (code / 32768) * R_ref, then convert resistance to temperature using the Callendar-Van Dusen equation R = R0 * (1 + A*t + B*t^2), solved for t, for t >= 0. Run a PID control loop every 100 ms, outputting a PWM duty cycle on GPIO18 at 1 kHz with pigpio range 1000 for 0-100% duty. Include a failsafe shutoff: if temperature exceeds 80°C, an SPI read fails, or any MAX31865 fault is detected, immediately set PWM duty to 0 and exit with an error. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM gracefully — turn off the heater, close SPI, terminate pigpio, exit cleanly. Load the target temperature and PID gains (Kp, Ki, Kd) from a JSON config file at startup, using defaults target=25°C, Kp=1.0, Ki=0.1, Kd=0.01 if the file is missing. Log errors to stderr and exit with nonzero status on critical failures.

prompt: Create a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that monitors a BMP180 sensor over I2C at address 0x77 on /dev/i2c-1, sampling once per second and logging timestamped temperature/pressure breaches outside predefined thresholds — temperature above 30.0°C or pressure below 950 hPa — to breach_log.txt. Use the Linux I2C dev interface (i2c-dev.h, open()/read()/write()/ioctl()) instead of wiringPi, and use integer arithmetic for the BMP180 calibration calculations, avoiding floating-point pow. Check every syscall, retry transient errors up to 3 times, and handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths. Include clean resource release on all exit paths with signal handling for SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Create a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that samples a BMP180 pressure/temperature sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x77 every 500 ms using a pigpio hardware timer callback, storing timestamped readings in a 60-entry circular buffer, and driving a cooling fan on GPIO18 (active-high) when temperature exceeds 30°C. Use pigpio for I2C and GPIO (never wiringPi). Read and validate the 11-word BMP180 calibration table from register 0xAA before sampling. Compute true temperature (°C) and pressure (Pa) using the BMP180 compensation formulas with OSS=0, without calling the temperature function from inside the pressure function. Check every i2cWrite/i2cRead return code and skip the sample on error. Handle SIGINT/SIGTERM by turning the fan off, closing the I2C handle, and calling gpioTerminate. Print each new reading to stdout, and keep the timer callback simple, avoiding blocking calls such as printf or I2C functions inside it where possible.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B, using the pigpio library, that toggles data logging from a BMP180 pressure sensor at I2C address 0x77 to a file named pressure_log.txt, with each logged line recording a timestamp together with the pressure reading in Pa. The toggle is driven by falling-edge detection on GPIO27, debounced with a 200 ms window so repeated edges from a single press are not counted twice. At startup and periodically thereafter, read the BMP180's calibration data and use it with the Bosch compensation formulas to compute pressure from the raw sensor bytes, writing a new log line every 2 seconds for as long as logging remains enabled. Handle I2C communication errors as well as pigpio library initialization failures without crashing the program. On receiving SIGINT or SIGTERM, clean up all open resources, including the I2C handle and the pigpio library instance, before the process exits.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to control a solid-state relay on GPIO17, modulating a resistive heater to maintain a target temperature read from a MAX31855 thermocouple amplifier over the hardware SPI peripheral (SPI0, CE0: GPIO8 CS, GPIO9 MISO, GPIO10 MOSI, GPIO11 SCLK) at 2 MHz. Log temperature and PWM duty cycle to heater_log.csv with ISO-8601 timestamps. Implement a PI controller with anti-windup and a safe maximum duty cycle of 80% to prevent overheating. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown — turn off the heater, close SPI, close the log file, terminate pigpio. The target temperature defaults to 25.0°C. Red, Green, and Blue cathodes connect to GPIO 17, 18, and 27 (BCM), with the common anode on 3.3 V and current-limiting resistors on each cathode line. Use hardware PWM via gpioPWM (range 0-255) on each pin; since the LED is common-anode, a channel is fully off at duty 255 and fully on at duty 0, so invert the desired brightness accordingly. Apply temperature thresholds from the millidegree sysfs value: below 40000 m°C, solid Blue (R=0,G=0,B=255); 40000-59999 m°C, solid Green (R=0,G=255,B=0); 60000 m°C and above, solid Red (R=255,G=0,B=0). Print the current temperature (m°C) and RGB values to stdout each cycle. Check the return value of gpioInitialise(); on failure, print an error to stderr and exit with non-zero status. When reading the temperature file, handle both fopen failure and short or failed reads (check ferror); on any read error, print a diagnostic to stderr and skip the update cycle rather than using a bogus value, and close the file handle on every code path. Install a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM, using a volatile sig_atomic_t flag and performing cleanup in main's exit path rather than inside the handler, so that Ctrl+C cleanly turns off all three channels (PWM duty 255 for common-anode off) and calls gpioTerminate() before exiting. Run an infinite loop until interrupted.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ to read humidity and temperature from a DHT22 sensor connected to GPIO4 (BCM numbering, physical pin 7), using the pigpio library for bit-banging the 1-wire protocol and libcurl for HTTP POST requests. Send a start signal by pulling the data line low for at least 1 ms, then read the 40-bit response. Parse the data, validate the 8-bit checksum, and POST the readings as a JSON payload to http://yourserver.com/api/humidity. Handle sensor-absent, checksum, and network errors gracefully with up to 3 retries. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including signal handling for SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library that toggles data logging from a BMP180 pressure sensor (I2C address 0x77 on bus 1) to pressure_log.txt via a push-button interrupt on GPIO4, containing timestamped pressure readings in hPa. Use a falling-edge ISR on GPIO4 with an internal pull-up to toggle logging on and off, debouncing in the ISR using pigpio tick comparison (at least 200000 us). Read the BMP180 calibration coefficients from registers 0xAA-0xBE at startup and validate them, failing cleanly if the sensor is absent or returns invalid data. Use oversampling OSS=3 for pressure measurements with the correct 26 ms conversion delay, and implement the full Bosch BMP180 compensation algorithm using integer arithmetic, with no floating-point pow calls. Log only when logging is enabled; when disabled, print a status message. Sample every 2 seconds. Handle SIGINT cleanly by closing the I2C handle and releasing pigpio resources before exiting. Check every I2C read/write return value and report errors to stderr.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads humidity from a DHT22 sensor on BCM GPIO 4 (physical pin 7) and POSTs the humidity value as JSON to http://your-server.com/api/humidity using libcurl, using the pigpio library (not wiringPi) for the timing-critical GPIO reads. Initialize pigpio with gpioInitialise() and check for errors, implement the DHT22 single-wire protocol with correct start-signal timing (pull the data line low for at least 1 ms, then high for 20-40 µs, then release), and read the 40-bit response with microsecond-level edge timing via gpioRead(). Validate the checksum and retry up to 3 times on sensor failure with a 2-second backoff. POST the humidity reading with Content-Type: application/json using libcurl, retrying up to 3 times on network or HTTP errors. Handle SIGINT/SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, calling gpioTerminate() and curl_global_cleanup() on all exit paths, and log to syslog. Include a command-line option -s <url> to override the default server URL. Read every 10 seconds in the main loop, handling all error paths: sensor absent, checksum failure, curl init failure, and non-2xx HTTP responses.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that actively manages the official Raspberry Pi 5 Active Cooler through the sysfs thermal framework, using no third-party GPIO libraries. Read the CPU temperature (millidegrees Celsius) from /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp every 5 seconds and write the fan state to /sys/class/thermal/cooling_device0/cur_state using a tiered speed map: below 45°C, state 0 (off); below 55°C, state 1; below 65°C, state 2; 65°C and above, state 3 (max). Validate the cooling device's max_state before writing, to ensure the requested state is within bounds. Check all file opens, reads, writes, and parses, and handle transient read failures by retrying on the next cycle. Use a linear mapping: 0% duty at 40°C and below, 100% duty at 70°C and above, with linear interpolation in between. Log the timestamp, temperature (°C), and PWM duty cycle (as a 0-100 percentage) to a comma-separated file cooling_log.csv with a CSV header, polling the temperature every 5 seconds. Check pigpio initialization, verify the PWM frequency and duty cycle calls, handle file I/O errors, and gracefully shut down on SIGINT/SIGTERM by turning off the fan and releasing resources.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to interface with two Sensirion SLF3S-1300F liquid flow sensors on I2C bus 1. Both sensors share the default I2C address 0x08, so assume they are connected through a Sensirion SF06 multiplexer breakout (or similar I2C hub) that maps them to addresses 0x08 and 0x09. Continuously poll both sensors every 1 second using the SLF3S-1300F continuous measurement command 0x3608, reading 3 bytes per sensor (2 data bytes plus 1 CRC byte) and validating the CRC-8 checksum, skipping the logging if the CRC fails. Convert readings using raw_value * 0.01 to get flow rate in ml/min. Log the flow rates to a comma-separated file named flow_log.txt (format YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,flow1,flow2). Handle I2C errors robustly with up to 3 retries per sensor. Implement clean shutdown on SIGINT/SIGTERM, closing all I2C handles and terminating pigpio.

Develop a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to monitor a magnetic rotary encoder built from two TMAG5110A1 Hall-Effect Latch sensors: Sensor A (Channel A) on GPIO17 and Sensor B (Channel B) on GPIO18. Since the TMAG5110A1 has an open-drain output, configure internal pull-up resistors on both pins. Implement a standard 2-bit quadrature state machine to track rotation increments over 360 pulses per revolution, logging every state change with a timestamp and the normalized angular position (0.00 to 360.00 degrees) to encoder_log.txt. Ensure robust error handling for GPIO initialization and file I/O, and implement clean resource release on SIGINT/SIGTERM using pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using libgpiod for GPIO and the Linux I2C character-device interface (linux/i2c-dev.h) to interface with an Analog Devices ADPD144RI red and infrared photometric sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default 7-bit address 0x39. Read the 16-bit red and IR channel data from the FIFO data register (0x60), handling I2C read/write errors and sensor-absent conditions. Trigger an LED on GPIO 17 (active-high) if the IR reading exceeds a threshold of 2000. Sample every 100 ms and log timestamped readings to adpd144ri_log.txt in CSV format (timestamp,red,ir). Handle SIGINT/SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, cleanly releasing all resources — the I2C file descriptor, GPIO lines, and log file — on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to read RPM from a Melexis MLX90254 magnetic speed sensor connected to GPIO 18 (physical pin 12, configured as input with a pull-down), which outputs 1 pulse per revolution. Calculate RPM over a 1-second interval by counting rising edges only, and log RPM values with timestamps to rpm_log.txt in append mode, flushed immediately. Use a pthread mutex to protect the pulse counter between the ISR and the main thread. Check pigpio initialization, ISR registration, and log file opening. Use a signal handler for SIGINT/SIGTERM for graceful shutdown that terminates pigpio, closes the log file, and destroys the mutex. If the sensor is absent (0 pulses), log 0.00 RPM.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 using the libgpiod API (not sysfs or wiringPi) to sample the analog audio output of an Adafruit MAX9814 Electret Microphone Amplifier. Connect the MAX9814 OUT pin to GPIO 17 (configured as input) and the GAIN pin to GPIO 18 (configured as output), setting GPIO 18 LOW to select 60dB gain. Since the MAX9814 provides an analog signal, rapidly poll the digital input pin, at a 10 ms interval, to detect rising edges (logic HIGH) as peak sound events. Log each detected peak to audio_log.txt with a timestamp formatted as 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS LEVEL', where LEVEL is 1 for a rising edge. Handle all libgpiod initialization and I/O errors robustly, checking the return value of every API call, and ensure clean release of all libgpiod resources on all exit paths via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling. Print a startup message and run indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to monitor flow rate from a Sensirion SLF3S-4000B Liquid Flow Sensor connected on I2C bus 1 at the default 7-bit address 0x36, for a microfluidic drug delivery system. Initialize the sensor by sending the 2-byte command 0x3608 to start continuous measurement. Every 1000 ms, read 3 bytes from the sensor: a 16-bit raw flow value (MSB first) followed by a CRC-8 byte, and validate it using the Sensirion CRC-8 algorithm (polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF); if the CRC check fails, log an error and skip that reading. Convert the raw 16-bit signed value to a flow rate in uL/min by dividing by 1000.0. Log each valid reading to a CSV file named 'flow_log.csv' in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,flow_rate_uL_min', opening the file once at startup in append mode, keeping it open, and flushing after each write rather than reopening repeatedly. Check every pigpio initialization, I2C open, write, and read call; on an I2C read or write failure, log the error to stderr and attempt to recover on the next loop iteration. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) gracefully by closing the I2C handle, flushing and closing the log file, and terminating pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to interface with a Honeywell MICS-VZ-89TE VOC sensor connected on I2C bus 1 at address 0x70. Read the 7-byte sensor state starting at register 0x00, extracting TVOC (ppb) from bytes 1-2 and eCO2 (ppm) from bytes 5-6 (big-endian), and compute an IAQ index using the formula IAQ = clamp(100 - (TVOC / 10.0) - ((eCO2 - 400) / 50.0), 0, 100). Every 5 seconds, log a timestamped line with the IAQ, TVOC, and eCO2 values to 'air_quality_log.csv'. Check every I2C read and write return value, and handle sensor-absent or bus-error conditions without crashing. Handle SIGINT gracefully by closing the I2C handle, flushing and closing the log file, and terminating pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 using the libgpiod v1 API to monitor a SainSmart TTP223B capacitive touch sensor connected to GPIO 17 (physical pin 11, active-high): the sensor outputs HIGH while touched and LOW when released. Open gpiochip0 by name and request the line as input with the consumer label "ttp223_tamper". Poll the line every 100 ms using CLOCK_MONOTONIC. If the sensor remains continuously touched for more than 5 seconds, print an intrusion alert to stdout once per touch event (not repeatedly), and reset the timer when the sensor is released. Check every libgpiod call for failure and print strerror(errno) on error; if a sensor read fails mid-loop, print an error and exit with EXIT_FAILURE after cleanup. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, releasing the line and closing the chip on all exit paths. Do not use sysfs or wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B to continuously sample audio data from the InvenSense INMP441 I2S MEMS microphone and log 16-bit PCM samples to a raw file named 'audio_capture.pcm'. The INMP441 outputs 24-bit data left-justified in a 32-bit frame; extract the 24-bit data and right-shift it to produce 16-bit PCM samples. Acquire the I2S data through the Linux ALSA subsystem (via /dev/snd/pcmC0D0c or the snd-pcm kernel interface). Use the libgpiod library to drive the microphone's L/R select pin on GPIO 17 to select the left channel. Handle I2S initialization, data acquisition, and file I/O errors robustly, and implement clean resource release on all exit paths, including signal handling for SIGINT (Ctrl+C).

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to monitor a SainSmart IR Flame Sensor Module (LM393 comparator, IR photodiode) connected to GPIO 4 (digital DO pin), which outputs LOW when a flame is detected and HIGH when no flame is present. Poll the sensor every 50 ms with 50 ms software debouncing. When a flame is detected, drive a PWM-controlled cooling fan on GPIO 18 using hardware PWM at 100 Hz, scaling the duty cycle from 0 to 80% based on flame duration using an exponential curve; turn the fan off immediately when no flame is detected. Log all events (system start, flame detected, flame ended, shutdown) with ISO-8601 timestamps to 'flame_log.txt'. Implement robust error handling: check pigpio initialization, verify every GPIO read, handle sensor-absent conditions with a timeout, and cleanly release all resources (stop PWM, reset pins, terminate pigpio) on SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to interface with a TI AWR1642 mmWave radar sensor via SPI channel 0 (CE0/GPIO8) at 1 MHz, mode 0, assuming the AWR1642 is pre-configured via the TI mmWave SDK to stream range-Doppler heatmap data over SPI. Initialize pigpio and open SPI0.0 at 1 MHz mode 0. prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to poll a KY-033 Obstacle Avoidance Sensor Module connected to GPIO 4 (BCM numbering, physical pin 7), which outputs LOW (0) when an obstacle is detected within its threshold and HIGH (1) otherwise. Initialize pigpio and verify success, printing an error to stderr and returning non-zero on failure. Configure GPIO 4 as input with the internal pull-up resistor enabled and poll it every 50 ms. On each detection (reading == 0), record a timestamp and the reading into a circular buffer of 100 entries that overwrites the oldest entry when full, and print an alert to stdout. On SIGINT (Ctrl+C), print the entire buffer contents in chronological order with human-readable timestamps, release all pigpio resources, and exit cleanly. Do not use any deprecated APIs.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 (64-bit Bookworm) that interfaces with an Omron D7S vibration sensor over I2C (up to 400 kHz, default 7-bit address 0x55) using the Linux I2C character-device API (open()/ioctl(I2C_SLAVE)/read()/write() on /dev/i2c-1, GPIO 2/3 for SDA/SCL) to detect subtle vibrations indicating pre-failure in a small cooling fan. Initialize the sensor by writing 0x10 to register 0x1D (MODE_CONTROL) to switch it from standby to active mode, then wait until the operating-status register (0x1B) bit 0 reads 1; if the sensor does not become active within 1 second, print an error and exit. Every 500 ms, read the 16-bit signed acceleration registers X (0x2A/0x2B), Y (0x2C/0x2D), and Z (0x2E/0x2F), little-endian with LSB first, and convert the raw values to g using the scaling factor 0.0009765625 g/LSB. Log each sample as a CSV row with an ISO-8601 timestamp to 'fan_health.csv' in append mode, writing a header row if the file is newly created. Check every I2C syscall return value; on a read/write/ioctl failure, print a diagnostic to stderr and retry on the next iteration rather than crashing. Handle SIGINT/SIGTERM cleanly by closing the I2C file descriptor and the CSV file, then exit. The program should run until interrupted by the user.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to interface with two Keywish KY-032 Infrared Obstacle Avoidance sensors (active-LOW outputs, logic 0 = obstacle detected) connected to GPIO 23 (Sensor 1 OUT) and GPIO 24 (Sensor 2 OUT), triggering an LED on GPIO 25 (through a 220-330 ohm resistor to GND) when an obstacle is detected within approximately 10 cm of either sensor. Poll both sensors every 100 ms. Turn the LED ON immediately when either sensor reads LOW, and turn it OFF when both read HIGH. Verify pigpio initialization, validate every gpioSetMode/gpioRead/gpioWrite return code, and ensure clean resource release (gpioTerminate) on all exit paths, including SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to monitor a conveyor belt with two E18-D80NK IR obstacle sensors connected to GPIO 17 and GPIO 18, which output LOW (0) when an object is detected and HIGH (1) when clear. A stall is confirmed when both sensors read LOW continuously for at least 2 seconds; on a confirmed stall, log a timestamped entry to 'stall_log.txt', avoiding duplicate log entries for the same stall event. Check pigpio initialization, validate every sensor read, handle file I/O errors, and ensure clean resource release on SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to interface with a Texas Instruments TMAG5170-Q1 I2C 3D Hall-Effect sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x0E (A0=A1=0). Configure the sensor for continuous-conversion mode with all three axes enabled and a 50 mT range. Verify the device ID register (0x00, expected value 0x8D) at startup, and write a CSV header row to 'magnetic_log.csv' if the file is newly created. Every 100 ms, read the X, Y, and Z magnetic field readings, convert the raw 16-bit two's-complement values to mT using the appropriate LSB scale factor for the 50 mT range, and log them with ISO-8601 timestamps to 'magnetic_log.csv'. Check every I2C read/write return code, and handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths by logging errors to stderr and continuing. Register a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler for clean resource release (close the I2C handle, close the file, call gpioTerminate). Run an infinite loop until interrupted by Ctrl+C.

Write a robust C daemon for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to monitor a SEN0193 Water Level Sensor (digital output) connected to GPIO 23, using a pull-down resistor on the input to avoid floating states when the sensor is dry. Poll the sensor every 2 seconds. When water is detected (logic HIGH), print an alert message to stdout and append a timestamped entry in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS ALERT: Water detected' to 'flood_log.txt'. Check pigpio initialization, handle GPIO read failures with an automatic re-initialization attempt after 60 seconds (logging error entries to the same log file), and ensure clean resource release on SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B (Bookworm or later) using the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to read RPM from a Melexis MLX90217 Hall-effect sensor via GPIO interrupts. The sensor output is connected to physical pin 7 (Broadcom GPIO 4), configured as input with the internal pull-up resistor enabled. Count rising-edge pulses in a 1-second window using an atomic add for the pulse counter, and compute RPM as pulses_per_second * 60, assuming one pulse per revolution. Every 1-second sample, log 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS <rpm>' to 'rpm_log.txt' (flushing the file after each write) and print it to stdout, logging RPM 0 rather than aborting when the sensor is absent or not rotating. Check every pigpio call and file-open call for errors and exit with a diagnostic message on failure. Install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers so Ctrl+C stops cleanly: disable the timer and alert callback, close the log file, and call gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to detect direction of rotation from two Melexis MLX90217 unipolar Hall-effect sensors connected to GPIO 17 (Sensor A) and GPIO 27 (Sensor B) via hardware pull-up resistors, physically offset by 90 degrees to produce a quadrature signal. Use pigpio alerts (gpioSetAlertFunc) for edge-triggered interrupts instead of polling, and implement a quadrature state machine that tracks the previous state to determine direction, protecting the shared state between the ISR and main loop with a mutex. Log each detected rotation event (CW or CCW) with a millisecond-precision timestamp (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS.mmm) to 'rotation_log.txt'. Check all error paths: gpioInitialise(), gpioSetAlertFunc(), gpioSetPullUpDown(), and file open. Use a signal handler (SIGINT/SIGTERM) for graceful shutdown, ensuring the log file is flushed/closed and pigpio is terminated. The main loop should wait on a condition variable or sleep, not busy-spin. Never use wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the libgpiod library's line request API to interface with a SainSmart TTP223B digital capacitive touch sensor whose OUT pin is connected to GPIO 23 (physical pin 16), and an LED on GPIO 18 (physical pin 12) with a current-limiting resistor. Poll the touch sensor every 50 ms (to avoid busy-waiting) and illuminate the LED only while the sensor is actively touched. Check all libgpiod calls, including chip opening, line requests, reads, and writes, handling the case where the GPIO chip is unavailable. Log all touch events, errors, and startup/shutdown messages to the system syslog using openlog/syslog. Implement graceful shutdown via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handlers to ensure the LED is turned off and resources are released before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the libgpiod library's line event interface to read touch input from a SainSmart TTP223B capacitive touch sensor connected to GPIO 17 (physical pin 11), which outputs HIGH (3.3 V) when touched and LOW when idle. On each rising-edge touch detection (with approximately 50 ms software debounce), toggle an LED connected to GPIO 18 (physical pin 12). Initialize the LED line as output and drive it LOW at startup. Check every libgpiod call (chip open, line request, event wait, read, write) and print meaningful messages to stderr on failure. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM gracefully: release all libgpiod resources (lines and chip) and exit cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to interface with two SainSmart TTP223B capacitive touch sensors (active-high) on GPIO 4 and GPIO 17, each controlling a distinct LED on GPIO 27 and GPIO 22 respectively, lit while the corresponding sensor is touched. Use a 50 ms polling loop for debounce. Log every touch and release event (sensor pin, Unix timestamp, and new state) into a 100-entry circular buffer in RAM with an overflow counter tracking how many events were overwritten once the buffer wraps. Check the return value of gpioInitialise and every gpioSetMode/gpioWrite/gpioRead call, printing a diagnostic to stderr on any failure. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, turning off both LEDs and calling gpioTerminate before exiting. On shutdown, print the full log buffer contents and the overflow count to stdout.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to monitor a Raindrop Sensor Module (digital output, active-low: reads LOW (0) when rain is detected, HIGH (1) when dry) connected to GPIO 17, with the internal pull-up resistor enabled so the input is defined when the sensor is disconnected. Poll the sensor every 500 ms and log only state transitions, writing timestamped 'Rain Detected' or 'No Rain' messages to /var/log/rain_events.log. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, closing the log file and releasing pigpio resources on all exit paths. Check the return value of every pigpio call and of fopen.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to monitor a rotating shaft's RPM using two DRV5032FJDBZR Hall-Effect sensors (push-pull outputs, 3.3 V) connected to GPIO 17 and GPIO 18. Implement a debounce mechanism (approximately 5 ms) to avoid false readings, and calculate and print the RPM to the console assuming 2 pulses per revolution. Log timestamps and sensor state changes to a CSV file named 'shaft_log.txt' in the format 'timestamp,sensor1_state,sensor2_state'. Handle potential GPIO initialization and file I/O errors gracefully, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including signal handling for SIGINT (Ctrl+C). Include all required standard headers (e.g., errno.h, string.h) so the code compiles cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to read heart rate and SpO2 data from a Silicon Labs Si1182 I2C-based optical sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x28. Initialize pigpio, open the I2C bus, and verify the sensor is present by reading the PART_ID register at 0x00. Configure the sensor for continuous measurement by writing to the CONFIG register at 0x30. Once per second, read heart rate data from register 0x02 and SpO2 data from register 0x04, and log each reading with a timestamp in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, Heart Rate: X BPM, SpO2: Y%%' to 'biometric_log.txt' in append mode, flushing after each write. Check every I2C read/write return value and handle failures; on communication errors, print a message to stderr and continue the loop. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) for graceful shutdown, closing the I2C handle and log file and terminating pigpio before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to monitor structural integrity of a miniature bridge model using two digital tilt sensors, which output HIGH when tilted beyond their threshold, connected to GPIO 17 (sensor 1) and GPIO 18 (sensor 2), both configured as inputs with internal pull-down resistors enabled. Connect an active-high alarm (buzzer/LED) to GPIO 27, initialized LOW. Poll at a 100 ms interval using gpioDelay. If either sensor reads HIGH continuously for more than 2 seconds, activate the alarm (GPIO 27 HIGH); when both sensors return to LOW, deactivate the alarm. Log all tilt-start, threshold-exceeded, and tilt-end events with ISO-8601 timestamps (YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS) to 'bridge_integrity.log'. Check pigpio initialization, log file opening, and gpioRead return values. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for clean shutdown (deactivate the alarm, close the log file, call gpioTerminate), ensuring the alarm is deactivated on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to interface with an Omron D7S-A0011 seismic sensor over I2C bus 1 (default 7-bit address 0x1D, SDA=GPIO2, SCL=GPIO3). Initialize the sensor by verifying its presence and clearing the power-down bit in CTRL1 (register 0x1F). Every 100 ms, poll the 3-axis acceleration registers (0x28-0x2D, little-endian, 6-byte block read) and compute the Euclidean vibration magnitude; if it exceeds a threshold of 500, turn on an LED on GPIO 17 for 1 second, then turn it off. Log every threshold-exceeding event with an ISO-8601 timestamp and the peak vibration value to 'seismic_events.log'. Handle I2C communication errors and sensor-absent conditions gracefully with up to 3 retries per read. Ensure all resources (I2C handle, pigpio library, log file) are released cleanly on Ctrl+C/SIGINT. Build with: gcc -O2 -Wall -o seismic seismic.c -lpigpio -lm -lrt.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 using the libgpiod library to read obstacle detection data from four Keywish KY-032 Infrared Obstacle Avoidance Sensors whose OUT pins are connected to GPIO 4, 17, 27, and 22 (active-low: 0 = object detected). If any sensor detects an object, turn ON an LED connected to GPIO 18; otherwise turn it OFF. Poll the lines every 50 ms. Robustly handle GPIO initialization errors (e.g., chip open, line request failures) and cleanly release all resources on SIGINT/SIGTERM. Do not use blocking delays that would prevent prompt signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using libgpiod (v1.6+) to monitor 5 Keyes KY-026 flame sensors on BCM GPIO 2, 3, 4, 17, and 27 (physical pins 3, 5, 7, 11, 13), wiring each sensor's digital output (LOW when a flame is detected, HIGH otherwise) to its GPIO and VCC/GND to 3.3V and GND. Poll all five lines once per second. On a rising-edge transition from no-flame to flame, confirmed by a 50 ms debounce re-read, append an event line to /var/log/flame_events.log formatted as '<ISO 8601 UTC timestamp> - Sensor ID: <id> (GPIO <pin>) - Flame Detected'. Use syslog (facility LOG_USER, ident 'flame_monitor') for startup, read-error, and shutdown messages. Check every libgpiod call (chip open, line get, line request, line read) and every file I/O call (fopen, flock, fprintf, fflush); log and continue on per-sensor read failures rather than aborting, aborting only if chip open or line acquisition/request fails. Install SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers that set a volatile sig_atomic_t flag, release all requested lines, close the chip, and call closelog() on both normal and error paths. Track individual line pointers in an array rather than using gpiod_line_bulk_* APIs. Compile with: gcc -O2 -Wall -Wextra -o flame_monitor flame_monitor.c -lgpiod.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the libgpiod v1.x API to read the 8 individual touch states from a TTP226 8-channel capacitive touch sensor whose outputs OUT0-OUT7 are connected to BCM GPIO pins 5, 6, 13, 19, 26, 12, 16, and 20 respectively. Poll all eight pins every 50 milliseconds, logging only state changes (touch detected / released) to the console with ISO-8601 timestamps and the sensor index plus BCM pin number. Implement robust error handling for GPIO chip initialization, line resolution, bulk line requests, and read failures, printing a descriptive error (including errno) and exiting with a non-zero status on unrecoverable failures. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including graceful shutdown on SIGINT (Ctrl+C). The code must compile cleanly with gcc -Wall -Wextra -lgpiod and must not rely on libgpiod v2-only APIs such as struct gpiod_line_bulk.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to implement an adaptive grow light system with a VEML7700 lux sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x10. Configure the sensor with ALS gain 1/8 (0x00) and ALS integration time 100 ms (0x00) by writing a 16-bit value to config register 0x00 (little-endian: low byte first, high byte second). Read ambient light from ALS register 0x04 (16-bit little-endian) once per second and convert it to lux using lux = raw * 0.0576. Control an LED on GPIO 18 via hardware PWM at 1000 Hz with range 0-100, using adaptive brightness logic: lux < 100 -> 100%, lux < 500 -> 75%, lux < 1000 -> 50%, lux >= 1000 -> 25%. Log each sample to 'grow_log.txt' with an ISO timestamp, lux value, brightness, and error code, flushing after each write. Check pigpio initialization, I2C open, sensor config write, ALS read, and PWM operations; log and handle sensor-absent/bus-error paths. On SIGINT/SIGTERM, turn off the LED, close I2C, close the log file, and terminate pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library for a simulated security keypad that interfaces with an 8-channel TTP226 capacitive touch sensor module whose 8 digital output channels are connected to GPIO 2-9 (BCM numbering), and an LED on GPIO 17 that lights whenever any touch is detected. Initialize pigpio and verify success, exiting with an error message on failure; configure GPIO 2-9 as inputs with pull-down resistors and GPIO 17 as an output. Poll the inputs every 50 ms and debounce each channel so a single touch is logged only once per press. Log each new touch event to 'touch_log.txt' in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS - Channel X Touched', where X (1-8) corresponds to GPIO 2-9. Turn the LED on when any channel transitions from untouched to touched, and off when all channels are released. Check all file I/O operations for errors and print diagnostics to stderr. Implement a clean signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM that turns off the LED, releases pigpio resources, and exits gracefully.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to read ambient light data from a Texas Instruments OPT3001 sensor for a smart greenhouse environment monitoring system. Use I2C bus 1 (/dev/i2c-1, pigpio bus 1), OPT3001 address 0x44, configuration register 0x01, and result register 0x00. Configure the sensor for continuous conversion mode with automatic full-scale range and a 100 ms conversion time using configuration word 0xC810; pigpio's i2cReadWordData/i2cWriteWordData use little-endian word order while the OPT3001 expects/reports big-endian (MSB first), so byte-swap the 16-bit values before writing and after reading. After writing the configuration, wait at least 100 ms for the first conversion before reading the result register. Once per second, read the 16-bit result register, where bits 15-12 are the exponent and bits 11-0 are the mantissa, and compute lux = mantissa * 0.01 * (2^exponent). Log each reading to 'light_data.txt' as 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, <lux_value>' with two decimal places, and also print the lux value to stdout for live monitoring. Check the return value of every pigpio and file I/O call; if i2cOpen or i2cReadWordData fails, print a descriptive error to stderr and skip that iteration, or exit gracefully on init failure. Install a SIGINT handler for clean shutdown: close the I2C handle and call gpioTerminate(). Ensure the log file is flushed and closed properly on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to monitor a KY-026 Flame Sensor whose digital output (DO) is connected to GPIO 4 (BCM), outputting LOW (0) when a flame is detected and HIGH (1) otherwise. Poll the sensor every 500 milliseconds and log every reading with a timestamp to 'fire_events.log' (append mode). When a flame is detected (LOW), trigger an alert by setting GPIO 17 (BCM) HIGH for 1 second, then LOW. Check pigpio initialization, log file opening, and every GPIO read/write call; handle sensor read failures by logging the error and continuing. Ensure clean resource release (close the log file, reset GPIO, terminate pigpio) on all exit paths, including SIGINT (Ctrl+C), using signal-safe cleanup and avoiding unsafe functions in signal handlers.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the libgpiod library to read capacitive touch events from a TTP223 touch sensor connected to GPIO4 (physical pin 7), configured as an input with a pull-down bias. Poll the line with a debounce interval of approximately 50 ms, and on every press or release transition append a line to the text file 'touch_log.txt' in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS: Touch Detected' or 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS: Touch Released', flushing the file after each write. Verify every libgpiod call and print a diagnostic to stderr on failure; if the log file cannot be opened, release all GPIO resources before exiting with a non-zero status. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown by releasing the line, closing the chip, closing the log file, and exiting cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library (never wiringPi) to monitor coolant flow in a miniature liquid cooling system with a Sensirion SLF3S-1300F liquid flow sensor on I2C bus 1 (GPIO2=SDA, GPIO3=SCL), address 0x08. To start continuous measurement, send the 2-byte command sequence 0x36, 0x08 (0x3608) and wait at least 2 ms before the first read. Each read must fetch exactly 3 bytes: a big-endian signed 16-bit raw flow value followed by a CRC-8 byte (polynomial 0x31, init 0xFF); validate the CRC and flag the reading as an error on failure. Convert the raw value to ml/min using raw / 90.0, sampling once per second. Log the flow rate, raw sensor flags, and a computed status string to a comma-separated 'cooling_log.csv', writing the header row 'Timestamp,Flow Rate (ml/min),Status' only when the file is newly created. Check every pigpio, I2C, and file operation for errors; on an I2C read failure or CRC failure, log the row with status ERROR and attempt recovery by re-initializing the I2C handle. Validate the converted flow rate against a plausible range of 0.0 to 100.0 ml/min, logging out-of-range values with status INVALID. Handle SIGINT for graceful shutdown, closing the I2C handle, closing the file, and terminating pigpio on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod library to poll three KY-033 obstacle-avoidance sensors (IR reflective, digital output) wired to GPIO17 (left), GPIO27 (middle), and GPIO22 (right). Handle SIGINT cleanly by releasing all GPIO lines, closing the chip, flushing, and closing the log file before exiting. When a flame is detected, print an alert with a timestamp to stdout and log the event, with its timestamp, to 'flame_events.txt'. Verify that the libgpiod chip and line requests succeed, handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the libgpiod library (not sysfs, not wiringPi) to interface with a TTP223 capacitive touch sensor on GPIO23 (BCM 23, input, active-high) and toggle an LED on GPIO24 (BCM 24, output). Use libgpiod line events on the rising edge (touch detected) with a 1-second poll timeout, toggling the LED on each event; debounce is not required since the TTP223 has built-in hardware debouncing. Log every touch event with an ISO-8601 timestamp and the new LED state to 'touch_log.txt'. Open GPIO chip /dev/gpiochip4; if it cannot be opened or its lines cannot be requested, exit with an error after cleaning up any partially initialized resources. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to read a SainSmart TTP223B capacitive touch sensor on GPIO4 (physical pin 7) and toggle an LED on GPIO17 (physical pin 11). Poll GPIO4 every 10 ms; on a rising edge (LOW-to-HIGH transition, not just level), toggle the LED and append a UTC ISO-8601 timestamped line to 'touch_log.txt'. Implement a 200 ms software debounce so a single touch does not register multiple events. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown by turning off the LED, closing the log file, and calling gpioTerminate(). Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (never wiringPi) to interface with three Texas Instruments TMAG5110A1 Hall-effect latch magnetic sensors on GPIO4, GPIO17, and GPIO27 (BCM numbering). Each sensor's open-drain OUT pin drives a GPIO input with an internal pull-up enabled: it pulls low when a south pole is present and releases high otherwise, so a logic low means magnet-present and a logic high means magnet-removed. Initialize pigpio and verify every GPIO mode and pull call returns 0. Poll all three sensors every 100 ms using gpioDelay, and on the first read record the initial state without falsely logging a transition. Log each state change, with an ISO-8601 timestamp and sensor identifier, to 'magnet_log.txt'. Handle sensor read errors gracefully by logging to stderr and continuing. Install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers for clean shutdown that close the log file and call gpioTerminate(). Include comments explaining the latch behavior.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (never wiringPi) to read heart-rate data from a Silicon Labs Si1182-A-GM optical heart-rate sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x4A. Verify the sensor's PART_ID register (0x00) reads 0x02 and HW_REV register (0x01) reads 0x01, aborting with a clear error if the sensor is absent or wrong. Configure the sensor by writing the LED current (0x3F), averaging (0x04), and enable (0x01) registers, checking each write. Read the 16-bit heart-rate register (0x2A) once per second using i2cReadWordData and convert the raw value to BPM using raw * 0.5. Apply a 5-sample moving average and validate that the filtered BPM is between 30 and 220 before logging. Append valid readings as 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,BPM' to heart_rate.csv with an immediate flush. Retry on transient I2C read errors without crashing, and implement robust error handling for sensor-absent and bus-error conditions throughout. Handle SIGINT gracefully, closing the I2C handle, terminating pigpio, and closing the log file on all exit paths.

When a falling edge is detected (HIGH-to-LOW transition, edge-triggered rather than level-triggered, to avoid duplicate alerts while the signal remains LOW), print 'FLAME DETECTED' to the console and append a line with the current timestamp and 'FLAME DETECTED' to 'flame_log.txt' in append mode, flushing immediately. Check every libgpiod call and file operation, and handle the case where the GPIO chip or line is unavailable. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler for graceful shutdown that releases the GPIO line, closes the chip, and closes the log file on all exit paths.

Connect TTP226 outputs OUT1-OUT8, each active-high (3.3 V touched, 0 V idle), to GPIO 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, and 12 respectively (BCM numbering), and drive the counter display on GPIO17 (bit 0, LSB) through GPIO24 (bit 7, MSB). Poll the sensor lines every 10 ms, tracking each line's previous state to detect rising edges (inactive-to-active) without double-counting while held; on each new touch, increment an 8-bit counter that wraps 255 to 0 and immediately update the 8 output GPIOs so bit b appears on GPIO 17+b. Log every touch event to 'touch_log.txt' in append mode as 'YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ, Channel: <1-8>, Counter: <0-255>' and also print 'Touch on channel <N> | Counter: <V>' to stdout. Include a 200 ms stabilization delay after requesting lines before entering the main loop. Check every libgpiod call, file open, and I/O operation, reporting errors with strerror(errno); if gpiod_chip_open fails, print an error and exit non-zero; if any line-request call fails, release everything acquired so far and exit non-zero; if a sensor read errors, log to stderr and skip that channel without crashing; if an output write fails, log to stderr and continue; if the log file cannot be opened, log a warning to stderr and continue with stdout output. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown by resetting all output pins to 0, releasing all libgpiod resources, closing the chip, and exiting cleanly with status 0. Each sensor output is active-low, where 0 means a line or surface is detected and 1 means none is detected. Use the modern libgpiod API (gpiod_line_request_input, gpiod_line_get_value) to poll all four sensors every 100 ms and append a row to a timestamped CSV file named 'tracking_log.csv' with columns timestamp, sensor1, sensor2, sensor3, sensor4, writing a header row if the file is newly created. Robustly check every initialization and read call; if a GPIO request or read fails, print a clear error to stderr and continue if possible. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, releasing all libgpiod resources and closing the CSV file, and flush the file after each write so data is not lost on abrupt termination.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the libgpiod API (not sysfs, not wiringPi) to monitor two Omron D7E-5 tilt sensors connected to GPIO lines 17 and 18 (BCM numbering, physical pins 11 and 12). Configure both lines as inputs with an active-low pull-up (BiasPullUp) so an unconnected sensor reads high and a tilt event pulls the line low. Poll both lines every 100 ms and use edge detection with a 50 ms debounce window to avoid duplicate logs. When a line transitions from inactive (1) to active (0), log a timestamped event to /var/log/tilt_events.log in the exact format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, Sensor X tilted\n', where X is 1 for GPIO17 and 2 for GPIO18. Handle chip-open failure, line-request failure, and read errors by printing a message to stderr and exiting or continuing gracefully. Install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that release all libgpiod resources (chip and lines) and close the log file cleanly before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod library (v2.x API, no sysfs, no wiringPi) to read digital reflectance data from two TCRT5000 IR obstacle-avoidance sensor modules on GPIO17 and GPIO27, each active-low (0 = obstacle detected, 1 = clear). Drive an LED on GPIO22 high when BOTH sensors read 0. Poll the sensors every 100 ms and log each sample to a comma-separated file 'obstacle_log.csv' with columns timestamp,sensor1,sensor2,led_state, flushing after each write. Check every libgpiod call, handle the case where gpiochip0 is unavailable, and verify the log file opens successfully. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) for graceful shutdown by turning off the LED, releasing all line resources, closing the chip, and closing the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to sample a TDK InvenSense ICS-40180 analog MEMS microphone via direct GPIO polling and trigger an LED as a visual alert on sound peaks. The microphone's analog output is fed to GPIO4 (physical pin 7), configured as a digital input, so the program treats the mic line as a binary signal: a HIGH reading constitutes a detected peak. The LED is wired to GPIO17 (physical pin 11) through a current-limiting resistor. Sample the GPIO4 input at approximately 8 kHz (a 125-microsecond period) using pigpio's gpioDelay for timing. On each HIGH reading, print a millisecond-precision timestamp to stdout and turn the LED on GPIO17 ON for 100 ms, then OFF. Check the gpioInitialise() return value, and check every gpioRead/gpioWrite return value, reporting errors to stderr. Use a volatile sig_atomic_t flag for signal handling, without calling pigpio functions from inside the signal handler itself, and implement clean shutdown on SIGINT: stop sampling, ensure the LED is OFF, and call gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the libgpiod library (not wiringPi) to read a SunFounder 3-Way Tracing Sensor (IR reflectance, digital GPIO) connected to GPIO17 (left), GPIO27 (center), and GPIO22 (right), configured as active-low inputs with pull-up enabled. Log the left, center, and right sensor states to the console every 100 ms. Implement robust error handling for GPIO initialization failures, line request failures, and read errors, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including signal handling for SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the Linux i2c-dev ioctl interface to read a Silicon Labs Si1175 optical heart-rate sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x49. Read the ALS visible data registers, LSB at 0x24 and MSB at 0x25, at 100 ms intervals, combine them into a 16-bit value, and log the raw sensor values to the console. Implement robust error handling for I2C initialization and read failures, handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including signal handling for Ctrl+C.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod C library (v1.x API, not wiringPi) to read a Keywish 3-Way Tracking Sensor (IR reflectance, digital GPIO) connected to Broadcom GPIO pins 2 (left), 3 (middle), and 4 (right). Poll all three lines every 100 ms and log the sensor values to stdout in the format 'L:<0|1> M:<0|1> R:<0|1>'. Use individual gpiod_line_request_input calls (not the bulk API) to maximize portability across libgpiod versions. Check every libgpiod call, including chip open, line get, line request, and line read, and handle the case where the gpiochip device is absent or permission-denied. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, using signal handling for SIGINT (Ctrl+C) to terminate gracefully.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod library (v1.x API: gpiod_line, gpiod_chip, gpiod_line_get_value; not wiringPi) to read a TTP226 8-channel capacitive touch sensor, whose 8 independent active-high output lines TP1-TP8 connect to BCM GPIO 5, 6, 13, 19, 26, 12, 16, and 20 respectively. Open gpiochip0 and request all 8 lines as inputs. Poll every 200 ms and log each channel's state (0 or 1) to the console in a single timestamped line using a monotonic clock, for example '[12.345s] CH1=0 CH2=1 CH3=0 CH4=0 CH5=0 CH6=0 CH7=0 CH8=0'. Handle errors at every step, including chip-open failure, line-request failure, and individual line-read failure, printing to stderr and exiting with non-zero status.
