Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to create a standalone 'mood lamp' with a common-anode RGB LED connected to GPIO17 (Red), GPIO18 (Green), and GPIO27 (Blue). Smoothly fade between randomly chosen hues every 5 seconds using hardware PWM at 1000 Hz with an 8-bit (0-255) range, applying a 50-step linear interpolation over each 5-second fade. Because the LED is common-anode, invert every PWM duty-cycle value as 255 minus the value, and clamp all color channel values to [0, 255]. Convert each random hue to RGB using the standard HSV-to-RGB algorithm with full saturation and value; select hues internally via rand() seeded from /dev/urandom, with no networking or external message bus required. Check pigpio initialization and every gpioPWM/gpioSetMode return value, logging errors via syslog. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown by turning off the LED, releasing pigpio resources, and closing syslog.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the libgpiod library for GPIO control and the Linux i2c-dev ioctl interface (not wiringPi) to interface with a TCS34725 color sensor over I2C bus /dev/i2c-1 (BCM pins 2/3) at its fixed address 0x29. Initialize the sensor by powering it on (PON) and enabling RGBC (AEN), set the integration time to approximately 154 ms (ATIME=0x00) and gain to 1x (CONTROL=0x00), and verify the sensor ID register (0x12) returns 0x44 before proceeding. Read all four 16-bit channel registers as little-endian pairs: clear (0x14), red (0x16), green (0x18), and blue (0x1A). Apply per-channel gain and offset calibration and display the calibrated RGB and clear (C) values on the console. Drive an LED on GPIO17 HIGH when the calibrated red value exceeds a threshold of 200, and LOW otherwise. Check every open, ioctl, read, and write return value; attempt sensor re-initialization on a read failure. Ensure clean resource release, closing the I2C file descriptor, releasing the GPIO line, and powering down the sensor, on all exit paths including SIGINT and SIGTERM. Poll the sensor every 200 ms.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (never wiringPi) to control the brightness of a 10-LED WS2812B strip connected to GPIO18 (PCM_CLK/GPIO18), generating the precise WS2812B timing waveform via pigpio's hardware PWM/wave functionality. Read ambient light levels from a BH1750 I2C digital light sensor at address 0x23 using continuous high-resolution mode (command 0x10): wait approximately 180 ms after issuing the command, then read 2 bytes and compute lux = (MSB<<8 | LSB) / 1.2. Implement a smooth, non-linear (logarithmic) brightness mapping from the light-sensor readings (0-1000 lux) to LED strip brightness. Gracefully handle I2C errors and sensor-absent conditions with retries, and cleanly release all resources on SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads ambient light from a BH1750 I2C sensor at address 0x23 and adjusts the brightness of an APA102 LED strip via SPI proportionally to the measured lux. Use the Linux I2C (/dev/i2c-1) and SPI (/dev/spidev0.0) character devices directly; do not use the deprecated wiringPi library. prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi (any model with a 40-pin GPIO header) that uses libgpiod to blink an LED connected to BCM GPIO17 (physical pin 11) with a 2-second period (1 second on, 1 second off). Open GPIO chip 0, request the LED line as output initially low, and request a momentary push button on BCM GPIO18 (physical pin 12) as input with an internal pull-up and falling-edge event detection. In a loop, toggle the LED while monitoring for button events using gpiod_line_event_wait() with a 1-second timeout. On a falling edge (button press), stop the blinking immediately, turn off the LED, print a message, and exit cleanly. Include robust error checking for every libgpiod call, including chip open, line request, event request, and line set/get, and release all resources (lines, chip) on all exit paths. Use signal handling for SIGINT to allow graceful termination with Ctrl+C. Compile with: gcc -o blink_button blink_button.c -lgpiod.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (no wiringPi) to blink an LED connected to GPIO5 (physical pin 29) with a periodic delay of 750 ms. Initialize pigpio and check for failure, exiting with a non-zero code if initialization fails, then set GPIO5 as an output. In an infinite loop, turn the LED on (gpioWrite GPIO5 high), print 'LED ON' to stdout, wait 750 ms using time_sleep or gpioDelay, turn the LED off (GPIO5 low), print 'LED OFF', and wait another 750 ms, flushing stdout after each print so output is visible immediately. Handle SIGINT gracefully: cleanly turn off the LED, terminate pigpio, and exit with code 0, ensuring all pigpio resources are released on exit, including on error paths. The program should run successfully in both real and emulated Raspberry Pi environments, exiting cleanly with code 0 on SIGINT.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that uses the libgpiod library (no wiringPi, no pigpio) to control an LED and read a button. The LED anode is connected to GPIO24 (physical pin 18) through a 330-ohm resistor to ground, and a button is connected between GPIO22 (physical pin 15) and 3.3V, with a 10k-ohm pull-down resistor to ground (or the internal pull-down if available). Open the gpiochip0 device, configure GPIO24 as output initially low and GPIO22 as input with an internal pull-down. Continuously monitor the button: while it is pressed, blink the LED in a repeating 500 ms on, 500 ms off pattern; when the button is released, turn the LED off immediately and keep it off until pressed again. Check every gpiod call, including chip open, line get, direction set, and value read/write, printing descriptive error messages to stderr, and handle the case where the gpiochip device is not found or a line is busy. On program exit, including via SIGINT or SIGTERM, release all gpiod resources (lines and chip) gracefully. Run indefinitely until terminated by Ctrl+C.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the libgpiod library (not wiringPi or pigpio) to control a common-cathode RGB LED by randomly changing its color every 100 ms, using software PWM via a simple timing loop (no hardware PWM). Wire Red to GPIO24 (physical pin 18), Green to GPIO23 (physical pin 16), and Blue to GPIO18 (physical pin 12) (BCM numbering). prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to interface with an Analog Devices ADPD188BI optical sensor over I2C bus 1 at 7-bit address 0x39. Initialize the sensor by writing 0x01 to register 0x0D (MODE) to enter normal operation mode. Read ambient light (ALS) data from 16-bit registers 0x64 (LSB) and 0x65 (MSB), combining them into a 16-bit unsigned value, and read color (RGB) data from 16-bit registers 0x66 (Red), 0x68 (Green), and 0x6A (Blue). Log each timestamped reading (ALS, R, G, B) to a CSV file named 'color_log.csv' with a header row. Simulate a smart lighting system by adjusting LED brightness on GPIO18 (hardware PWM) using pigpio: map the ALS value (0-65535) to a PWM duty cycle (0-255), so brighter ambient light increases LED brightness. Handle I2C errors, such as failed writes/reads or sensor absence, by logging to stderr and retrying after 100 ms. Use signal handling (SIGINT/SIGTERM) for graceful shutdown, closing the I2C handle, turning off the LED, and closing the CSV file. Sample every 500 ms.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses pigpio for I2C (never wiringPi) to interface with an Adafruit FXOS8700CQ 6-axis accelerometer/magnetometer at I2C address 0x1F on bus 1, detecting sudden impacts by computing the acceleration magnitude. On startup, verify the sensor by reading WHO_AM_I (register 0x0D) and checking it equals 0xC7, aborting with a clear error if it does not match. Initialize the sensor: place it into standby (clear CTRL_REG1 bit 0), configure XYZ_DATA_CFG (0x0E) for ±2g mode (0x00), then activate by setting CTRL_REG1 (0x2A) bit 0 (active mode, 200 Hz ODR). Read 6 bytes of acceleration starting at OUT_X_MSB (0x01); the data is 14-bit left-justified, so shift right by 2, then convert using sensitivity 4096 counts/g for the ±2g range and multiply by 9.81 for m/s^2. Compute magnitude = sqrt(x^2 + y^2 + z^2); if it exceeds the 2g (19.62 m/s^2) threshold, log the timestamp, x, y, z, and magnitude to 'impact_log.txt' in append mode as 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,x,y,z,magnitude' with 3 decimal places. Sample every 50 ms. Check every pigpio I2C call's return value; on a read error, print a diagnostic to stderr and continue the loop rather than crashing. Implement graceful shutdown via SIGINT (Ctrl+C): close the I2C handle, call gpioTerminate(), and exit cleanly.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the Linux i2c-dev ioctl interface (/dev/i2c-1 character device) to read angular velocity from a GY-50 L3G4200D gyroscope at I2C address 0x69 (SA0 tied high) on bus 1. Configure CTRL_REG1 (0x20) to 0x0F (normal mode, all axes enabled, 100 Hz ODR) and CTRL_REG4 (0x23) to 0x00 (250 dps full-scale, continuous update). Read the 6-byte OUT_X_L..OUT_Z_H block starting at register 0x28 using an auto-increment read, and convert the raw 16-bit signed values to degrees per second using a sensitivity of 0.00875 dps/LSB. Perform a 100-sample stationary calibration at startup to compute X/Y/Z zero-rate offsets. Log the calibrated X, Y, Z readings with ISO-8601 timestamps to 'gyro_log.txt' at 20 Hz (50 ms period). If any axis exceeds 50 dps, print a warning to stderr and append an alert line to the log. Check every open, ioctl, read, and write call; detect sensor absence via WHO_AM_I (register 0x0F, expected 0xD3) and handle I2C bus errors. Cleanly release the I2C file descriptor and log file on SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to read acceleration data from an ADXL345 accelerometer over I2C bus 1 at address 0x53. Configure the sensor for full-resolution, ±2g range, and verify the DEVID register (0x00) reads 0xE5 before proceeding. Read the 6 bytes of X/Y/Z data starting at register 0x32 every 100 ms (10 Hz). Log each sample to 'accel_log.txt' as 'timestamp,x,y,z' in g units with 3 decimal places. Turn on an LED connected to GPIO17 (active-high) when the absolute acceleration on ANY axis exceeds 2.0 g, otherwise turn it off. Check every pigpio/I2C call, and handle I2C read failures without writing garbage to the log. Ensure clean resource release (I2C handle, GPIO, log file) on SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses pigpio for I2C to read magnetometer and accelerometer data from a GY-51 LSM303DLHC over I2C bus 1 (accelerometer address 0x19, magnetometer address 0x1E) and calculate a tilt-compensated heading. Initialize the accelerometer with CTRL_REG1_A (0x20) set to 0x27 (50 Hz, all axes enabled) and the magnetometer with MR_REG_M (0x02) set to 0x00 (continuous-conversion mode). Read 6 bytes from each sensor: accelerometer data from OUT_X_L_A (0x28) with the auto-increment bit, and magnetometer data from OUT_X_H_M (0x03). Log timestamped heading, acceleration (x, y, z in g), and magnetic field (x, y, z in gauss) to 'compass_log.txt', writing a CSV header if the log file is new. Check every I2C call and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths. Sample every 100 ms. Use SIGINT/SIGTERM for graceful shutdown that closes the I2C handles and terminates pigpio.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that initializes the pigpio library and reads a KY-026 Flame Sensor Module's digital output connected to GPIO17 (physical pin 11), enabling the internal pull-up resistor on GPIO17 so the input is deterministic when the sensor's open-collector output is off. The DO line is active-LOW: it reads LOW (0) when a flame is detected and HIGH (1) when no flame is present. Check for pigpio initialization failure, then open 'flame_events.log' in append mode and verify the file handle is valid. In a main loop, poll the sensor every 500 ms; on each poll, log a timestamped line of the form 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS - Flame detected: YES|NO' to the log file and immediately flush it, and when a flame is detected (LOW), print 'FLAME DETECTED!' to the console to simulate a fire alarm. Install a SIGINT handler so Ctrl+C sets a flag that stops the loop cleanly, and on any exit path close the log file if open and call gpioTerminate(). Handle sensor read errors (gpioRead returning PI_BAD_GPIO) by logging an error line rather than a false positive.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that interfaces with an Omron D7S-0001 vibration sensor over I2C at slave address 0x53 on bus /dev/i2c-1, using the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface directly (open/read/ioctl) rather than wiringPi, to simulate a structural integrity monitoring system. The D7S-0001 exposes acceleration in registers 0x28-0x2D (X_LSB, X_MSB, Y_LSB, Y_MSB, Z_LSB, Z_MSB); combine each axis as signed 16-bit (MSB<<8 | LSB). Sample the sensor every 100 ms and log X, Y, and Z axis acceleration data to a CSV file named 'vibration_log.csv' with header 'Timestamp,X,Y,Z' and ISO-8601 UTC timestamps. Check every open/ioctl/read call, detect sensor-absent paths (e.g. an I2C read returning 0xFF or failing), and handle bus errors gracefully without crashing; if a read fails, print a diagnostic to stderr and skip that sample rather than terminating. Install a SIGINT handler so Ctrl+C cleanly closes the I2C file descriptor and the CSV file before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses libgpiod (v1.6+ API) to monitor a conveyor belt safety system by reading the digital output of two TI DRV5032 digital Hall-Effect sensors connected to GPIO17 and GPIO27, configured as inputs with internal pull-ups enabled via bias flags. Log timestamps with millisecond precision and the sensor states to 'conveyor_log.txt' every 50 ms, and if both sensors read logic 1 (triggered), halt the conveyor, simulated with a print statement. Include robust error handling for GPIO access (chip opening, line requests, reads) and log file I/O, and handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, releasing all libgpiod resources cleanly on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B running a 64-bit OS that interfaces with a GY-45 MMA8452Q 3-axis accelerometer over I2C using the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface (no third-party GPIO/I2C libraries such as wiringPi). The sensor's SA0 pin is tied high, so use I2C address 0x1D on bus /dev/i2c-1. Verify the sensor identity by reading the WHO_AM_I register (0x0D) and checking it equals 0x2A, printing an error and exiting if it does not match. Initialize the sensor by reading CTRL_REG1 (0x2A), clearing bit 0 to place it in standby mode, setting the data rate to 100 Hz (bits 3-5 = 0b010), and then setting bit 0 to switch to active mode. Continuously poll the accelerometer at roughly 100 Hz (10 ms loop interval), reading the six data registers (0x01-0x06) in a single I2C block read for atomic sampling, combining MSB/LSB and right-shifting by 4 to form signed 12-bit values, and compute the tilt angle of the X-axis relative to gravity using atan2(x, sqrt(y*y + z*z)). When the absolute tilt angle exceeds 45 degrees, log a timestamped line containing the raw 12-bit X, Y, Z values to fall_log.txt, opened once in append mode at startup. Handle all I2C syscall failures (open, ioctl, read, write) by printing strerror(errno) and exiting or skipping the iteration as appropriate. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that closes the I2C file descriptor and the log file before exiting, keeping the log file open for the program's lifetime and flushing after each entry rather than reopening it on every write.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that interfaces with an Adafruit LIS3MDL Triple-Axis Magnetometer over I2C on /dev/i2c-1 at address 0x1E, using the Linux i2c-dev ioctl interface for I2C access since libgpiod has no I2C API. Configure the sensor for continuous-conversion mode at 80 Hz ODR with high-performance mode on all axes (CTRL_REG1=0x70, CTRL_REG4=0x0C, CTRL_REG3=0x00), and verify the sensor is present by reading WHO_AM_I (0x0F) and checking it equals 0x3D. Continuously read the 6-byte little-endian X/Y/Z magnetic-field output registers starting at 0x28, apply fixed offset/scale calibration constants, convert to milliGauss using the +-4 gauss sensitivity of 0.146 mG/LSB, and append comma-separated X,Y,Z values to 'magnetic_log.txt' at 10 Hz. Check every I2C read/write for errors and retry initialization up to 3 times; handle SIGINT/SIGTERM cleanly by closing the I2C file descriptor and the log file, which should be opened once and flushed after each write. Include a simple metal-detector threshold alert printed to stderr when the total field magnitude exceeds 800 mG.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library over SPI channel 0 (CE0/GPIO8), 1 MHz clock, SPI Mode 0, to read acceleration data from an Analog Devices ADXL354B accelerometer. The ADXL354B outputs 20-bit signed acceleration data in 3 consecutive bytes per axis (XDATA at 0x08, YDATA at 0x0B, ZDATA at 0x0E); use the +-2g range sensitivity of 3.9 microg/LSB (0.0000039 g/LSB). SPI reads use bit 7 = 1 for read and bit 6 = 1 for multi-byte. Implement a proper device reset sequence: write 0x52 to the RESET register (0x1F), wait 1 ms, then set the measurement mode by clearing the RUN bit in POWER_CTL (0x2D), waiting for the STABLE bit in STATUS (0x04), then setting the RUN bit. Log X, Y, and Z axis readings with timestamps every 100 ms to a file named 'vibration_log.txt'. Handle SPI communication errors with retries, check sensor presence by reading PARTID (0x01, expected 0x1D), and implement graceful shutdown via SIGINT/SIGTERM with proper resource cleanup: close the SPI handle, close the file, and terminate pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library's spiOpen and spiXfer APIs (not deprecated wiringPi) to interface with an Analog Devices ADIS16362 IMU over SPI channel 0 (CE0/GPIO8), baud rate 1 MHz, SPI Mode 3 (active-high clock, sampled on trailing edge). The ADIS16362 read protocol sends the register address with the MSB set followed by a dummy byte, with the requested register's data returned on the next 16-bit transfer; implement a robust read function that sends the address, waits for the conversion, and retrieves the data, handling stall/error returns from spiXfer. Continuously read 3-axis gyroscope from X_GYRO=0x04, Y_GYRO=0x06, Z_GYRO=0x08 and 3-axis accelerometer from X_ACCL=0x0A, Y_ACCL=0x0C, Z_ACCL=0x0E, scaling with 0.05 deg/sec/LSB for gyroscope and 0.0025 g/LSB for accelerometer, sampling at approximately 100 Hz (10 ms delay between reads). Log timestamped readings to a comma-separated file 'imu_log.csv' starting with the header 'Timestamp,X_Gyro,Y_Gyro,Z_Gyro,X_Accel,Y_Accel,Z_Accel', using high-precision UNIX epoch timestamps (seconds.nanoseconds). Check pigpio initialization, SPI open, file open, and spiXfer return codes; if spiXfer fails, print an error to stderr and skip the logging iteration. Implement graceful shutdown via SIGINT (Ctrl+C) using a signal handler that safely closes the SPI handle, flushes and closes the log file, and calls gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the libgpiod library (not the deprecated sysfs interface, and not wiringPi) to read an E18-D80NK IR obstacle sensor connected to GPIO17. The E18-D80NK outputs LOW (0) when an obstacle is detected within its detection range, adjustable up to about 80 cm and configured here for roughly 30 cm, and HIGH (1) when the path is clear. Open the gpiochip device for GPIO17 on the Raspberry Pi 5 (gpiochip4) and request the line for input direction using modern libgpiod APIs such as gpiod_chip_open_by_name, gpiod_line_open, gpiod_line_request_input, and gpiod_line_get_value. Poll the sensor every 1 second; when an obstacle is detected (line reads LOW), trigger a simulated "self-parking" sequence logged to the console with timestamps ("Self-parking sequence started" / "completed"). Check all libgpiod calls, handle the case where the gpiochip or line is unavailable and exit gracefully, and handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) for clean shutdown, releasing the GPIO line and closing the chip on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses libgpiod (v2 API) to interface with two Keyes KY-032 IR obstacle avoidance sensors connected to GPIO17 and GPIO27 (physical pins 11 and 13, BCM numbering). The KY-032 output is active-low: the sensor reads 0 when an obstacle is detected and 1 when the path is clear. Use a single gpiochip and request both lines together for input, reading both lines in a single call via the libgpiod v2 bulk-read API gpiod_line_request_get_values. Poll both sensors every 100 ms and log the obstacle detection status to the console with a timestamp, simulating a basic collision avoidance system for a small robot, running in an infinite loop until interrupted. Check every libgpiod call, handle the case where the gpiochip or lines are unavailable, and ensure clean release of all resources on all exit paths including SIGINT (Ctrl+C). Compile cleanly with -Wall -Wextra against libgpiod >= 2.0.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the modern libgpiod library for SPI chip-select line control together with the Linux spidev interface for SPI communication (not the deprecated bcm2835 or wiringPi libraries) to periodically read gyroscope data from an Analog Devices ADIS16266 connected on SPI0 (CE0 on GPIO8), configured for SPI Mode 3, MSB first, at a 1 MHz clock speed. Initialize the SPI device (/dev/spidev0.0) and a libgpiod line for the CS pin, write to the MSC_CTRL register (0x24) to enable data ready mode, then periodically read the X, Y, and Z angular rate output registers (0x04, 0x06, 0x08) using the ADIS16266 two-transfer read protocol (send the address with the MSB set, then read 2 bytes). Convert the raw 16-bit signed values to angular rates using the scale factor of 0.02 deg/sec/LSB and log the results to the console every 100 ms. Include robust error handling: check all SPI and GPIO initialization calls, handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including SIGINT, running in a loop until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses only the pigpio C API, not wiringPi, to read accelerometer and gyroscope data from an STMicroelectronics LSM6DSR connected via I2C bus 1 at the 7-bit address 0x6B. Initialize the pigpio library and open the I2C bus, then verify the sensor is present by reading the WHO_AM_I register and checking it returns 0x6B. Configure the accelerometer for +-2g full-scale at 104 Hz (CTRL1_XL = 0x42) and the gyroscope for +-250 dps at 104 Hz (CTRL2_G = 0x42). Every 100 ms, burst-read 12 bytes starting at OUTX_L_G (0x22) covering gyro X/Y/Z then accel X/Y/Z, convert to physical units using gyro sensitivity mdps/LSB = 8.75 (i.e. 0.00875 dps/LSB) and accel sensitivity mg/LSB = 0.061 (i.e. 0.000061 g/LSB), and print one line to stdout. Handle all error paths: pigpio init failure, I2C open failure, WHO_AM_I mismatch, register write failures, and short or failed burst reads, printing to stderr and exiting non-zero; check every I2C call's return value and never use hard-coded sleeps that ignore errors. Install a SIGINT handler so Ctrl+C triggers a clean shutdown that closes the I2C handle and calls gpioTerminate() before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to read accelerometer and magnetometer data from an Adafruit FXOS8700 breakout board over I2C at address 0x1D on bus 1 (GPIO2/GPIO3 for SDA/SCL). Initialize the sensor into hybrid mode by configuring CTRL_REG1 (0x2A), CTRL_REG2 (0x2B), M_CTRL_REG1 (0x5B), and M_CTRL_REG2 (0x5C) so both the accelerometer and magnetometer produce data. Every 100 ms, read the 12-byte combined data block starting at register 0x01 (OUT_X_MSB), which contains 6 bytes of 14-bit left-aligned accelerometer data followed by 6 bytes of 16-bit magnetometer data, and log the raw X, Y, and Z values for both sensors to the console each cycle. Handle I2C communication errors robustly: check every pigpio I2C call, verify the sensor is present by reading the WHO_AM_I register (0x0D, expected value 0xC7) before initialization, and retry on transient read failures. Clean up all resources — close the I2C handle and terminate pigpio — on SIGINT/SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that interfaces with an ADXL345 accelerometer over I2C at address 0x53 using the Linux i2c-dev interface via /dev/i2c-1, not wiringPi, since libgpiod itself has no I2C API. Read X, Y, Z data from registers 0x32-0x37, calculate tilt angles using atan2, and log events with timestamps every 100 ms. Log tilt events exceeding a threshold of 30.0 degrees to '/var/log/tilt_events.log'. Include robust error handling for I2C communication failures, explicitly handling sensor-absent and bus-error paths, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including signal handling for Ctrl+C.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library, and no wiringPi, to monitor ambient noise levels via a KY-038 sound sensor connected to GPIO17 (physical pin 11). The KY-038 OUT pin is active-high and pulses when sound exceeds its onboard comparator threshold. Accept a single command-line argument — an integer threshold representing the minimum number of high-readings per 5-second window required to trigger an alert — and validate it, rejecting non-numeric or non-positive values. Continuously sample GPIO17 every 1 ms for 5 seconds, counting how many times the pin reads high; at the end of each 5-second window, print a timestamped ALERT to stdout if the high-reading count exceeds the threshold, otherwise print a normal status line. Run in a continuous loop until signaled to stop, with a 1-second pause between monitoring windows. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM gracefully, terminating pigpio and exiting cleanly, and check every pigpio call for failure (gpioInitialise, gpioSetMode), printing clear error messages to stderr on any failure.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the libgpiod C API, never wiringPi, to control two 12V electromagnetic door locks actuated by 5V active-HIGH relay modules driven via TIP120 transistors on GPIO17 (Door A) and GPIO27 (Door B), based on a randomly generated 6-digit security code. Initialize GPIO17 and GPIO27 as outputs, both defaulting to LOW (locks energized/closed); a HIGH signal de-energizes the relay and unlocks the corresponding door. Generate a random 6-digit code between 100000 and 999999 at startup and print it to stdout. In a loop, prompt the user to enter the code via stdin; if it matches, unlock Door A (GPIO17 HIGH) for 5 seconds, then re-lock it (LOW), log the successful entry to 'access_log.txt' as a CSV row 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,NNNNNN', and generate a new random code. If the code does not match, print 'Access denied' and continue; handle invalid non-numeric stdin input gracefully by clearing the buffer and re-prompting. Check every libgpiod call (chip open, line get, line request) and file open, printing meaningful errors to stderr and exiting non-zero on initialization failure. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that sets a volatile sig_atomic_t flag so the main loop exits cleanly; on exit, drive both GPIO outputs LOW (locked), release all libgpiod resources (lines and chip), and close any open file handles. Compile with: gcc -Wall -o door_access door_access.c -lgpiod.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the standard Linux /dev/i2c-1 ioctl interface, not the unmaintained bcm2835 library, to read illuminance from a BH1750FVI light sensor over I2C bus 1 (GPIO2/GPIO3). The sensor's ADDR pin is tied to GND, so the I2C address is 0x23. Write the One-Time High-Resolution Mode 2 command (0x21) to the sensor, wait for the maximum conversion time of 180 ms, then read 2 bytes of data and calculate the illuminance in lux using the formula: (raw_value * 5) / 6 (equivalent to raw_value / 1.2). Log the sensor readings to a file named 'light_log.txt', formatting each entry as 'Timestamp: <timestamp>, Lux: <lux_value>', continuously every 5 seconds until interrupted. The program must handle potential I2C write/read errors and sensor-absent paths (e.g., failing to open the bus or read bytes), and implement clean resource release on all exit paths, including signal handling for SIGINT (Ctrl+C).

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses pigpio for I2C and hardware PWM to implement a theremin using an MPR121 capacitive touch sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x5A. The program acts as a TCP server listening on port 12345; when a client sends a message starting with 'MOTION_DETECTED:' and containing the shared secret 'MySecretKey', the theremin plays tones for 5 seconds based on capacitive touch readings, using hardware PWM on GPIO18. Initialize the MPR121 with proper soft-reset and electrode configuration, and map the maximum electrode filtered data value to a frequency in the range 220-880 Hz using a logarithmic scale, sampling touch values every 20 ms during the 5-second playback window and logging each frequency to 'frequency_log.txt'. Handle errors for pigpio initialization, I2C open/read, and socket/bind/listen/accept. On SIGINT/SIGTERM, stop PWM, close I2C and sockets, and terminate pigpio cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that interfaces with an LSM303DLHC magnetometer via I2C bus 1 at default address 0x1E, connected to the physical SDA1/SCL1 pins, and controls an LED on GPIO17. Use libgpiod for GPIO/PWM control and the standard Linux I2C interface (/dev/i2c-1, ioctl) for sensor communication, not wiringPi. Initialize the magnetometer by writing 0x18 to CTRL_REG1_M (0x20) for 10 Hz continuous conversion, and read 6 bytes of data starting from OUT_X_L_M (0x08) in a single I2C block read. The program must read X, Y, Z magnetic field data, compute the magnitude of the Z-axis field, and adjust the LED brightness proportionally using hardware PWM, sampling every 100 ms in the main loop. Handle I2C errors (e.g., sensor absent, bus errors) gracefully by logging the error and skipping the sample without crashing, and implement clean resource release on SIGINT/SIGTERM by releasing the PWM, closing the I2C file descriptor, and closing any log files.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that implements a smart lighting system, using libgpiod to drive three 5V relay modules on BCM GPIO17, GPIO27, and GPIO22, and reads ambient light from a BH1750 sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x23 through the Linux i2c-dev ioctl interface. Configure the BH1750 for continuous high-resolution mode (0x10) and wait at least 120 ms for the first conversion; read the 2-byte lux value and compute lux = raw / 1.2. Drive the relays by lux thresholds: below 50 turn on the RED relay, 50-150 the GREEN relay, 150-300 the BLUE relay, and above 300 turn on all three. Every 1 second, log the timestamp, lux value, and relay states to lighting_log.txt. Check every I2C and file I/O call, handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths, and release all GPIO lines, the I2C file descriptor, and the log file on every exit path, including SIGINT and SIGTERM signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to independently control two DC motors driven by an L298N controller: Motor A on GPIO17 (IN1) and GPIO18 (IN2), Motor B on GPIO22 (IN3) and GPIO23 (IN4). Each motor is controlled from its own simulated ultrasonic distance sensor reading (range 10-100 cm, already sampled and passed as an argument — do not call random number generators inside the motor-control function). Map distance to a PWM duty cycle so closer obstacles drive higher speed (255 at 10 cm, 0 at 100 cm), clamped to [0,255], using a 1 kHz PWM frequency with a 0-255 range on the IN2/IN4 pins. Per motor, if distance is below 50 cm drive forward (IN1/IN3 high, IN2/IN4 PWM duty); if 50 cm or above, drive backward (IN1/IN3 low, IN2/IN4 PWM duty). Run the control loop every 100 ms. Check gpioInitialise() and every gpio call for failure, and ensure the motors stop and pigpio cleans up on every exit path, including SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program using the pigpio library on a Raspberry Pi to drive a 28BYJ-48 unipolar stepper motor through an L293D H-bridge, simulating an automatic door lock. Drive the coils in full-step (two-phase) mode with the standard 4-step sequence on BCM GPIO17, GPIO18, GPIO27, and GPIO22 (mapped to L293D inputs IN1-IN4), using a 2 ms inter-step delay. A momentary button on BCM GPIO24 (wired to ground, internal pull-up, active-low) rotates the motor 512 steps (a quarter turn) clockwise to lock; a momentary button on BCM GPIO23 (same wiring) rotates 512 steps counter-clockwise to unlock. Prevent re-triggering while a button is held down. Handle pigpio initialisation failure and check every GPIO configuration return code. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, de-energize the motor coils and release all pigpio resources before exiting. Print console feedback for lock and unlock actions and for exit events.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses an MPU-6050 accelerometer/gyroscope on I2C (SDA GPIO2, SCL GPIO3, bus /dev/i2c-1, address 0x68) to detect tilt and drive a PWM-controlled servo on GPIO18 (hardware PWM via sysfs at /sys/class/pwm/pwmchip2/pwm0) to adjust a miniature solar panel's angle. Access I2C through ioctl and linux/i2c-dev.h, with exponential-backoff retries on sensor-absent or bus-error paths. Log timestamped, comma-separated pitch, roll, and servo position values to solar_tracker.log. Release all resources cleanly on every exit path via SIGINT and SIGTERM signal handling. Do not use external networking or JSON libraries — limit the program to local sensor reading, PWM control, and file logging.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to control four relay-controlled lamp actuators on GPIO4, GPIO17, GPIO27, and GPIO22, simulating a smart home lighting system with a sunrise/sunset effect driven by a 24-hour schedule read from lighting_schedule.txt (format HH:MM:SS,relay_number,on/off). Check the schedule every second and, when the current time matches an entry, smoothly fade the lamp's brightness using PWM (100 Hz, 0-100 duty range) over a 1800-second (30-minute) transition. Handle file read errors, GPIO initialisation failures, and invalid schedule entries gracefully. Use SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling to turn off all relays and release GPIO resources cleanly on exit, and avoid calling non-reentrant functions such as fopen and localtime inside the signal handler.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to build a rudimentary theremin from an HC-SR04 ultrasonic distance sensor (trigger on GPIO23, echo on GPIO24) and a PWM buzzer on GPIO18. Linearly map distances from 2 cm to 30 cm to frequencies from 200 Hz to 2000 Hz, clamping the result to that range before applying it. Generate the 10 microsecond trigger pulse with gpioDelay and measure the echo pulse width with microsecond-precision gpioTick timing. Run the main loop at roughly 50 Hz with at least a 60 ms gap between measurements to avoid trigger/echo overlap. Handle pigpio initialisation and HC-SR04 read failures robustly, including sensor-absent and timeout paths, logging failures to stderr. On SIGINT, silence the buzzer and deinitialise pigpio before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to simulate a color-based proximity alert. Drive a common-anode RGB LED, with red, green, and blue elements on GPIO17, GPIO22, and GPIO27 respectively through current-limiting resistors, using pigpio hardware PWM at 1 kHz so the LED smoothly transitions between red, green, and blue based on a simulated proximity value in the range 0.0 to 1.0, generated internally (for example from a sine wave over time) rather than read from a network socket. Handle pigpio initialisation errors gracefully and check every GPIO operation. On every exit path, including SIGINT, turn off the LED and call gpioTerminate to release resources cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B to read angular velocity from an MPU-6050 gyroscope on I2C bus /dev/i2c-1 (SDA GPIO2, SCL GPIO3) at address 0x68, using the Linux i2c-dev kernel interface (open/ioctl/read on /dev/i2c-1) rather than wiringPi, which is deprecated. Wake the sensor by writing 0x00 to PWR_MGMT_1 (register 0x6B), then read the 6 bytes of gyroscope data starting at register 0x43 with a block read. Convert each signed 16-bit value to degrees/second using the ±250 deg/s sensitivity factor of 131.0 LSB/(deg/s). Every 100 ms, log a timestamped x, y, z reading to gyro_log.txt. Check the return value of every open, ioctl, read, and write call, handling sensor-absent paths, and close all file descriptors cleanly on SIGINT or SIGTERM. No network logging or configuration-file parsing is required.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to implement a musical doorbell. A button on GPIO17 (internal pull-up enabled, active-low) triggers playback of a custom melody stored in a const lookup table in flash memory, played through a piezo buzzer on GPIO18 (hardware PWM0) using gpioHardwarePWM() for tone generation at a 50% duty cycle for volume. Debounce the button with a minimum 50 ms gap between presses; a second press during playback must gracefully stop the melody. Check the return value of every pigpio call, including gpioInitialise, gpioSetMode, gpioSetISRFuncEx, and gpioHardwarePWM. The interrupt handler must not block — use a volatile flag checked by the main loop to control playback. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, stop the PWM, release all resources, and call gpioTerminate for a clean shutdown.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the libgpiod API (gpiod_line_request_input, gpiod_line_event_wait, gpiod_line_event_read) to read an SW-420 vibration sensor's active-high digital output on GPIO17 (physical pin 11), rather than the deprecated sysfs /sys/class/gpio interface. Poll for both rising and falling edges, using a poll timeout in milliseconds taken as a single command-line argument (default 1000 ms if omitted). Log every edge event with an ISO-8601 timestamp and the raw value (0 or 1) to vibration_events.log, opening the file once and flushing or fsyncing after each write rather than reopening it per event; handle file open/write errors gracefully without terminating. Implement a basic earthquake early-warning simulation: maintain a sliding window of the last 5 events, and if 3 or more of them read HIGH, print an EARTHQUAKE ALERT message with the timestamp to the console. Check every libgpiod call and syscall for errors, printing diagnostics to stderr. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that sets a volatile sig_atomic_t flag so the main loop exits cleanly, releasing the line and closing the log file.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads calibrated magnetic-field data from an LSM303DLHC magnetometer over I2C and logs it to a CSV file named mag_log.csv, using the Linux I2C-dev interface (/dev/i2c-1, linux/i2c-dev.h, ioctl-based SMBus reads/writes) rather than wiringPi, which is deprecated and unmaintained. The magnetometer's 7-bit I2C address is 0x1E, with SDA on physical pin 3 (GPIO2) and SCL on physical pin 5 (GPIO3). Configure continuous-conversion mode by writing 0x00 to MR_REG_M (register 0x02), and optionally set the output data rate to 15 Hz by writing 0x14 to CRA_REG_M (register 0x00). Read the six data registers 0x03-0x08 (X MSB, X LSB, Z MSB, Z LSB, Y MSB, Y LSB) and assemble them into signed 16-bit X, Y, and Z values. Apply hard-iron calibration offsets X_OFFSET=10, Y_OFFSET=-5, Z_OFFSET=20 to produce calibrated float values, then compute the compass heading in degrees from the calibrated X and Y values using atan2f, normalized to 0-360 degrees, and map it to one of eight compass directions (N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW), printing the direction and numeric heading to the console. Once per second, append a row to mag_log.csv with columns Timestamp, Calibrated X, Calibrated Y, Calibrated Z, Heading, writing a header row first if the file does not already exist. Check the return value of every open, ioctl, read, write, and fopen call; on an I2C read failure, print a diagnostic to stderr and skip that sample rather than crashing. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler so Ctrl+C cleanly closes the I2C file descriptor and the CSV file, freeing all resources on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library to toggle a 5V relay on GPIO17 via a TTP223 capacitive touch sensor on GPIO4. The TTP223 outputs HIGH (3.3 V) on touch and LOW when released; configure GPIO4 with a pull-down resistor. Debounce touches in software with a minimum 200 ms gap between registered touches inside the ISR callback, and on each valid touch toggle the relay and append a JSON object to relay_log.json in the form {"timestamp":"<ISO 8601>","relay_state":"ON|OFF"}. Check every pigpio call for errors and abort cleanly if gpioInitialise() or gpioSetISRFunc() fails. On SIGINT, turn the relay OFF, append a final OFF entry to the log, and call gpioTerminate() before exiting. Do not use any deprecated library such as wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the libgpiod library (not wiringPi, which is deprecated) to run a smart irrigation system controlling four 5V relay modules on BCM GPIO17, GPIO23, GPIO24, and GPIO25. Open the gpiochip once and request the four lines as outputs with an inactive (OFF) drive of 1, since the relays are active-low; do not call the setup function more than once. Every 10 seconds, generate a simulated soil-moisture value from 0 to 100 using rand(), seeded once at startup. If the moisture reading is below 30, sequentially activate each relay (drive the line to 0) for 5 seconds, then deactivate it (drive to 1), leaving a 1-second gap between relays. Log every activation with an ISO-8601 timestamp, relay number, and moisture level to irrigation_log.txt in append mode, flushing after each write. Check every libgpiod call and file operation for errors, printing diagnostics to stderr. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, deactivate all relays, release the lines, close the chip and the log file, and exit cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to run a miniature automated plant watering system with two SG90 servo motors: a water valve servo on GPIO17 (physical pin 11) and a directional nozzle servo on GPIO18 (physical pin 12), driven by simulated soil-moisture readings that cycle every second through the hardcoded values 20, 40, 60, 80, 100. Control both servos with gpioServo() using pulse widths in the 500-2500 microsecond range (500 us is about 0 degrees, 1500 us about 90 degrees, 2500 us about 180 degrees): the valve servo is closed at 0 degrees and open at 90 degrees, and the nozzle servo sweeps through 0, 45, 90, 135, and 180 degrees during watering. If the moisture reading is below the 50 threshold, open the valve to 90 degrees, sweep the nozzle through all five angles at 2 seconds per step, hold for 5 seconds, then close the valve to 0 degrees; if it is 50 or above, skip watering. After each cycle, wait 5 seconds before reading the next moisture value. Check the return value of gpioInitialise() and exit on failure. Retry each gpioServo() call up to 3 times with a 100 ms backoff on failure; abort the watering cycle if the valve fails to open, print a critical warning if it fails to close, and log an error and continue to the next angle if a nozzle position fails. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM using volatile sig_atomic_t flags: stop both servos with gpioServo(..., 0), call gpioTerminate(), and exit cleanly, never calling gpio functions before gpioInitialise() or after gpioTerminate() in the signal handler. Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B to read X, Y, and Z axis angular velocities from an MPU-6050 gyroscope on I2C bus 1 (GPIO2=SDA, GPIO3=SCL) at address 0x68, using the Linux I2C-dev interface (/dev/i2c-1 via linux/i2c-dev.h and sys/ioctl.h) instead of the deprecated wiringPi. Wake the sensor by writing 0x00 to PWR_MGMT_1 (register 0x6B), then read the 6 bytes of gyroscope data starting at GYRO_XOUT_H (register 0x43) with a burst read. Convert the raw 16-bit big-endian values to degrees/second using the ±250 deg/sec sensitivity factor of 131.0 LSB/(deg/s). Sample at 10 Hz and log each timestamped reading to gyro_log.txt in CSV format (timestamp, x, y, z). Check every I2C syscall, handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths, and ensure clean resource release — closing all file descriptors — on every exit path via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling.

Write a C program using the pigpio library on a Raspberry Pi to drive a 28BYJ-48 unipolar stepper motor through an L293D motor driver, simulating an automatic door lock with full-step (single-coil) excitation. Drive the coils on BCM GPIO4, GPIO17, GPIO27, and GPIO22 (mapped to L293D inputs IN1-IN4) with a 3 ms inter-step delay. Two momentary push-buttons use internal pull-ups: LOCK on BCM GPIO24 and UNLOCK on BCM GPIO23 (active-low). Pressing LOCK rotates the motor 512 steps clockwise (about a quarter turn); pressing UNLOCK rotates 512 steps counter-clockwise. Check the return value of gpioInitialise() and report an error on failure, and check every gpioWrite, gpioSetMode, and gpioSetPullUpDown return code. De-energize all coils after each rotation completes to reduce power consumption and motor heating. Handle SIGINT by de-energizing the coils and calling gpioTerminate(). Debounce button reads with a short delay so a single press does not trigger multiple rotations, and print clear console messages for lock and unlock actions and for errors.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B (64-bit, Bookworm) that reads distance from an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor once per second and logs the value in centimeters to distance_log.txt, using the libgpiod v2.x API (gpiod.h) rather than wiringPi, which is deprecated. Request the trigger line on BCM GPIO17 as output and the echo line on BCM GPIO18 as input with active-high polarity. Generate a 10 microsecond high pulse on the trigger, then measure the echo pulse width with a busy-wait loop using a 50 ms timeout for both the rising and falling edges; convert the pulse width to distance with distance_cm = duration_us * 0.01715 (speed of sound 343 m/s). On timeout or any libgpiod call failure, log "-1" to the file and print an error to stderr; also report GPIO initialisation failures to stderr. Open the log file once in append mode at startup and keep it open for the program's lifetime. Enforce a 60 ms minimum guard between measurements to avoid false echoes. Handle SIGINT/SIGTERM by releasing all libgpiod resources and closing the log file. Assume the HC-SR04's 5 V echo output is reduced to 3.3 V by a voltage divider or level shifter before reaching the Pi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B implementing a proximity-based automated door system using a VL53L1X time-of-flight sensor on I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x29, with the pigpio library used for both I2C and GPIO control. Perform a software reset of the VL53L1X (register 0x0000 = 0x00), then initialise it by setting the ranging mode and starting continuous ranging (register 0x0080 = 0x01). Poll the sensor every 100 ms: check the interrupt status register 0x0044 for data readiness, then read the 16-bit distance result from registers 0x0096 (MSB) and 0x0097 (LSB). Log the current distance to stdout each cycle, and drive a relay on BCM GPIO18 HIGH to simulate opening the door when the distance is 50 cm or less, otherwise LOW. Check every pigpio and I2C return value, handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths, and log all errors to stderr. On SIGINT, close the I2C handle, set the relay LOW, and terminate pigpio for a clean shutdown.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ to read angular velocity from an MPU-6050 gyroscope on the hardware I2C bus (GPIO2/SDA, GPIO3/SCL) at address 0x68, using the Linux i2c-dev ioctl interface on /dev/i2c-1 — libgpiod has no I2C API, so it cannot be used for this, and wiringPi is deprecated. Initialise the sensor by waking it from sleep (PWR_MGMT_1, register 0x6B) and setting the gyroscope full-scale range to ±250 dps (GYRO_CONFIG, register 0x1B). Continuously read the 6 bytes of gyroscope data starting at register 0x43, convert the raw signed 16-bit big-endian values to degrees/second using the 131.0 LSB/dps sensitivity factor, and log the x, y, and z axis readings to the console. Check every I2C read/write syscall, handling sensor-absent or bus-error paths gracefully, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths using SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the libgpiod v1 API to control four 5V relay modules on BCM GPIO17, GPIO18, GPIO27, and GPIO22 (physical pins 11, 12, 13, 15), rather than the deprecated sysfs /sys/class/gpio interface or wiringPi. Open gpiochip0 and request all four lines as outputs with active-low semantics, setting all lines HIGH (inactive) at startup. Simulate an automated plant watering system that activates each relay sequentially for 5 seconds every 86400 seconds (24 hours), starting immediately on launch, and log each watering cycle's start time in 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS' format to watering_log.txt. Run the main loop on a 60-second polling interval. Check every libgpiod call and file I/O operation for errors, including the case where the GPIO chip cannot be opened. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that releases all GPIO lines, closes the chip, and exits cleanly. Compile with gcc -o watering watering.c -lgpiod.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library (rather than the deprecated wiringPi) to control four SRD-05VDC relay modules on BCM GPIO17, GPIO18, GPIO27, and GPIO22 (equivalent to wiringPi pins 0, 1, 2, 3), simulating a smart lighting 'sunrise' effect that gradually raises light intensity over 30 minutes using hardware PWM to simulate dimming. Run the sunrise simulation in 1-second steps, incrementing the duty cycle progressively across all four relays simultaneously, using a 1 kHz PWM frequency with duty cycles from 0 to 255. Check the return value of gpioInitialise(), verify each GPIO pin's mode setup, and handle PWM initialisation failures gracefully. Log every event with a timestamp to smart_lighting.log. Implement clean resource release on all exit paths, including SIGINT and SIGTERM signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library (not wiringPi) for both I2C and GPIO to read angular velocity from a single MPU-6050 gyroscope on I2C bus 1 (address 0x68, GPIO2=SDA, GPIO3=SCL). Initialise the sensor by writing 0x00 to PWR_MGMT_1 (register 0x6B) to wake it, 0x07 to SMPLRT_DIV (register 0x19) for a 1 kHz sample rate, and 0x00 to GYRO_CONFIG (register 0x1B) for the ±250 deg/s full-scale range (131 LSB/deg/s sensitivity); do not configure the accelerometer. Verify the WHO_AM_I register (0x75) reads 0x68 during initialisation to confirm the sensor is present. At 20 Hz (a 50 ms period), read the 6 bytes of gyroscope data starting at GYRO_XOUT_H (register 0x43), convert the signed 16-bit big-endian values to degrees/second, and store each reading with its timestamp in a 100-entry in-memory circular buffer. Turn on an LED on GPIO17 whenever the absolute value of any axis exceeds 250 deg/s, and turn it off when all axes drop below that threshold. Check every pigpio call for errors: if I2C initialisation fails, print an error and exit; if a read fails, attempt re-initialisation up to 3 times before exiting. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, close the I2C handle, set the GPIO low, and call gpioTerminate() for a clean shutdown.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B to read X, Y, and Z axis angular rates from an MPU-9250 gyroscope over SPI, using the standard Linux spidev interface with libgpiod for chip-select control rather than the unmaintained bcm2835 library. Open /dev/spidev0.0 and configure SPI at 1 MHz, mode 0, 8 bits per word, MSB first. Manually control chip select on GPIO8 (CE0) via libgpiod (/dev/gpiochip0, line offset 8), asserting it LOW during transfers and HIGH otherwise. Every 10 ms, read gyroscope data from registers 0x43-0x48 (GYRO_XOUT_H through GYRO_ZOUT_L) as a single 6-byte burst, and convert the raw 16-bit two's-complement values to degrees per second using a scale factor of 131.0 for the ±250 dps range. Log each reading with an ISO-8601 timestamp including nanoseconds to gyro_log.txt in CSV format: timestamp,x_rate,y_rate,z_rate. Retry SPI communication errors up to 3 times; on persistent failure, log to stderr and continue. Handle file write errors gracefully, and check every system and library call. Clean up the SPI handle, the GPIO chip-select line, and the log file on SIGINT/SIGTERM. The program should run indefinitely until interrupted.

Handle SPI initialisation failures and sensor read failures (check for zero or invalid data). On SIGINT (Ctrl+C), print the entire circular buffer as CSV with columns Timestamp, X, Y, Z, then release the SPI handle and GPIO resources on every exit path. The program should simulate a basic stability monitoring system.

prompt: Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library (not wiringPi) — pigpio has no support for the Raspberry Pi 5's RP1 I/O controller, so the earlier Pi 4 Model B is used instead — to read tilt from an MPU-6050 accelerometer/gyroscope on I2C bus 1 at address 0x68. Wake the sensor by writing 0x00 to PWR_MGMT_1 (register 0x6B) and set the accelerometer full-scale range to ±2g by writing 0x00 to ACCEL_CONFIG (register 0x1C), verifying successful configuration. Every 100 ms, read the 6 bytes of raw accelerometer data from registers 0x3B-0x40, and compute roll = atan2(y, z) * 180/pi and pitch = atan2(-x, sqrt(y^2 + z^2)) * 180/pi. Turn on an LED on GPIO21 if the absolute roll exceeds 45 degrees or the absolute pitch exceeds 45 degrees, otherwise turn it off. Log each reading to tilt_log.txt in CSV format with a timestamp (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS), roll, and pitch, and print roll and pitch to the console each cycle. Check the I2C open, sensor initialisation, and every read operation; on a sensor read failure, log the error and continue without crashing. On SIGINT (Ctrl+C), turn off the LED, close the I2C handle, and terminate pigpio, with signal handling and resource cleanup on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ to interface with a Si1145 optical biometric sensor (assumed register-compatible with the Si1182-A-GM) over I2C, using the Linux I2C-dev interface (/dev/i2c-1, ioctl, read/write) for the sensor and libgpiod (gpiod_line_set_value, etc.) for GPIO — not wiringPi and not pigpio. The sensor is at I2C address 0x5A (8-bit). Read the 2-byte little-endian ambient-light value from register 0x20 and the 2-byte little-endian proximity value from register 0x22 every 100 ms. Log each timestamped reading in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS,AmbientLight:XXXX,Proximity:XXXX' to biometric_log.txt in append mode. If the proximity value exceeds 100, set GPIO17 high to simulate a presence-detected LED; otherwise set it low. Handle I2C communication errors with up to 3 retries and a 10 ms delay between attempts. Install SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handlers for graceful cleanup: close the I2C file descriptor, close the log file, and turn off the LED.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library for SPI and GPIO (not wiringPi) to read angular rate data from an Analog Devices ADXRS290 dual-axis gyroscope on SPI channel 0 (CE0, GPIO8) at a 1 MHz clock, SPI mode 0 (CPOL=0, CPHA=0). The X and Y axis angular-rate registers are at addresses 0x02 and 0x04; each returns 16-bit two's-complement data, high byte first. To read a register, send its address OR'd with 0x80 (the read bit) followed by a dummy byte — the response is the second byte of the transfer. The sensitivity is 200 LSB/deg/s. Sample both axes at approximately 100 Hz (a 10 ms delay between samples) and log each sample to gyro_data.csv with columns: timestamp (seconds since epoch, microsecond precision), X rate (raw int16), and Y rate (raw int16). If a read fails, attempt to reinitialise SPI up to 3 times before exiting. Check every pigpio call (gpioInitialise, spiOpen, spiXfer) and file operation for errors. Use a SIGINT handler to cleanly close SPI, flush and close the file, and terminate pigpio, releasing all resources on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library to detect seismic activity with two Omron D7E-2 tilt sensors on BCM GPIO23 and GPIO24. The D7E-2 is a normally-open mechanical tilt switch that closes to ground when tilted beyond about 60 degrees; wire each sensor between its GPIO pin and 3.3V with a 10 kOhm pull-down resistor to ground, so the GPIO reads HIGH when tilted. Register edge-triggered pigpio callbacks for both rising and falling edges on each sensor. When both sensors simultaneously read HIGH for a continuous duration of at least 500 milliseconds, trigger an alert by setting GPIO17 HIGH for 2 seconds, then LOW. Log each seismic event to seismic_events.txt with an ISO-8601-style timestamp, e.g. '2024-01-15 14:30:00 - Seismic event detected!'. Check pigpio initialisation, the log file open, and callback registration for errors. Install SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handlers that close the log file, set the alert pin LOW, and terminate pigpio. The program should run indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that reads an Analog Devices ADXRS290 dual-axis MEMS gyroscope over the hardware SPI0 bus (CE0 on GPIO8, SCLK on GPIO11, MOSI on GPIO10, MISO on GPIO9) using only the pigpio library, not wiringPi. Continuously read the 16-bit two's-complement X-axis angular-rate register (RATE_XL at address 0x02 and RATE_XH at address 0x03), combine the bytes, and convert to degrees per second using the 200 LSB/deg/s sensitivity. For each SPI read, set the MSB (bit 7) of the register address to 1 to indicate a read, transmit the address, and read the data payload, using a 1 MHz SPI clock and mode 0 (CPOL=0, CPHA=0). Timestamp each reading with clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC) and store it in a thread-safe, in-memory circular buffer with a capacity of 100 entries. If the absolute angular velocity exceeds a threshold of 20.0 deg/s, turn on an LED on GPIO17 as a visual warning, turning it off again once the rate drops back below the threshold. Check the return values of all pigpio initialisation and SPI transfer calls, and on SIGINT or SIGTERM exit gracefully with proper resource cleanup: close SPI, turn off the LED, and terminate pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W implementing a 'smart sunset simulator' with three relay-controlled dimmable lamps on GPIO17, GPIO18, and GPIO27 (physical pins 11, 12, 13), using the pigpio library's hardware PWM rather than the sysfs PWM interface. Accept a single command-line argument: the total fade duration in seconds (integer, 1-3600). Fade each lamp sequentially from full brightness (100% PWM duty cycle) to off (0%) over the specified duration, with each lamp starting its fade only after the previous one completes, using a PWM range of 0-255 at 100 Hz. Validate the user-supplied duration and check every pigpio initialisation call. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM gracefully by turning off all lamps and releasing resources, ensuring proper cleanup on every exit path. Print status messages at startup, during each lamp's fade, and upon completion or termination.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using libgpiod (not wiringPi, which is deprecated) to drive four 5V relay modules on BCM GPIO17, GPIO22, GPIO23, and GPIO24 as a traffic light simulator. The relays are active-low (LOW turns a relay ON, HIGH turns it OFF). Cycle through the states red (10 seconds), red+yellow (2 seconds), green (10 seconds), and yellow (3 seconds), then repeat indefinitely. Check libgpiod initialisation, the chip open, the line request, and every GPIO operation for errors. Use SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling to gracefully release all GPIO lines and exit. Print each state transition to stdout. The program should run indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B using the pigpio library — chosen because pigpio has no support for the Raspberry Pi 5's RP1 I/O controller — to control a 5V relay on GPIO17, triggered by a capacitive touch sensor MPR121 on I2C bus 1 at address 0x5A. The relay simulates a light switch: touching electrode 0 toggles it on or off. Initialise pigpio and set GPIO17 as output, default LOW. Open the I2C device at address 0x5A on bus 1 and configure the MPR121 by writing: reset (register 0x80 = 0x63), stop mode (0x5E = 0x00), enable electrode 0 (0x5D = 0x01), touch threshold (0x41 = 0x0A), release threshold (0x42 = 0x08), debounce (0x5B = 0x21), charge time (0x5C = 0x0D), and run mode (0x5E = 0x0D). Read the touch status from registers 0x00 (LSB) and 0x01 (MSB) every 10 ms, debouncing touch events with a 100 ms delay. Log all I2C, GPIO, and configuration errors with timestamps to touch_relay.log. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to cleanly close the I2C handle, the GPIO, and the log file. Use only pigpio functions, not wiringPi, and check every initialisation and I2C operation for errors, logging and exiting gracefully on failure.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the libgpiod GPIO interface — not the deprecated sysfs /sys/class/gpio interface, and not wiringPi — to monitor a KY-026 flame sensor's digital output on GPIO17 (active-low: LOW means flame detected). When flame is detected, activate a buzzer on GPIO18 and an LED on GPIO23; both remain active for as long as flame is detected and turn off once it clears. Debounce the sensor reading with three consecutive reads at 50 ms intervals. Log each flame-detection event with a timestamp and the message 'Flame Detected' to flame_log.txt. Implement robust error handling for all GPIO operations, release all resources on any error exit path, and handle SIGINT/SIGTERM for graceful cleanup by releasing the GPIO lines and closing the log file. The program simulates a basic fire alarm.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pigpio library to control two 12V push-pull solenoids connected through TIP120 Darlington transistors to GPIO17 and GPIO27, simulating a simple pneumatic dispensing system. Initialise pigpio, handling initialisation failure by printing an error and exiting, and configure GPIO17 and GPIO27 as outputs with error checking. On each dispense cycle, activate solenoid 1 for half of a 1000 ms total dispense duration, then activate solenoid 2 for the remaining half, then deactivate both, using gpioDelay() (microseconds) for timing; repeat the dispense every 5 seconds in a continuous loop. Log each dispense event, with timestamp, solenoid pins, and duration in milliseconds, to dispense_log.txt, handling file open failures. Each function should return 0 on success and non-zero on failure, with main checking every return value and printing error messages to stderr. Register a SIGINT handler to gracefully deactivate both solenoids, terminate pigpio, and exit on Ctrl+C. Compile with -lpigpio.

Develop a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that controls two DC motors via an L298N dual H-bridge using only the pigpio library (gpioInitialise, gpioSetMode, gpioPWM, gpioWrite, gpioDelay, gpioTerminate — no wiringPi or other deprecated API). Motor A uses GPIO17 (forward) and GPIO18 (backward); Motor B uses GPIO22 (forward) and GPIO23 (backward); the L298N's enable pins ENA (GPIO24) and ENB (GPIO25) must be held HIGH to allow PWM control, with all motor speeds clamped to +/-255. Simulate a self-balancing robot: an internal PID controller (Kp=1.0, Ki=0.01, Kd=0.1) generates motor commands every 50 ms from a simulated tilt error (a random float between -10.0 and 10.0 degrees). Also simulate an ultrasonic distance sensor returning a random value between 2.0 and 400.0 cm; if the distance is below 20 cm, reverse both motors at 50% speed for obstacle avoidance. Handle pigpio initialisation failure by printing an error and returning 1; handle log file open failure by printing an error, terminating pigpio, and returning 1; on an invalid motor character, log the error and skip. On SIGINT, stop the motors, close the log file, and terminate pigpio gracefully. Log every control cycle to balance_log.txt with columns: timestamp (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS), tilt_error, distance, motor_a_speed, and motor_b_speed.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library (not wiringPi, which is deprecated) to toggle a 5V relay on GPIO17 (physical pin 11) using a TTP223 capacitive touch sensor on GPIO4 (physical pin 7), simulating a smart light switch: each touch toggles the relay on or off. The TTP223 outputs logic HIGH when touched; assume an external pull-down resistor, or configure the internal pull-down via pigpio. The relay is active-high, energized when GPIO17 is HIGH. Debounce each touch with a delay of at least 50 ms after detection. Check every pigpio initialisation call and GPIO operation, handling sensor-absent or bus-error conditions gracefully, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling. The program should run indefinitely until terminated by Ctrl+C.

Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ using the pigpio library (not wiringPi) to implement a 'mood light' driven by ambient noise from ALSA audio capture. Drive a common-cathode RGB LED on GPIO17 (red), GPIO18 (green), and GPIO27 (blue), each with a current-limiting resistor, using pigpio software PWM (gpioPWM) for smooth color control. Configure ALSA to capture from the 'default' device at 8000 Hz, 16-bit signed little-endian, 1 channel, with a period size of 1024 frames. Continuously read samples, compute the RMS amplitude, and map it to RGB PWM values using a non-linear transition — cool colors for low amplitude, warm colors for high amplitude. Accept an optional command-line sensitivity-scaling argument (default 1.0, must be positive). Check every pigpio and ALSA call: recover from buffer overruns (EPIPE) with snd_pcm_prepare, and from a suspended state (ESTRPIPE) with snd_pcm_resume. Include a 10 ms delay between updates, print status messages to stdout and errors to stderr, and release all resources — pigpio, ALSA, and allocated memory — on exit via SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handlers. Gate ALSA support behind an ALSA_AVAILABLE compile-time macro: when ALSA is unavailable, simulate the audio input with a sine-wave amplitude so the mood light still cycles through colors, and ensure all exit paths remain clean with no resource leaks in either mode.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod library to implement a sunrise/sunset lighting simulator controlling four independent 5V relay modules connected to lamps. The relays are active-low and wired to physical pins 11, 13, 15, and 17 (BCM GPIO17, GPIO27, GPIO22, GPIO23). Cycle repeatedly and indefinitely through four phases: sunrise, a gradual brightness increase over 1 hour; daytime, full brightness for 6 hours; sunset, a gradual brightness decrease over 1 hour; and nighttime, off for 14.4 hours. Simulate brightness with PWM-like relay toggling rather than true PWM, using an increasing duty cycle during sunrise and a decreasing duty cycle during sunset, with all four lamps running the same phase simultaneously. Use only the libgpiod functions gpiod_chip_open_by_name, gpiod_line_get, gpiod_line_request_output, gpiod_line_set_value, gpiod_line_release, and gpiod_chip_close. Handle initialization failures from gpiod_chip_open_by_name and gpiod_line_request_output with clear error messages and a graceful exit. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, turn off all relays and release GPIO resources cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to detect motion with a Keyes KY-033 IR Obstacle Avoidance Sensor on GPIO 17 (physical pin 11), which outputs an active-low digital LOW signal when an obstacle is detected. On motion detection, execute raspivid to record a 5-second video saved to /home/pi/videos/ with a timestamp-based filename such as 20250321_143022.h264, and log each event with an ISO 8601 timestamp to /home/pi/logs/motion_log.txt. Implement debouncing with a 200 ms minimum interval between triggers. Handle errors gracefully by checking pigpio initialization, file operations, and system command execution. Install a SIGINT signal handler for clean shutdown that closes the log file and terminates pigpio, and keep the program running continuously until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to read X, Y, and Z angular velocities from an MPU-6050 gyroscope over I2C bus 1 at address 0x68 (AD0 pin low), for a basic vibration monitoring system. Initialize the sensor by writing 0x00 to register 0x6B to wake it, 0x07 to register 0x19 to set the sample rate divider to 125 Hz, and 0x00 to register 0x1B to set the gyroscope full-scale range to ±250°/s. Read the raw signed 16-bit gyroscope values from registers 0x43-0x48 (X_H, X_L, Y_H, Y_L, Z_H, Z_L) using a combined I2C block read, and convert them to degrees per second using a sensitivity of 131.0 LSB/(°/s). Sample at 100 Hz (10 ms interval) and log each reading to gyro_log.csv with columns timestamp (Unix epoch seconds with millisecond precision), X_degps, Y_degps, Z_degps. On a read failure, attempt sensor re-initialization (re-wake and re-configure) up to 3 times before logging an error and continuing. Check every pigpio call (gpioInitialise, i2cOpen, i2cWriteByteData, i2cReadI2CBlockData). Use a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler to close the log file and release the I2C handle, and run indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to control four SainSmart 5V relay modules on BCM GPIO pins 4, 17, 27, and 22 for a simulated smart greenhouse irrigation system. Each relay corresponds to one irrigation zone, and a simulated moisture sensor using rand() % 101 produces readings from 0 to 100 every 5 seconds, with the random generator seeded from time(NULL). If a zone's reading is below 30, drive its relay LOW to activate it, since the relays are active-low; otherwise drive it HIGH to deactivate it. Append each sensor reading, relay state, and a timestamp to irrigation_log.txt. Check pigpio initialization, the log file open, and every GPIO operation. On SIGINT or any error, safely deactivate all relays (drive HIGH), close the log file, and terminate pigpio, installing the handler with signal().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to read accelerometer data from an Analog Devices ADXL345 over I2C at address 0x53. Configure the sensor for ±2g range with full resolution by writing 0x0B to the DATA_FORMAT register (0x31), and enable measurement mode by writing 0x08 to the POWER_CTL register (0x2D). Every 100 ms, read 6 bytes starting from the DATAX0 register (0x32) for the X, Y, Z axis data, and convert the raw signed 16-bit values to g-force using a scale factor of 256 LSB/g. Detect a freefall event when all three axes have an absolute value below 0.2g for a continuous 0.5 seconds, confirmed by reading twice with a 0.5 second delay. On a confirmed freefall, drive GPIO27 high to simulate an alarm, hold it for 5 seconds, then set it low. Log each freefall event to freefall.log in CSV format with a timestamp (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS) and x, y, z values to 3 decimal places. Handle I2C errors by printing to stderr and continuing operation, checking every pigpio and I2C call. Use a SIGINT handler to close the I2C handle, set GPIO low, and terminate pigpio.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to measure distance with an interrupt-driven HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor, TRIG on GPIO4 and ECHO on GPIO18 (BCM numbering). Send a 10 µs trigger pulse every 200 ms and measure the echo pulse width using rising-edge and falling-edge interrupt callbacks, correctly handling wrap-around of the 32-bit tick counter, which wraps roughly every 71.6 minutes. If the echo pulse width exceeds 23200 µs (about 4 meters, the sensor's maximum range) or no echo arrives within 100 ms of the trigger, discard the reading. Log each valid distance measurement in centimeters with a nanosecond-precision timestamp to distance_log.txt in CSV format: timestamp_ns,distance_cm. Protect the shared pulse-timing variables, which are updated from interrupt context, with a mutex. Handle pigpio initialization failure, file open failure, invalid pulse widths, and sensor timeouts. Use a SIGINT handler to cancel callbacks, close the file, terminate pigpio, and destroy the mutex, and run the measurement loop indefinitely.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the pigpio library to read acceleration data from an Adafruit LIS3DH accelerometer over I2C bus 1 at address 0x18, implementing a basic fall detection system that triggers a buzzer on GPIO17. Initialize pigpio and I2C with error checking, and configure the LIS3DH for a 100 Hz data rate and ±2g full scale by writing 0x77 to CTRL_REG1 and 0x00 to CTRL_REG4. Continuously read 16-bit signed acceleration values starting from register OUT_X_L (0x28), converting to g using a sensitivity of 16384 LSB/g. Detect freefall when the acceleration magnitude drops below 0.2g, then detect impact when it exceeds 1.5g; on impact, activate the buzzer for 1 second. Accept optional command-line freefall and impact thresholds. Handle I2C communication failures with up to 3 retries and perform graceful cleanup on SIGINT. Handle sensor absence and bus errors robustly, and ensure resources are released on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to precisely control two 28BYJ-48 stepper motors, each driven through a ULN2003 board, simulating a basic CNC plotter that draws a simple square. Motor 1 (X-axis) uses IN1=GPIO4, IN2=GPIO17, IN3=GPIO27, IN4=GPIO22; Motor 2 (Y-axis) uses IN1=GPIO5, IN2=GPIO6, IN3=GPIO13, IN4=GPIO19. Assume the 28BYJ-48's 1/64 gear ratio gives 2048 steps per revolution, use a 1000 microsecond step delay, and drive the coils with a 4-step wave drive (single-coil excitation) sequence. Draw a square with 50 mm sides using a conversion factor of 10 steps per mm. Set all GPIO pins as outputs, checking the return of every gpioWrite and gpioSetMode call, and check pigpio initialization. Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) to safely stop both motors and release resources, handle any motor movement failures gracefully, and set all GPIO pins low before termination.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the pigpio library to read X, Y, and Z acceleration data from a single Adafruit LIS3DH accelerometer over I2C at address 0x18 (overridable via a -a hex argument, valid range 0x08-0x77). Configure the sensor for ±2g range, high-resolution mode (12-bit left-justified), and 100 Hz output data rate by writing 0x57 to CTRL_REG1 and 0x88 to CTRL_REG4. Read acceleration at 10 Hz (100 ms interval), computing g as the 16-bit signed raw value shifted right 4 bits, then scaled by 0.0009765625 (2g / 2048). If the absolute acceleration on any axis exceeds a user-defined threshold in g (default 2.0g, overridable via a -t float argument), log the event with timestamp and axis values to /var/log/high_acceleration.log, then immediately trigger a system shutdown via `sudo shutdown -h now`. Use the pigpio I2C functions i2cOpen, i2cReadI2CBlockData, and i2cWriteI2CBlockData, but use i2cWriteByteData for single-byte register writes since i2cWriteI2CBlockData returns 0 on success rather than a byte count. Support only one sensor. Handle I2C open/configuration errors with cleanup and exit, handle sensor read errors gracefully by returning zeros and continuing, and validate the I2C address range (0x08-0x77) and threshold (greater than 0) from the command line. Register a SIGINT handler that closes I2C and terminates pigpio, and allow a graceful exit with code 0 when pigpio initialization or I2C open fails in a non-hardware environment.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the libgpiod API to autonomously navigate a line-following robot using a SunFounder 3-Way Tracking Sensor (IR reflectance, digital GPIO). Sensor pins are LEFT=GPIO4, CENTER=GPIO17, RIGHT=GPIO27, where 0 means a line is detected and 1 means no line; an alert pin on GPIO22 drives an active-high LED or buzzer. Poll the sensors every 10 ms and log each reading (left, center, right) into a circular buffer of size 5. If the center sensor reads 'no line' for 5 consecutive readings, drive GPIO22 HIGH for 2 seconds as an alert. Implement line-following logic: move forward when the center sensor detects a line, turn left when the left sensor detects a line, turn right when the right sensor detects a line, and stop when all three sensors read 'no line'; motor control functions may be placeholders. Check every libgpiod initialization and line-request return value, handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths, and ensure clean resource release on every exit path via SIGINT and SIGTERM handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to read magnetic field data from a Silicon Labs Si7210 Hall effect sensor over I2C bus 1 at its default address 0x30, and trigger a relay on GPIO 17 (active high) when the field strength exceeds a 5.0 mT threshold, sampling every 100 ms. Perform a one-shot measurement by writing 0x01 to register 0xC1 to start a conversion, polling register 0xC1 until it reads 0x00, then reading 2 bytes from register 0xC0 (byte 0 LSB, byte 1 MSB) and combining them into a signed 16-bit value: field_raw = (msb << 8) | lsb. Convert to milliTesla units of 0.01 mT with field_mT_x100 = field_raw * 25 / 1000, and compare against threshold * 100. If register 0xC1 does not clear after 50 poll attempts, log a timeout error and skip the cycle. Check every pigpio call (gpioInitialise, i2cOpen, i2cReadByte, i2cWriteByte, i2cReadByteData, i2cWriteByteData); if i2cOpen fails, log the error and exit, and on any read/write failure, log the error, deactivate the relay, and retry on the next cycle. Append timestamped entries in ISO 8601 format to magnetic_events.txt for every field reading, relay state change, and error. Install a SIGINT handler that closes the I2C handle, deactivates the relay, terminates pigpio, and logs the shutdown.
