Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library, not wiringPi, to interface with two Sensirion SLF3S-1300F liquid flow sensors (40 ml/min version) on I2C bus 1: sensor 1 at address 0x08 and sensor 2 at 0x09. Initialize pigpio and open both I2C handles with flags=0, checking for errors and cleaning up partially-initialized resources on failure. Send the SLF3S start-measurement command (bytes 0x36, 0x08) to each sensor and verify the write returns 0, aborting with full cleanup on failure. Configure GPIO 18 (BCM) as an output and initialize it low (de-energized), checking the return code. In a 100 ms polling loop, read 3 bytes (2 data + 1 CRC-8) from each sensor and validate the CRC-8 (polynomial 0x31, init 0xFF, no final XOR); on a read error or CRC mismatch, log a warning to stderr and skip that cycle without updating the relay. Convert each signed 16-bit big-endian raw value to ml/min using the scale factor 1/1500.0. If both reads succeed and either sensor reports flow below 5.0 ml/min, energize GPIO 18 (active-high relay, write 1); de-energize (write 0) when both sensors are at or above 5.0 ml/min. Log every successful cycle's flow rates with millisecond timestamps to flow_log.txt in append mode, flushing after each write. Install a single SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that sets a volatile flag so the main loop can exit cleanly; on shutdown, de-energize the relay, close both I2C handles if open, call gpioTerminate(), and print a shutdown message. The code must compile cleanly with gcc -Wall -Wextra.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the pigpio library to implement a single-process rain-actuated window controller. A Seeed Studio Rain Sensor v1.0 on GPIO 17 (BCM), configured as input with a pull-up, pulls its DO pin LOW when rain is detected and HIGH when dry; poll it every 200 ms. An L298N drives the window-closing DC motor via ENA on GPIO 22, IN1 on GPIO 23, and IN2 on GPIO 24 (all BCM). Only trigger the close-window sequence on a rising-edge dry-to-wet transition, never re-triggering while rain persists: set ENA HIGH, IN1 HIGH, IN2 LOW, hold for 5 seconds, then set ENA LOW and both IN1/IN2 LOW to stop, verifying each gpioWrite call. After completing the sequence, suppress further triggers until the sensor reads dry for at least 3 consecutive polls (about 600 ms). Check gpioInitialise()'s return value, logging and exiting on failure, and check every gpioWrite return code, logging warnings on failure. Log via syslog (facility LOG_USER, identifier "rain_window") using LOG_INFO for startup, rain detected, motor start/stop, and shutdown, and LOG_ERR/LOG_WARNING for failures. Implement everything in a single process with one main loop, with no fork(). Use gpioDelay() or usleep(), never busy-waiting, for the 200 ms poll interval and the 5-second motor run. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown: stop the motor (all GPIOs LOW), call gpioTerminate(), close syslog, and exit cleanly.

Write a C program that uses the pigpio library to control a door-lock servo on a Raspberry Pi. The servo is connected to GPIO 18 (physical pin 12, BCM 18). Two momentary push-buttons are wired to GPIO 21 (BCM) and GPIO 22 (BCM), each connecting its pin to ground when pressed, so internal pull-ups must be enabled. Pressing the GPIO 21 button drives the servo to the locked position with a 2000 µs pulse width; pressing the GPIO 22 button drives it to the unlocked position with a 1000 µs pulse width. Check the return value of gpioInitialise() and exit with an error message on failure, and verify that gpioServo() succeeds for both pulse-width commands. Implement button debouncing so a single press is not registered multiple times, waiting for release plus a short debounce delay, and poll the buttons in a tight loop with a small sleep to avoid high CPU usage. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler so Ctrl+C cleanly stops the servo (pulse width 0) and calls gpioTerminate() before exiting. Print status messages to stdout for lock, unlock, and shutdown events.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to implement a smart security light. Monitor a PIR motion sensor on GPIO 4 (physical pin 7, input). On a rising edge (motion detected), activate a relay-controlled 12V LED floodlight on GPIO 17 (physical pin 11, output) for exactly 60 seconds, then turn it off. Log every activation event with an ISO-8601 timestamp and every deactivation event with timestamp and measured duration in seconds to security_log.txt in append mode. Check pigpio initialization, every gpioSetMode/gpioWrite/gpioRead return code, and every fopen/fprintf/fclose result; on a file error, turn off the floodlight before exiting. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler so Ctrl+C cleanly turns off the floodlight, releases pigpio resources, and exits with code 0. Poll at a 100 ms interval to avoid busy-waiting, and ensure the floodlight is off on every exit path. Do not use wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the pigpio library to toggle a 5V relay on GPIO17 via an MPR121 capacitive touch sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x5A. Perform a full MPR121 initialization: issue a soft-reset, configure baseline filtering (MHD/NHD/NCL/FDL), set debounce (register 0x5B), set FFI/SFI/CDT (register 0x2C), set auto-config (registers 0x7B-0x7D), and enable exactly 12 electrodes by writing 0x0C to register 0x5E. Read touch status from register 0x00, a 16-bit word whose lower 12 bits are the electrode touch states. Toggle the relay only on a fresh (rising-edge) touch of electrode 0, with a 200 ms debounce. Include robust error handling for every pigpio/I2C call, checking return values and handling sensor-absent and bus-error paths, with clean resource release on every exit path via SIGINT/SIGTERM handling, and set the relay to a known OFF state on both startup and shutdown.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the modern libgpiod API, not wiringPi, for all GPIO operations and listens for TCP commands on port 5000 to control a servo motor (BCM GPIO17) and read a PIR sensor (BCM GPIO4). Drive the servo with a software PWM thread that toggles the line via gpiod_line_set_value at 50 Hz with a 1-2 ms pulse width spanning 0-180°. Parse commands of the form 'SERVO <angle>' (0-180) and 'PIR', which returns 'PIR:0' or 'PIR:1' over the socket. Log all activation events, commands, and errors to both syslog (LOG_USER facility) and a local file named security.log with ISO 8601 timestamps. Check every libgpiod call, socket syscall, and file I/O operation; if GPIO initialization fails, log the error and exit with a non-zero status. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, releasing all libgpiod resources, closing the socket, and closing the log file. Include stdarg.h for variadic functions so the code compiles cleanly with -Wall -Wextra.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to read ambient light levels from a BH1750 sensor at I2C address 0x23 on I2C1 (GPIO2=SDA, GPIO3=SCL). Trigger a relay on GPIO23 to activate a grow light when the lux reading falls below 150, and deactivate it when lux is 150 or above. Use the BH1750 One-Time High-Resolution mode (command 0x20) and wait at least 120 ms for the conversion before reading the 2-byte result, converting to lux with lux = raw / 1.2. Log timestamps and lux values to grow_log.txt, sampling every 2 seconds. Implement robust error handling for I2C communication failures by checking the return codes of i2cOpen, i2cWriteByte, i2cReadDevice, and file operations, and handle sensor-absent and bus-error paths by logging errors and retrying on the next cycle. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths — close the I2C handle, close the log file, deactivate the relay, and call gpioTerminate — with SIGINT and SIGTERM signal handling.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod library, not wiringPi, to read weight from a TAL220B load cell via an HX711 amplifier, with DOUT on GPIO23 (physical pin 16) and SCK on GPIO24 (physical pin 18), and to trigger a solenoid lock on GPIO25 (physical pin 22), which is driven HIGH for 200 ms whenever the measured weight exceeds a threshold of 1000 grams. Implement the HX711 bit-bang read protocol: wait for DOUT to go LOW (data ready), clock out 24 bits MSB-first, then send one additional clock pulse to select Channel A / Gain 128, and convert the 24-bit two's-complement reading to a signed 32-bit integer. Average 5 readings per measurement cycle and compute weight as (average_raw - tare_offset) / scale, performing a startup tare by averaging 10 readings. Check every libgpiod call; if DOUT does not go LOW within 1 second, log an error and retry up to 3 times before exiting. Release all GPIO lines and chips, close syslog, and ensure the solenoid is set LOW on every exit path, handling SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown. Log informational and error messages via syslog. Accept optional command-line arguments --threshold <grams>, --scale <factor>, and --duration <ms>, and poll weight every 500 ms in the main loop.

In the message callback, treat the payload as a NUL-terminated string: ON sets GPIO17 HIGH (relay energized) and OFF sets it LOW (relay de-energized); log every received message, and if the payload is empty or anything other than ON/OFF, log an error via syslog(LOG_ERR, ...) and leave the relay state unchanged. prompt: Write a robust C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to implement a smart chicken coop lighting system. Control a 12V relay-connected LED strip via GPIO 17 (active-high) based on ambient light read from a BH1750 sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x23. The relay activates at dusk, when lux falls below 50, and deactivates at dawn, when lux exceeds 200, using a hysteresis loop to prevent rapid toggling. Poll the sensor every 5 seconds, waiting at least 180 ms after issuing the One-Time High-Resolution Mode 2 command (0x21) before reading the 2 bytes of lux data, and convert the raw data to lux by dividing by 1.2. Log all sensor readings and relay state changes to chicken_coop_log.txt in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS: Lux = XXX, Relay = ON/OFF'. Implement comprehensive error handling for pigpio initialization, I2C bus communication, and file I/O; if the sensor fails to respond, log the error and safely turn off the relay. Ensure clean resource release of the I2C handle, the relay GPIO, and the log file on all exit paths, including graceful shutdown via SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to control a 5V relay on GPIO 17 (physical pin 11) via a TTP223 capacitive touch sensor on GPIO 4 (physical pin 7); each valid touch toggles the relay state. Initialize pigpio and check for errors, configure GPIO 4 as input and GPIO 17 as output, and implement software debouncing with a 50 ms stabilization delay, toggling only when the sensor reads HIGH both before and after the delay. Wait for the touch sensor to return LOW before allowing the next toggle (edge detection on touch-release). Log every relay state change to the console with an ISO-8601 timestamp and the new state (ON/OFF). Handle SIGINT (Ctrl+C) for graceful shutdown by turning the relay OFF, releasing pigpio resources, and printing an exit message. Check the return value of every pigpio call (gpioInitialise, gpioSetMode, gpioWrite) and report errors to stderr. Use a 10 ms main-loop sleep to reduce CPU usage, and do not include MQTT or networking code.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the pigpio library to read flow rate from a YF-S201 water flow sensor on GPIO 17 (physical pin 11), computing liters per minute (LPM) from its 450 pulses-per-liter calibration as LPM = (pulses / 450.0) * 60.0. Trigger a solenoid valve on GPIO 27 to shut off when the rate exceeds 5.0 L/min, reopening only when it drops below 4.5 L/min (0.5 L/min hysteresis); the solenoid is open (HIGH) by default and closes (LOW) above the threshold. Initialize pigpio and validate all return codes (gpioInitialise, gpioSetMode, gpioWrite, gpioSetISRFuncEx), using a 1-second ISR debounce timeout on the flow sensor pin. Protect the shared pulse counter with a pthread mutex; sample the pulse count every 1 second and reset it after computing LPM. Log every LPM reading and every solenoid state change with timestamps to water_flow.log; if the log file cannot be opened, clean up all initialized resources and exit with a non-zero status. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM by logging the event, reopening the solenoid to its safe state, closing the log file, destroying the mutex, and calling gpioTerminate.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the pigpio library, not bcm2835 or wiringPi, to read data from an HX711 load cell amplifier connected to GPIO 23 (DATA) and GPIO 24 (SCK), calibrate the readings using a known weight, and control an SG90-style servo motor on GPIO 18 via hardware PWM to dispense a pre-determined amount of ingredient based on the weight. The program must act as a TCP server listening on 127.0.0.1:12345: receive a target weight in grams from a client, open the servo to dispense, wait 1 second for the load cell to stabilize, read the actual weight from the HX711, send the actual weight back to the client, and log each dispensing event (date, time, target weight, actual weight, and any error message) as a JSON object appended to dispensing_log.json. Implement robust error handling for pigpio initialization, HX711 communication timeouts (sensor absent or not ready), servo control failures, file I/O, and network errors. Use signal handlers (SIGINT, SIGTERM) for clean shutdown of GPIO, sockets, and the servo. Read calibration_factor, server_ip, and server_port from a config.ini file, falling back to defaults if the file is missing or malformed. Read the HX711 using bit-banged GPIO with a 1 µs clock pulse width, timing out if DATA stays HIGH for more than 1000 attempts. Map the target weight to the servo's 1000-2000 µs pulse-width range.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to toggle a 5V relay on GPIO 17 upon detecting a touch on a TTP223 capacitive touch sensor on GPIO 4, implementing a touch-controlled on/off switch for a desk lamp. The TTP223 module idles LOW and drives HIGH while touched. Implement a 50 ms polling-based software debounce with stable-level confirmation, overridable via an optional command-line argument -d <milliseconds>, and robust error handling for every pigpio call (gpioInitialise, gpioSetMode, gpioWrite). On each valid rising edge (LOW to HIGH), toggle the relay. Log every relay state change to the console with a timestamp in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS Relay: ON' or '... Relay: OFF'. Install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers for graceful shutdown: turn the relay OFF, release pigpio resources, and exit cleanly. Keep the program self-contained, with no networking, Redis, or ZeroMQ code.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 or 5 (40-pin header) that uses the pigpio library, not WiringPi or direct /dev/mem register access, to control a standard hobby servo such as an SG90 connected to GPIO18 (physical pin 12) via hardware PWM. The user increments or decrements the servo angle via keyboard input without pressing Enter (raw terminal mode): '+' increases the angle by 10°, '-' decreases it by 10°, and 'q' quits, with the angle clamped to 0-180°. Use 50 Hz PWM (20 ms period) with a pulse width of 500-2500 µs spanning 0-180°, starting at 90° (1500 µs), and drive it with gpioServo() rather than raw register writes. Check the return value of gpioInitialise(), printing to stderr and exiting non-zero on failure, and validate that computed pulse widths stay within [500, 2500] µs. On 'q' or SIGINT (Ctrl-C), stop PWM pulses on GPIO18, call gpioTerminate(), and restore the terminal settings, saving and restoring termios even on an unexpected exit. Print the current angle after each change.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the modern libgpiod API, not wiringPi, to monitor a conveyor-belt motor using an A3144 Hall-effect sensor on GPIO 17 (physical pin 11, BCM). A two-pole magnet on the motor shaft produces one pulse per revolution, detected on the rising edge. Configure GPIO 17 as input with the internal pull-up enabled via the GPIOD_LINE_REQUEST_FLAG_BIAS_PULL_UP bias flag, since the A3144's open-collector output requires a pull-up. Use edge-triggered event detection (gpiod_line_event_wait) to count pulses, with a 2 ms debounce window to reject contact bounce and double-edge noise. Every 5 seconds, compute RPM = (pulseCount / 5.0) * 60.0, append the sample to motor_rpm.log in CSV format (timestamp in ISO 8601, rpm_value to 2 decimal places), flushing after every write, and print the current RPM to stdout. Check the return values of gpiod_chip_open, gpiod_chip_get_line, and gpiod_line_request_input_flags, printing clear diagnostics to stderr and exiting non-zero on failure. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown: stop the main loop, release the GPIO line, close the chip, close the log file, and exit cleanly. Use the monotonic clock (clock_gettime with CLOCK_MONOTONIC) for timing, not clock().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the pigpio library to control a 5V relay on GPIO17 based on a TTP223 capacitive touch sensor on GPIO4, which outputs 3.3V logic HIGH when touched and LOW otherwise; the relay module is active-HIGH. On the rising edge of a touch, toggle the relay state, polling the sensor every 50 ms. Implement a failsafe: if the touch sensor remains continuously HIGH for more than 10 seconds, force the relay OFF and ignore further toggles until the sensor is released. Check the return value of gpioInitialise() and every gpioSetMode()/gpioWrite()/gpioRead() call; if gpioRead() returns PI_BAD_GPIO, log the error and exit. Install handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM that set a volatile flag so the main loop can exit cleanly; perform the actual cleanup — releasing the relay (set OFF) and calling gpioTerminate() — in main() after the loop exits, not inside the signal handler itself.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library, not wiringPi, to implement a closed-loop flow control system for an ASCO RedHat 8210 series proportional solenoid valve. Drive the valve via PWM on GPIO 18 (BCM, hardware PWM 0), with enable/direction control on GPIO 23 (BCM), active-high, and count pulses from a YF-S201 flow sensor on GPIO 24 (BCM) via an interrupt-driven, rising-edge pulse counter. Accept the target flow rate in L/min as a command-line argument (-t, e.g. -t 5.0), validating it and exiting with an error message if missing or invalid. Sample the flow rate every 100 ms, computing L/min from the pulse count accumulated over the interval using the YF-S201 calibration of 450 pulses per liter, and use a proportional controller (Kp = 1.0) to adjust the valve PWM duty cycle (0-255), clamped to [0, 255], to maintain the target flow rate. Log timestamp_ms, flow_rate, and valve_position to flow_log.csv on every control iteration, logging only to this local file with no UDP or network logging. Enable the valve (GPIO 23 high) at startup; on shutdown, set PWM to 0, drive GPIO 23 low, close the log file, and cleanly terminate pigpio. Check pigpio initialization, GPIO mode setup, ISR registration, and file open, exiting with a diagnostic on any failure, and handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown and resource release.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to implement a two-factor authentication system controlling two YLI YM-180 electromagnetic lock actuators on GPIO 17 and GPIO 27. The locks are normally engaged (powered = locked); disengage them by driving their GPIO pins LOW for 5 seconds, then re-engage them (HIGH). Authentication requires both factors in sequence: a valid RFID tag read via SPI channel 0 at 100 kHz, where the reader returns 10 bytes and an all-zero response means 'no tag present' rather than an error, matched against the 10-byte valid tag {0x01..0x0A}; then a button press on GPIO 22 (active-low with internal pull-up, 50 ms debounce). On successful two-factor authentication, drive both lock pins LOW for 5 seconds, then re-engage. Log all access attempts — successful, invalid tag, RFID read failure, and button press without a valid tag — with ISO-8601 timestamps to /var/log/door_access.log. Check gpioInitialise(), spiOpen(), spiXfer(), gpioWrite(), and the log file open, handling SPI read failures gracefully without crashing. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler for clean shutdown: close SPI, release both locks to the engaged state, close the log file, and call gpioTerminate(). Use a non-blocking polling loop with gpioDelay, avoiding busy-wait.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the libgpiod library, not wiringPi, to control two L298N-driven DC motors, implementing a PID controller (KP=1.0, KI=0.1, KD=0.01, 100 ms sample time) to maintain a target rotational speed for each motor, measured by quadrature encoders with 600 pulses per revolution. Motor 1 uses ENA on GPIO 23, IN1 on GPIO 24, IN2 on GPIO 25; Motor 2 uses ENB on GPIO 12, IN3 on GPIO 16, IN4 on GPIO 20. Encoder 1 uses A on GPIO 5, B on GPIO 6; Encoder 2 uses A on GPIO 26, B on GPIO 19. Decode the quadrature signals using libgpiod BOTH_EDGES edge events on each A pin, reading the corresponding B pin to determine direction, and drive each motor with software PWM via libgpiod line toggling at a fixed frequency such as 100 Hz, with duty cycle proportional to the PID output. Target RPMs may be hardcoded, for example 60 RPM for both motors. Log motor speeds (RPM), the PID P/I/D components, and the PID output to motor_log.csv with a header row, flushing after each write. Check all libgpiod calls (chip open, line request, edge event setup) and file operations, and handle encoder read failures gracefully. Use threads for encoder event monitoring so it does not block the main control loop, protecting shared encoder counts with mutexes. Install signal handlers (SIGINT, SIGTERM) that stop the motors, release the GPIO lines, close the chips, and close the log file, and run the control loop indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library for both I2C and GPIO control to interface with a single MPR121 capacitive touch sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x5A, toggling a 5V relay module on GPIO 17. Implement a robust MPR121 initialization sequence: a soft reset, configuring filtering, setting touch and release thresholds for all 12 electrodes, and enabling run mode. In the main loop, poll the MPR121 touch status registers 0x00 and 0x01 every 50 ms; if any electrode is touched, activate the relay (GPIO 17 HIGH), otherwise deactivate it (GPIO 17 LOW). Log every relay state change to a timestamped text file, relay_log.txt. Include comprehensive error handling: check pigpio initialization and every I2C open/read/write operation, and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths gracefully. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including signal handling for SIGINT (Ctrl+C) to shut down the relay and close the I2C handle properly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the libgpiod library, not wiringPi or pigpio, to control two Adafruit Solenoid Valves (Product ID 997), each a 12V, 0.7A valve switched through a relay module rather than driven directly, implementing a timed water distribution schedule for a miniature automated greenhouse. Valve 1's relay is on GPIO 17 (BCM) and Valve 2's relay is on GPIO 18 (BCM), where GPIO HIGH means the relay is ON and the valve is open, and GPIO LOW means the relay is OFF and the valve is closed. Run the schedule indefinitely until interrupted: activate Valve 1 for 500 ms, then pause 5 seconds; activate Valve 2 for 1000 ms, then pause 10 seconds. Implement robust error handling for GPIO chip initialization failures, gpiod_line_request_output failures, and file I/O errors for logging. Log every valve activation event with an ISO 8601 timestamp to valve_log.txt. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to ensure clean GPIO release and file closure, releasing all GPIO lines and closing the log file on exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library, not wiringPi, to toggle a 5V relay on GPIO17 upon each successful touch event from an MPR121 capacitive touch sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x5A (SDA=GPIO2, SCL=GPIO3). Initialize the MPR121 in stop mode, set the touch threshold (0x10) and release threshold (0x0A) for all 12 electrodes, configure the filter/charge time (0x20) and electrode current (0x01), then enter run mode with ELE_EN=1 (0x20) and wait 100 ms for stabilization. Set the relay pin as output, initially off. In a loop with a 100 ms delay, read the touch status registers (0x00-0x01); if any electrode is touched (touch_status > 0), toggle the relay and print the status. Include robust error handling for all I2C operations, GPIO operations, and initialization failures, opening the I2C bus with error handling. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown by closing I2C and terminating pigpio.

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the pigpio library to detect motion via an HC-SR501 PIR sensor on GPIO 17 (input with pull-down). On a rising-edge motion detection (0 to 1), activate a 5V relay on GPIO 18 (output) for 500 ms to momentarily unlock an electric door strike. Implement rate limiting: ignore subsequent motion events for 2 seconds after each unlock. Log all events — motion detected, door unlocked, and rate-limited events — with millisecond-precision timestamps to door_events.log. Handle pigpio initialization failure gracefully with a clear error message and exit code 1. Ensure proper cleanup on SIGINT or normal exit: close the log file, terminate pigpio, and set the relay off. Use a single thread with non-blocking polling at a 50 ms interval and edge detection, using no sensors or GPIOs beyond the ones specified.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to modulate the speed of two eccentric rotating mass (ERM) vibration motors, Precision Microdrives 310-101, on GPIO pins 17 and 27, generating randomized haptic feedback patterns. Each pattern consists of a sequence of 5 to 15 steps, where each step specifies a PWM duty cycle from 0 to 255 for each motor and a duration of 50-200 ms. Use gpioPWM for PWM control and gpioDelay for timing. Implement robust error handling: check the gpioInitialise return value, verify GPIO mode setting, handle memory allocation failures, and ensure graceful shutdown on SIGINT (Ctrl+C) by stopping the motors and releasing resources, using a volatile sig_atomic_t shutdown flag. Seed the random number generator with time(NULL), and run indefinitely, generating and playing patterns until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library, not wiringPi, to read weight from an HX711 load cell amplifier with its data pin on GPIO4 and clock pin on GPIO17, and control a solenoid lock on GPIO27 (active high to lock). Initialize pigpio with error checking, then load calibration data (scale_factor and offset, space-separated) from calibration.txt, or use defaults of scale=1.0 and offset=0.0 if the file is missing or invalid. Perform a one-time startup calibration by averaging 100 readings to determine the offset, assuming zero load, and save the calibration data back to the file. In a loop, read the sensor every 500 ms, convert the raw value to weight using the calibration, and if it exceeds a calibrated threshold of 10.0 kg, drive the solenoid pin high to engage the lock, otherwise drive it low to release it. Log each reading with a timestamp to weight_log.txt. Handle HX711 read timeouts of 0.5 seconds gracefully by skipping that iteration. Handle SIGINT for a clean shutdown that releases the GPIO and closes the files.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to automatically close a window when rain is detected by a Seeed Studio Grove Rain Sensor on GPIO4 (BCM), driving an L298N motor driver connected with IN1 to GPIO17, IN2 to GPIO18, and PWM enable to GPIO27. The rain sensor outputs LOW when rain is detected and HIGH when dry; debounce by taking 5 readings at 50 ms intervals and treat rain as detected when at least 3 readings are LOW. To close the window, set IN1=1, IN2=0, and drive the PWM enable at 1000 Hz with duty cycle 150 out of 255; run the motor for 5 seconds, then stop it by setting IN1=0, IN2=0, and PWM=0. Check the sensor every 60 seconds, and after closing the window wait 60 seconds before checking again. Log every rain event and motor action with a timestamp to /var/log/window_control.log via syslog. Handle all GPIO initialization failures with error messages and exit codes. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, stop the motor, release GPIO resources, and close the log before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to monitor a kitchen ingredient stock level with a single TAL220B load cell read through an HX711 amplifier, with the amplifier's DT line on GPIO23 and SCK line on GPIO24. Check the weight every 1 second; when it drops below 100 g, activate a solenoid lock on GPIO17 for 5 seconds. Log each activation event with a timestamp to stock_events.txt. Implement robust error handling for HX711 reads, including timeout and data-line-stuck-high conditions, for GPIO control by checking every return value, and for file I/O. The program must run continuously and perform a clean shutdown on SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to read weight from an HX711 load cell amplifier over its bit-banged GPIO protocol (the HX711 is not an I2C device) and control a solenoid door lock. Connect the HX711 data pin to GPIO4 and clock pin to GPIO17, with clock high and low delays of at least 1 microsecond, and read raw 24-bit signed values with correct timing. At startup, calibrate the load cell by prompting the user to place a known weight, reading the raw value, computing a calibration factor as raw divided by the known weight in kilograms, and saving it to calibration.txt. Continuously read the weight; whenever it exceeds 5.0 kg, log the event with a timestamp and the weight to security.log, drive the solenoid lock on GPIO27 high for 5 seconds, then set it low to unlock. Handle pigpio initialization failure, file open and write failures, calibration read errors, and HX711 communication timeouts where the data line stays high for more than 100 ms. Install a SIGINT handler to gracefully unlock the solenoid and terminate pigpio, and release all resources, including closing files and terminating pigpio, on every exit path.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod library to monitor a Keywish KY-022 IR obstacle avoidance sensor on GPIO16 (BCM) and toggle a Songle SRD-05VDC-SL relay module on GPIO20 (BCM). The sensor is active-low, reporting an obstacle by driving its output LOW, and the relay trigger is active-high. Continuously monitor the sensor; each time an obstacle is detected, toggle the relay state from ON to OFF or OFF to ON, and log the new relay state together with a timestamp in ISO 8601 format to relay_events.log. Use only libgpiod APIs — gpiod_chip_open_by_name, gpiod_chip_get_line, gpiod_line_request_bulk_inputs/outputs, gpiod_line_get_value, gpiod_line_set_value, gpiod_line_release, and gpiod_chip_close. Handle GPIO initialization errors such as a missing chip or a failed line request, sensor read errors, and log file write errors, printing descriptive error messages and cleaning up resources. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, release all GPIO lines and exit cleanly.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the libgpiod library to detect motion from an HC-SR501 PIR sensor on GPIO17 (BCM numbering), which is active-high, and activate a 5V buzzer, also active-high and driven through a transistor or relay rather than directly from GPIO, on GPIO18 for exactly 2 seconds before deactivating it. Use gpiod_line_set_value with usleep for the 2-second timing rather than a busy-wait loop. Append each motion event's timestamp, formatted as YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, to motion_log.txt. The program must run continuously until interrupted. Check every libgpiod call, including gpiod_chip_open and gpiod_line_request_input/output, and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths by printing an error and exiting cleanly. Install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers to turn off the buzzer, close the log file, and release all GPIO resources before exit.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the libgpiod library to run a timed watering system controlling a Parker Hannifin Series 9 General Purpose Miniature Solenoid Valve (12V, 1.6W). Since the Pi cannot drive a 12V, 1.6 W solenoid directly, the valve is driven through an external N-channel MOSFET or relay module connected to GPIO18 (BCM numbering). Initialize the libgpiod chip and line, requesting GPIO18 as output with active-low set to 0 and a default output value of 0 (valve off). Read the watering duration from a configuration file 'watering.conf' containing a single line in the format 'duration=<seconds>', where seconds must be a positive integer between 1 and 3600; reject empty files, malformed lines, and out-of-range values. Activate the valve by setting the line high, wait for the configured duration using a signal-safe sleep that SIGINT or SIGTERM can interrupt early, then set the line low. Install SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers that set a volatile sig_atomic_t flag; the main loop must check this flag and turn the valve off before exiting. On every exit path — normal completion, signal, or error — release the GPIO line and close the chip, ensuring the valve is always left off. Check every libgpiod call for errors and print descriptive messages to stderr, and print status messages to stdout showing the configured duration and each valve on/off transition.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that uses the pigpio library to implement a line-following robot with a Keywish 3-Way Infrared Tracking Sensor and two DC motors driven through an L298N motor driver. The three active-low IR sensors are connected to GPIO4, GPIO17, and GPIO27; the motor driver's PWM inputs are connected to GPIO22, GPIO23, GPIO24, and GPIO25 and run at 1 kHz. Initialize pigpio with error checking, then read all three sensors every 10 ms and apply this control law: if the middle sensor reads low, drive straight at a base speed of 150 out of 255; if only the left sensor reads low, turn right by halving the left motor's speed; if only the right sensor reads low, turn left by halving the right motor's speed; if no sensor reads low, stop both motors. Log each control cycle to trace_log.txt with an ISO 8601 timestamp, the three sensor states as 0 or 1, and the left and right motor speeds. Include robust error handling for pigpio initialization, file opening, and GPIO operations, use only the pigpio API and never wiringPi, and on SIGINT stop the motors, close the log file, terminate pigpio, and release all GPIOs before exiting.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library to read illuminance from a BH1750 light sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x23, using continuous high-resolution mode (command 0x10) with a 180 ms measurement delay. Trigger a relay connected to GPIO23 to activate a grow lamp whenever the lux reading falls below 150. Log every lux reading and every relay state change to grow_log.txt with millisecond-precision timestamps. Handle I2C errors gracefully: if the sensor is not detected or a read fails, log the error and continue without crashing. The program must run indefinitely until SIGINT is received, then cleanly release all resources — close the I2C handle, turn off the relay, and terminate pigpio. Use only C and standard POSIX APIs.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi that uses the pigpio library to control a door lock with a servo motor on GPIO18 (PWM-capable) and two push buttons, a lock button on GPIO21 and an unlock button on GPIO22, each using an external or internal pull-up so that pressing reads as active-low (0). When the lock button is pressed, move the servo to the locked position with a pulse width of 1000 microseconds (about 0 degrees); when the unlock button is pressed, move it to the unlocked position with a pulse width of 2000 microseconds (about 180 degrees). Debounce each button press with a 100 ms delay. Constrain the servo pulse width to the safe range of 500-2500 microseconds at all times. Handle initialization failures gracefully, print status messages, use only pigpio API calls and never wiringPi, and cleanly release all resources on exit through a SIGINT signal handler.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the libgpiod library to run a haptic feedback system pulsing two Precision Microdrives 310-101 vibration motors, which require 3 V at 60 mA typical and must not be connected directly to GPIO. Drive motor 1 through a driver circuit such as an NPN transistor with a flyback diode on GPIO17, and motor 2 the same way on GPIO27. Pulse motor 1 for 200 ms, then motor 2 for 300 ms, repeating this sequential pattern indefinitely. Use gpiod_line_request_output() and gpiod_line_set_value() with error checking on every call. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM to gracefully stop the motors and release the GPIO lines, including robust handling of line request failures, value write failures, and signal handler registration, and call gpiod_line_release() for cleanup on all exit paths.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that uses the libgpiod library to implement a sound-triggered alarm as a single executable with two modes selected by a command-line argument. In sound_sensor mode, poll an LM393 sound sensor's active-low DO pin on GPIO17 every 10 ms (logic 0 means sound above threshold was detected) and publish alerts via ZeroMQ on tcp://*:5555 under topic SOUND_ALERTS. In alarm_node mode, subscribe to tcp://localhost:5555 on topic SOUND_ALERTS and light an alarm LED on GPIO27 for 1 second whenever a message arrives. Include robust error handling for every GPIO and ZeroMQ call, handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for a clean shutdown, and release all resources — GPIO lines, the GPIO chip, and the ZeroMQ sockets and context — on every exit path. Do not use wiringPi.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library to decode NEC IR remote signals from an IR receiver such as a TSOP38238 connected to GPIO17 (BCM). Register a pigpio alert callback on the falling edge to capture pulse timings, and decode the 32-bit NEC frame using its 9 ms mark plus 4.5 ms space header, 560 microsecond bit marks, 1690 microsecond spaces for logic 1, and 560 microsecond spaces for logic 0. Validate the decoded command against its inverted copy — extended NEC frames are allowed, so inverted-address validation is not required — and log the decoded address and command to syslog. Publish each decoded command as JSON to an MQTT broker at localhost:1883 on topic ir/decoded, using paho-mqtt v2 callback semantics, with the MQTT client initialized once at startup and its network loop serviced from the main loop. Check pigpio initialization, handle GPIO initialization failures, guard against pulse buffer overflow, validate the NEC checksum, and cleanly release pigpio, MQTT, and syslog resources on SIGINT or SIGTERM.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that reads ambient light levels from four BH1750FVI sensors on the I2C-1 bus at 7-bit addresses 0x23, 0x24, 0x25, and 0x26, using the standard Linux I2C ioctl interface (<linux/i2c-dev.h> with open() and ioctl(I2C_SLAVE)) rather than wiringPi. Note that the BH1750 natively supports only addresses 0x23 and 0x5C via its ADDR pin, so addresses 0x24-0x26 require an I2C multiplexer or level-shifted address lines; assume the hardware is wired accordingly. For each sensor, open /dev/i2c-1 (a single shared file descriptor or one per sensor is acceptable), set the slave address with ioctl(I2C_SLAVE, addr) before each transaction, write the One-Time High-Resolution mode command byte 0x20, wait 180 ms for conversion, then read 2 bytes. Convert the big-endian result to lux using lux = ((data[0] << 8) | data[1]) / 1.2. Once per second, broadcast all four readings as a single UDP multicast packet to 239.255.255.250:5005, formatted as semicolon-separated sensor_id,lux pairs, e.g. 1,120.5;2,85.0;3,210.5;4,45.0. If any sensor fails — open error, address-set error, write error, read error, or partial read — report NaN for that sensor and continue. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM by setting a flag to exit the loop cleanly, and close all file descriptors, both I2C and UDP socket, on every exit path.

Support command-line options -a for the I2C address (default 0x37), -i for the interval in seconds (default 1), and -f for the output filename (default seismic_data.csv).

prompt: Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that continuously reads ambient light from a BH1750 sensor at I2C address 0x23 on /dev/i2c-1, using the standard Linux I2C character-device API (open, ioctl(I2C_SLAVE), read, write) rather than wiringPi. Initialize the sensor by sending the power-on command 0x01 followed by the continuous high-resolution mode command 0x10. Every 1 second, read the 16-bit big-endian raw value, convert it to lux using lux = raw / 1.2, and broadcast the value as a floating-point string over UDP multicast to 239.255.255.250:5000 with TTL set to 1. Check every I2C write and read operation for failure, and on sensor absence or a bus error, print an error and retry after 1 second. Use a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM to properly clean up the I2C file descriptor and socket on exit, and run indefinitely using standard POSIX sockets until interrupted.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ that uses the pigpio library for UART access, never wiringPi, to interface with a Texas Instruments AWR1642 mmWave radar sensor over /dev/ttyS0 at 921600 baud. Continuously read the asynchronous TLV byte stream, synchronize on the 8-byte magic word 0x0204 0x0306 0x0805 0x0709 (little-endian), validate the TLV payload, and extract each detected object's range and velocity. For each detected object, write a row to radar_data.csv with columns timestamp, object_index, range_m, velocity_mps. Check every UART read, handle partial reads and buffer overflows gracefully, skip malformed frames, and log errors to stderr without crashing. On all exit paths, including SIGINT and SIGTERM, close the UART, flush and close the CSV file, and call gpioTerminate().

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B running a 64-bit OS that periodically reads range-detection data from a Texas Instruments AWR1642 mmWave radar sensor connected to the primary UART at /dev/serial0 (GPIO14/GPIO15). The radar emits ASCII lines in the format <unix_timestamp_seconds>,<range_meters> terminated by '\n' at 115200 baud, 8N1. Open and configure the UART using termios.h in non-canonical mode with a 0.5 s inter-byte timeout, use select() with a 2-second timeout to detect data availability and handle sensor-absent or bus-error paths, and accumulate partial reads into a line buffer, parsing only complete newline-terminated lines. Log each valid detection to stdout as 'Timestamp: YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, Range: X.XX meters'. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, closing the UART on all exit paths, and check every syscall — open, tcgetattr, tcsetattr, read, select, strdup — printing errno-based diagnostics on failure. Use only standard POSIX C libraries: stdio, stdlib, string, fcntl, termios, unistd, errno, sys/select, signal, and time.

Write a C program for a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that uses the pigpio library, not wiringPi, to read a Keywish 3-Way Tracking Sensor (KY-033) with its left, middle, and right IR emitter/detector outputs connected to GPIO4 (pin 7), GPIO17 (pin 11), and GPIO27 (pin 13) respectively, each configured as an input with pull-up resistors enabled; the sensor's 5V and GND are wired to the Pi's 5V and GND pins. Each output reads digital LOW when an obstacle or line is detected and HIGH when clear. If pigpio initialization fails, print an error and exit with code 1; if a gpioRead call fails, print an error and continue rather than exiting. Running the main loop at 10 Hz (a 100 ms period), read all three sensors each cycle and log their states to the console with a timestamp, using 0 for obstacle detected and 1 for clear. If all three sensors read 0 simultaneously, send the string \"EMERGENCY STOP!\\n\" over the serial port /dev/ttyAMA0 at 115200 baud, 8N1, with no flow control, handling any serial write error by printing it and continuing rather than exiting. Register SIGINT and SIGTERM handlers to close the serial port and terminate pigpio before exit, and release all resources on any error path.
